  description: 'Removes child rows whose parent was deleted before the FK existed.',
  group: 'Data repairs',
  leaves_behind: 'zz_backup_orphans_<stamp>',
  fo…
• Routes (admin only): GET /api/ops-tasks (catalog + last ten runs each), POST /api/ops-tasks/:key/run with { "execute": true } for a real run (dry by default; 409 while one runs), GET /api/ops-tasks/runs/:id (status, progress, outcome, output tail), POST /api/ops-tasks/runs/:id/cancel (cooperative — the task checks rc.cancelled() between chunks). • The output tail lives in the process that ran the task; the run row itself is durable. • In a test, createTestContext().runTask(key, { execute }) runs the task with a recording context.

Rows of a configuration collection an extension owns the definition of — a warehouse list, a category map, a set of reference values — are checked in beside its code and registered with ctx.seeds.register(...). A seed is never applied at boot: it becomes the operational task seed:<key> whose dry run is the drift report (every row where the database differs from the file, which columns, and who last changed the row) and whose real run applies the file through the items service, as the admin who clicked, with _change_reason naming the seed. Rows match on match_by columns, never on id, so a seed survives an id-space difference between databases.
ctx.seeds.register({
  key: 'my-extension:warehouse-ordering',
  collection: 'warehouses',
  match_by: ['name'],
  rows: [
    { name: 'North DC', ordering_system: 'api' },
    { name: 'South DC', ordering_system: 'manual' }
  ],
  mode: 'f…
• fill-only creates rows the database lacks and fills columns that are empty there; a value someone set stays and is reported as drift. authoritative writes the file's values back over differing columns. • A row that matches several database rows is ambiguous: reported, never written. • GET /api/config-seeds lists the seeds; GET /api/config-seeds/:key/drift is the report as JSON (admin only). The task appears under Ops Tasks like any other.

ctx.helpVideos lets an extension ship help videos with itself. declarePage({ key, label, app }) names a page key in the registry the Videos button and the editor's Where picker use, so authors can place a video on the extension's own screens before anyone has opened them. registerStarter({ package, ids, contexts }) points at a help-video package inside the extension folder — the file Content Promotion → Help videos exports — and addContexts(videoId, contexts) adds screens (a collection, a collection at one pipeline step, or a page) to one video of it.
ctx.helpVideos.declarePage({ key: 'acme.orders.board', label: 'Orders board', app: 'admin' })
ctx.helpVideos.registerStarter({
  package: 'videos/starters.tar',             // relative to the extension folder
  contexts: [{ kind: 'page', ke…
• A starter video is imported once per database, after register() returns and in the background, as a DRAFT: never published, visible to authors only, never required viewing, rendered only when someone publishes it. An author reviews it, chooses who can watch and publishes it. • The import runs the same checks as an administrator importing the package (manifest, sizes, checksums, media probes, edits re-normalized). Screens on a collection or step this instance does not have are skipped. • A video id that already exists here is left alone, and so is one that was imported once and deleted since: each import leaves a help-video-starter-import activity row naming the video, and a later boot reads it and does nothing. • The package path must stay inside the extension folder — an absolute path, .., or a link that leads outside is refused. A bad declaration is logged and skipped; it never stops the extension loading. • Music uploaded to a starter video is dropped (an uploaded music file needs an owner); library music is kept when this instance has the track. • Self-hosted only for now: in cloud mode the declarations are recorded on the registry sheet but nothing is written. Every declaration appears on the Extensions registry sheet under Help videos; createTestContext() records them under registered.helpVideos.

An extension cannot import api/src — the API compiles with rootDir: src, and a mounted extension runs against a built image that ships no source. @nivaro/extension-kit is the contract instead: the extension context (ExtensionContext), the default export shape (ExtensionDefinition, checked by defineExtension), and every registration the context accepts — bulk and item actions, readiness and integrity checks, notes providers, mail types, digest sections, obligation kinds, signals, import processors, flow operations and triggers. The API imports its own extension contract from the same package, so the two cannot drift.
• Types are exported with export type; importing one costs nothing at runtime. • Two helpers are runtime code: hasColumn(db, table, column) — a per-database column probe for a writer that must keep working before a migration reaches the database — and requesterInsertFields / requesterSelectColumns for the ERP submission tables. • Members are only ever added to the context. An extension built against an older kit keeps compiling; a member that arrived in a later core release is documented as such on the type. • In the monorepo the kit is a workspace package; a mounted extension resolves it from the image. Released with pnpm kit:release.

nivaro ext init <id> (the CLI that ships with @nivaro/sdk) writes api/extensions/<id>/ with an index.ts on defineExtension — one setting, one hook, one scheduled job with a description, and one route behind requireAuth — a passing test on createTestContext(), and a README naming the context members it uses. The id must be kebab-case and the directory must not exist yet; --dir writes somewhere else. Restart the API and the extension appears on the Extensions page.
npx nivaro ext init acme-orders            # → api/extensions/acme-orders/
cd api && npx vitest run extensions/acme-orders
npx tsc -p extensions/tsconfig.json

A context member on its way out is listed in the kit as data — KIT_DEPRECATIONS, each entry naming the member, its replacement and the kit version it leaves in — because a @deprecated tag is invisible at runtime. The loader watches every listed member on the context it hands register(): the first use per extension per boot logs a warning, the Extensions registry sheet lists the members in use under "Deprecated members in use" with a use count, and the readiness check "Extensions avoid deprecated kit members" warns while any loaded extension still reads one. In a test, createTestContext().calls.deprecations holds one sentence per read. Nothing is deprecated today.

createTestContext() from the kit is a context whose every effect is recorded instead of sent — notifications, external calls, activity rows, flow emits, obligations — and whose registrations the test can run: runHooks(collection, action, timing, ctx), runCron(id), deliverEvent(type, payload), and invoke(method, url, req) for a route the extension registered. Its database is createTestDb({ tables }), an in-memory knex-shaped fake that covers the chain extensions use (where, whereIn, first, pluck, count, insert, update, del, raw, schema.hasColumn, transaction); joins are accepted and ignored, so seed the joined columns on the row you expect back. Nothing boots the API.
import { createTestContext } from '@nivaro/extension-kit'
import ext from './index.js'

const ctx = createTestContext({ tables: { orders: [{ id: 1, owner: 'u1' }] } })
await ext.register(ctx)
await ctx.runHooks('orders', 'create', 'after', …

Extensions are loaded at startup. Reload without restarting:
POST /api/extensions/reload
Authorization: Bearer <admin-token>

// Returns list of newly loaded extensions and any errors
Extensions are auto-discovered from api/extensions/*/index.{ts,js}. Each must have a unique id. Duplicate IDs are logged and skipped.

An extension declares the variables it reads on its export. A required one that is not set fails GET /api/preflight and the readiness scorecard by name, the loader logs it at boot, and the Extensions registry sheet lists every declared variable as set or not set — never its value. Declare a credential with secret: true; leave required off for a variable whose absence only switches a behaviour off.
export default {
  id: 'my-extension',
  env: [
    { name: 'PARTNER_BASE_URL', required: true, description: 'The partner API this extension pushes to' },
    { name: 'PARTNER_CLIENT_SECRET', required: true, secret: true },
    { name: 'PAR…

A long, multi-step operator script (a data conversion, a cutover chain) can be declared as a runbook. The admin Environments page lists it under Runbooks and runs it from the machine the API runs on — local development only — as a detached process, so a run that takes hours outlives the API restarting. The console shows each step, how long it took and what it said, the log tail, and offers Cancel and Resume from the step that failed.
• A real run needs a finished dry run of the same target from the last 24 hours, and the target typed back. • One runbook runs at a time on the machine. A target listed in refuse_targets is refused. • The script is started as npx tsx <script> <args> --events from the api directory, with target_env set to the target. It prints @@steps ["a","b"], then @@event {"step","status":"start|ok|fail|skip|refused","secs","lines"} per step, and ends with ### DONE — <summary> or ### FAILED at <step>: <reason>. • Resume passes resume_flag and the failed step name; the script skips the steps before it.
export default {
  id: 'my-extension',
  runbooks: [
    {
      key: 'convert',
      label: 'Data conversion',
      script: 'extensions/my-extension/scripts/convert.ts',
      dry_args: ['--dry-run'],
      go_args: ['--execute'],
      …

A runbook declared with runs_on: 'host' runs on another machine — the one that can reach what it needs (the database server, a file share). Every instance lists it, local or deployed. Starting it QUEUES the run; the host agent on that machine claims it, runs it, and streams its output back every second while the console shows the phases, the live log and an estimate.
• Install the agent on the host with cron: * * * * * bash -lc 'cd <checkout>/api && npx tsx src/scripts/runbook-agent.ts --once' (or pnpm --filter @nivaro/api run runbook:agent -- --once). Each tick checks in, then claims the oldest queued run for a runbook the extensions on that checkout declare. RUNBOOK_AGENT_HOST overrides the host name. The console says when no agent is checking in. • command (an argv starting with bash, sh, node, npx or tsx and naming a file inside the extension) runs instead of npx tsx <script>; --events is not appended. phases ([{key, label}]) draws the track before any event arrives and offers "start from phase", passed through resume_flag. • The same rules as local runbooks: a real run needs a finished dry run of the target from the last 24 hours and the target typed back; one queued or running run per runbook; Cancel takes a queued run out of the queue and stops a running one (SIGTERM to its process group, SIGKILL 30 seconds later). • Exit 75, or a ### REFUSED: <reason> line, records the run as refused (a lock, another job, an unreachable database) rather than done. A run whose agent stops reporting for 3 minutes reads as lost; the next tick re-attaches while the process still runs, and records its exit status (kept in a file beside the agent's lock) when it has finished. • A wrapped runbook's own step events can be printed as @@sub {…} lines: they show as the progress of the phase that is running, never as phases of their own. • Estimates: every successful phase and sub-step is timed into nivaro_runbook_step_timings. A phase's typical time is the median of its last 7 passes in the same mode; the console shows how long a full run (or a run from any phase) usually takes, and during a run the elapsed time, the current phase and sub-step, the share done, the ETA, and a stall warning when the run has been quiet longer than that phase ever was (10 minutes without history). • history_dirs ([{path, mode}], relative to the repository root) feed the estimates from runs started outside the console, such as a nightly cron: one directory per run with a summary.txt of === <n>-<phase> END … exit=0 elapsed=<m>m<s>s === lines and per phase a <n>-<phase>.log whose ─── <step> done in <m>m<ss>s ─── lines are its sub-steps. A run directory holding .nivaro-runbook-run is skipped (the console already timed it).
runbooks: [
  {
    key: 'rebuild',
    label: 'Rebuild the rehearsal database',
    runs_on: 'host',
    command: ['bash', 'extensions/my-extension/scripts/rebuild.sh', 'nightly'],
    dry_args: ['--dry'],
    go_args: [],
    resume_flag:…
The ctx object passed to register() provides access to the entire Nivaro platform. Every extension receives the same context object.

Property | Type | Purpose / app | FastifyInstance | Register routes, decorators, hooks. Scoped to /api prefix. / database | Knex | MSSQL connection via Knex query builder. / logger | FastifyBaseLogger | Structured pino logger prefixed with extension id.

Property | Type | Purpose / hooks | { before, after } | Intercept CRUD operations. Tagged for enable/disable per extension. / cron | { schedule, unschedule } | Recurring jobs. Paused/resumed when extension toggled. / cache | { registerWarm(name, fn, { budgetMs? }) } | An expensive READ of your own (fill your Redis cache, run the query that warms the database), run by the cache warm after a boot and at 06:30 on weekdays, after the core queries, inside the same time budget. fn({ signal, budgetMs }) gets its own timeout (default 60 s, never more than the run has left); on timeout the signal aborts and the warm moves on. Errors are logged, never thrown. Must not write. Not run in cloud mode. Id = <extension>:<name>. / reads | { route(handler, { label? }) } (optional) | The heavy-read gate for your own expensive GET routes. reads.route(handler) returns a handler whose whole body holds one of the few heavy-read slots per process (the ones custom queries, widget renders and queue items use), so a burst of them never takes every database connection from the cheap reads around them. Reads inside the body that are gated themselves run in the same slot. A client that leaves while queued gets 499 and the handler never runs; a wait shows as Server-Timing: gate;dur=. Older APIs do not offer it — call ctx.reads?.route(h) ?? h. / pipelines | { ownedItemIds(userId, collection) } (optional) | Record ids of a collection whose CURRENT pipeline step the person owns: the same answer as My Work and a queue's My Items (owner groups, manual owners, teams, delegation). Resolving it scans every open record, so a cold call takes seconds; the answer is kept a minute per person and cleared whenever owners change. Use it for a "mine" filter, never per row. Older APIs do not offer it — ctx.pipelines?.ownedItemIds. / access | { readFilter(user, collection) } (optional) | The role's read access for your own raw-SQL read model. Pass the request's req.user: allowed is false when the role cannot read the collection at all, and apply(query, alias) adds the role's row filter for rows of that collection under alias, exactly as the items API narrows them. User Scopes are not included — apply your own. Admins: allowed, nothing applied. A raw SQL list that skips this shows rows the person could never open. Older APIs do not offer it — fall back to a narrower audience, never a wider one. / sql | { runLong, announceWrites, triggerSafeReturning? } | runLong(sql, { timeoutMs }) runs one long statement on its own timeout; announceWrites(collection, ids) tells open pages a raw write changed records. triggerSafeReturning: true says every core write that reads ids back (.returning()) works on a table that carries a trigger — SQL Server refuses a plain OUTPUT there (error 334). Never put a trigger on a table the core writes while it is missing (older APIs).

Property | Type | Purpose / callExternalApi | Function | Call configured external API by name/ID. Auth resolved automatically. / flows | Object | Register flow ops/triggers. Emit trigger events to execute flows. / notifyUser | Function | notifyUser(userId, {subject, message, category?, collection?, item?}) — deliver through the full channel stack (inbox, socket, push, optional email) honouring the recipient's notification rules. Never insert nivaro_notifications rows directly. / approvalBrief | Object | approvalBrief.registerLine(collection, async ({collection, item}) => ({label, text, tone?}) | null) — one short line on the transition confirm's approval brief for records of that collection: a fact the approver should see before the click that the record's own history cannot supply. A provider that throws, returns null or takes longer than 4 seconds is dropped for that brief.

Property | Type | Purpose / bulkActions | Object | Register selection bar buttons for collections. / itemActions | Object | Register toolbar buttons on item edit pages. / dashboardWidgets | Object | Register custom dashboard widget types. / collectionViews | Object | Register custom collection view modes (Kanban, calendar, etc). / notificationChannels | Object | Register delivery channels (Slack, SMS, custom).

Property | Type | Purpose / fieldTypes | Object | Register custom field types with serialize/deserialize. / validators | Object | Register field validation operators. / importParsers | Object | Register file format parsers for import wizard. / storage | Object | Register file storage adapters (S3, Azure, etc).

Field | Description / collection | Table name, e.g. articles / action | read | create | update | delete / data | For write operations: the new row data. For reads: query result. / itemId | Primary key of the affected record (update/delete). / userId | ID of the Nivaro user who initiated the action.

ctx.callExternalApi(
  nameOrId: string | number,  // API name or numeric id from nivaro_external_apis
  options?: {
    endpoint?: string | number; // predefined endpoint name or id — sets method/path/body/query/headers defaults
    method…
Auth type | What happens automatically / bearer | Authorization: Bearer <token> injected. / api_key | Key injected as header or query param per config. / basic | Authorization: Basic base64(user:pass) injected. / oauth2_cc | Client credentials token fetched from token_url, then Bearer injected.
callExternalApi throws if the API name/ID is not found or the API is disabled. Wrap in try/catch for graceful error handling.

Extensions can register custom operation types and trigger types. Once registered, they appear in the flow editor alongside built-in ops and triggers — no custom UI code required. Config fields are described with a schema and the editor renders them automatically.

ctx.flows.registerOperation({
  type: 'my-ext:send-sms',        // namespace with extension id
  label: 'Send SMS',
  description: 'Send a text via Twilio',
  color: '#7c3aed',               // optional badge color
  fields: [
    { key: 't…

Field | Type | Description / key | string | Key written into / read from the operation's options object / label | string | Display label in the flow editor config panel / type | 'string'|'number'|'boolean'|'select'|'textarea'|'json' | Input type rendered in the editor / options | Array<{ value, label }> | Required when type is select / placeholder | string? | Input placeholder text / required | boolean? | Shows a red asterisk in the editor (validation is up to the handler) / description | string? | Help text shown below the input / defaultValue | unknown? | Initial value populated in the editor

// 1. Register the trigger type (call during extension register())
ctx.flows.registerTrigger({
  type: 'my-ext:crm-contact-updated',
  label: 'CRM Contact Updated',
  description: 'Fires when a contact is updated in the external CRM',
  fie…
ctx.flows.emit() is fire-and-forget. It looks up all active flows with trigger = 'my-ext:crm-contact-updated' in the database and executes them asynchronously. Safe to call from hooks, cron callbacks, or route handlers.

Method | Path | Description / GET | /api/flows/registered-operations | List all extension-registered op types (without handler fn). Auth required. / GET | /api/flows/registered-triggers | List all extension-registered trigger types. Auth required.

A full working example is at examples/my-project/extensions/example-flows/index.ts. It registers two triggers (record-flagged, daily-digest) and two operations (format-text, db-lookup) with complete field schemas and handlers.

Beyond hooks, cron, and routes, extensions can register capabilities that plug into specific admin UI surfaces and server pipelines. Working examples for every type live in examples/my-project/extensions/.

Appear as buttons in the collection browser selection bar when rows are selected. The execute function runs server-side and returns a toast message.
ctx.bulkActions.register({
  id: 'mark-fulfilled',
  label: 'Mark fulfilled',
  icon: 'CheckCircle2',
  collections: ['orders'],   // omit for all collections
  async execute({ ids, collection }) {
    const n = await ctx.database(collectio…

Appear as buttons in the item editor toolbar alongside Save. Useful for "Push to ERP", "Generate PDF", "Send notification" patterns.
ctx.itemActions.register({
  id: 'push-to-erp',
  label: 'Push to ERP',
  variant: 'outline',        // 'default' | 'outline' | 'destructive'
  collections: ['invoices'],
  async execute({ itemId, collection }) {
    await ctx.callExternalA…
Add choose when the person must pick one of a per-record list first, such as which attached file to send. When the button is pressed, the record form and the row menu fetch the options from GET /api/item-actions/:id/choices?collection=&item=. With two or more options they show a picker; with exactly one they use it without asking; with none the action runs without a pick. The pick reaches execute as payload[key]. Bulk runs never ask, so execute must handle a missing pick.
ctx.itemActions.register({
  id: 'push-to-erp',
  label: 'Push to ERP',
  collections: ['invoices'],
  choose: {
    key: 'file_id',
    label: 'File to send',
    body: 'The ERP accepts one file. Pick the one to attach.',
    async options…

Replace local disk storage with any cloud provider. The adapter interface matches the local adapter exactly — put, get, delete, url.
ctx.storage.register('s3', {
  async put(key, stream, meta) { /* upload to S3 */ },
  async get(key) { /* return readable stream from S3 */ },
  async delete(key) { /* delete from S3 */ },
  async url(key) { return getSignedUrl(client, key)…

Add view modes to the collection browser (Kanban, calendar, Gantt, map). The view renders via a UI bundle URL that receives collection data via postMessage.
ctx.collectionViews.register({
  id: 'kanban',
  label: 'Kanban',
  icon: 'Columns3',
  bundleUrl: '/api/extensions/my-ext/ui.js',
  fieldMappings: [
    { key: 'statusField', label: 'Status field', required: true },
    { key: 'titleField'…

An extension can give assistants its own tools: ctx.mcp.registerTool adds a tool MCP clients (Claude, ChatGPT, Codex) can call, and ctx.ai.registerTool adds one Ask AI may call while it answers. Both take the same declaration, so one definition can serve both. Every handler runs as the person calling — read data with tools.readItems, never raw SQL — and a disabled extension’s tools disappear from every assistant.
const openDeals = {
  name: 'open_deals',                       // 3–48 lower-case letters, digits, _
  description: 'Open deals for an owner. Use when someone asks what is still open.',
  input_schema: {
    type: 'object',
    properties:…

• A bad declaration (name, missing description or handler, a schema that is not an object) is logged and skipped — registerTool returns false and never throws. • A name a built-in tool already uses is never offered; two extensions cannot share a name. • tools.assertFieldsReadable(collection, fields) refuses a field the caller cannot read (dotted paths are walked link by link). For Ask AI tools, field_lists: [{ fields_key, collection_key }] makes the core run that check on the input before your handler. • tools.linkLabels(refs) labels linked records as the caller; a record they cannot read keeps no label. • tools.api_key_scopes holds the collection scopes of the API key the caller is using (null when nothing narrows them). readItems already honours them; a handler that reaches data any other way — an external API, a flow, raw SQL — must refuse what the scopes do not cover. • An Ask AI answer that used an extension tool stays the asker’s, unless the tool is read_only and declared replayable — then a shared answer is re-run as each reader and shown only when their result matches. • A call is cut off after 30 seconds. Calls and failures since start show on AI Quality → Extension tools and on Assistant Tools.

ctx.chat.registerMessageAction adds an item to a message’s ⋯ menu. when limits it to room kinds (general, channel, entity, dm), record-room prefixes, messages with text or attachments, your own messages, or text matching a pattern. The handler runs as the person clicking, in a room they can see; text it returns as post is sent through the normal send path (as a thread reply with in_thread), reply is a private line, and open_url opens a link or an app path.
ctx.chat.registerMessageAction?.({
  id: 'log-to-record',
  label: 'Log to record',
  description: 'Copy this message into the record’s call log',
  when: { room_kinds: ['entity'], has_text: true },
  async handler(message, { userId, room }…

Extensions can include an admin UI bundle (ui.js) that injects React components into named slots in the admin interface. This works at runtime — no rebuild of Nivaro required. Docker volume mounts are the primary deployment mechanism.
When an extension has a manifest.json declaring a uiBundle, Nivaro serves the bundle at /api/extensions/<id>/ui.js. The admin SPA fetches the manifest on boot and injects a <script> tag for each enabled plugin. Each script self-registers by calling window.__NIVARO__.registerPlugin(plugin).

• API starts → scans extensions/ → reads manifest.json → registers route to serve ui.js • Admin boots → fetches GET /api/extensions/manifest → injects <script> for each UI plugin • Script executes → calls window.__NIVARO__.registerPlugin(plugin) → plugin components appear in slots • Disabling an extension via the Extensions page removes it from the manifest response → its UI is not loaded on next boot

Nivaro exposes a global object so plugin bundles can use React without bundling their own copy (which would cause hook errors):
Property | Type | Description / React | typeof React | The React object — use for createElement, Fragment, etc. / useState | Hook | React.useState / useEffect | Hook | React.useEffect / useCallback | Hook | React.useCallback / useMemo | Hook | React.useMemo / useRef | Hook | React.useRef / registerPlugin | (plugin) => void | Self-register the plugin and its slot components
Plugin bundles must NOT bundle React — they must reference it exclusively via window.__NIVARO__.React (or destructure from window.__NIVARO__). Bundling a second React instance causes "invalid hook call" runtime errors.

Slots are named injection points in the admin UI. A plugin registers components for one or more slots. Multiple plugins can fill the same slot — all matching components are rendered in registration order.
Slot name | Where it renders | Context props / external-api-detail | Bottom of the External API edit page | { api } — the full External API object including integration_type and integration_config / item-detail-sidebar | Sidebar panel on item edit pages | { collection, item } — collection name and the full item record / nav-sidebar | Extensions section at the bottom of the sidebar nav | { section, label, icon, href } — declares the link, not a component / settings-tab | New tab injected into the Settings page | none — component receives no props / collection-toolbar | Toolbar area on collection list pages | { collection, selectedIds } — collection name and currently selected row IDs / list-row-action | Action items in collection list row menus | { collection, item } — collection name and the row record

The nav-sidebar slot is declarative — provide metadata, not a component. Nivaro renders the link using the standard NavItem component:
slots: {
  'nav-sidebar': {
    section: 'extensions',   // 'main' | 'automation' | 'system' | 'monitoring' | 'extensions'
    label: 'Oracle EBS',
    icon: SomeIcon,          // React component (lucide or custom SVG)
    href: '/extension…

blocks.h: Building a UI Plugin — Full TypeScript Guide
blocks.t: Plugin UI bundles are compiled to IIFE-format JavaScript. You write TypeScript + JSX; Vite compiles it. React must not be bundled — it comes from window.__NIVARO__ at runtime. This guide walks through every step from an empty folder to a running plugin.

my-plugin/              ← this folder is mounted into /app/extensions/my-plugin
  src/
    ui.tsx            ← React component source (TypeScript + JSX)
    api.ts            ← API-side source (routes, hooks, cron)
    types.ts          ← s…

{
  "name": "@my-org/nivaro-plugin-my-plugin",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "build": "vite build && tsc -p tsconfig.api.json",
    "build:ui": "vite build",
    "build:api": "tsc -p tsconfi…

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2020",
    "module": "ESNext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "jsx": "react-jsx",
    "strict": true,
    "lib": ["ES2020", "DOM"],
    "types": ["node"]
  },
  "include": ["src/ui.tsx", "sr…

{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2022",
    "module": "NodeNext",
    "moduleResolution": "NodeNext",
    "outDir": ".",
    "rootDir": "src",
    "strict": true,
    "lib": ["ES2022"]
  },
  "include": ["src/api.ts", "src/types.ts…

# Install deps
pnpm install   # or npm install

# Build everything: ui.js (Vite IIFE) + index.js (tsc)
pnpm build

# Watch mode during development
pnpm dev
After pnpm build, your plugin directory contains ui.js (admin bundle), index.js (API side), and manifest.json. These three files are everything Nivaro needs.

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  nivaro:
    image: nivaro:latest
    volumes:
      - ./my-plugin:/app/extensions/my-plugin
    environment:
      - DB_HOST=...
After mounting the volume, hot-reload the API side without restarting the container:
curl -X POST https://your-nivaro/api/extensions/reload \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <static-token>"
The UI bundle is served immediately — no reload needed on the API. Open the admin in a fresh browser tab to load the new script.

blocks.h: Step 13 — Wire up in the admin
blocks.t: • Go to External APIs and open or create an API entry • Set Integration Type to my-plugin (or whatever string your filter checks) • Save — the My Plugin panel now appears at the bottom of the edit page • Use the panel to enter the client ID and configure the integration

• Edit src/ui.tsx → pnpm dev rebuilds ui.js on save • Hard-refresh the admin tab to reload the script (or use loadedExtensions.delete from browser devtools) • Edit src/api.ts → pnpm build:api → POST /api/extensions/reload to hot-swap routes • Type-check everything: pnpm tsc --noEmit (both tsconfig files)
The component: MyPanel as unknown as never cast is required because the SDK's PluginSlots interface uses unknown for components (the SDK is framework-agnostic). The cast is safe — Nivaro passes the correct props at runtime.

Every External API record has an optional integration_type field — a free-form string tag (e.g. "sat-ng", "oracle-ebs"). Plugins use this to identify which External APIs they manage and render targeted UI panels.
Set the integration type in the External API edit page under the "Integration Type" card. Leave blank for APIs that no plugin manages.
Field | Type | Description / integration_type | string | null | Free-form tag identifying the plugin that manages this API (e.g. "sat-ng") / integration_config | object | null | JSON config blob. Plugins write and read this to store integration-specific metadata (client IDs, expiry dates, etc.). Not exposed in the base form — plugins manage it directly via API calls.

A batch of platform primitives for integrating with and extending Nivaro: a server-sent event stream, feature flags, a durable extension event outbox, declared extension settings, and capability manifests.

GET /api/events/ticket            → { data: { ticket, expires_in: 60 } }   (authenticated)
GET /api/events/stream?ticket=…&collections=a,b   (text/event-stream)

event: collection.update
data: {"collection":"articles","item":"42","action":"…
The stream carries field NAMES, never values — a consumer fetches the changed row through /items, where permissions apply. EventSource cannot set headers, so header-less consumers mint a one-shot ticket first (60-second TTL, single use); Bearer/session auth works directly. Per-collection filtering drops unauthorized collections silently.
With several API processes, a stream hears every process’s writes (read from the record-event stream, REALTIME_EVENT_STREAM). Before 2026-10-23 it heard only the writes of the process it connected to. Behind a realtime tier, route /api/events/stream to the realtime processes (see Realtime tier).

Admin → Feature Flags registers flags with an on/off switch, per-role gating, and a stable percentage rollout (each user hashes into a fixed bucket, so a 20% rollout shows the same 20% of people every day). Clients read their effective set from GET /api/feature-flags/mine; the useFeatureFlag(key) hook (shared/react) resolves unknown flags and fetch failures to false, so a flag can gate new code with zero risk to the old path.

Extensions get durable at-least-once eventing: ctx.events.publish(type, payload) lands a row in nivaro_extension_events; a per-minute sweep delivers to ctx.events.on(type, handler) registrations with exponential backoff (2^attempts minutes, cap 60), dead-lettering after 8 attempts. Admin → Extensions → Events lists rows with Retry / Discard.

An extension may declare settings: [{key, label, type, default}] (string / number / boolean / secret) — the Extensions page renders a form from the schema, secrets are masked, and ctx.settings.get(key) reads typed values with declared defaults. Extensions may also declare capabilities; the loader records which context surfaces the extension actually touched, and observed-but-undeclared capabilities show amber on the Extensions page.

After a staging database is rebuilt from production, quality checks compare what the conversions produced with what production held. They answer one question: did the conversion change anything it should not have?

Each check returns a list of keyed rows. A row is a stable key, an optional label and a set of values. The same check runs twice: once on the fresh clone, before anything is converted (the baseline), and once after the conversions (the current shape). The two lists are compared key by key.
The baseline is a snapshot of the clone. Nothing reads production while the checks run, and the snapshot is stored with the run, so a later run is never compared with a newer production.
• A key in both lists with equal values matches. • A key in both lists with different values is a mismatch. • A key only in the baseline, or only in the current list, is a mismatch too. • A list check has an empty baseline. Every current row is then a finding.

A staging rebuild runs seven phases. Quality checks take part in three of them.
Phase | What happens / refresh | The database is restored from production. / capture | Every check runs its baseline query on the fresh clone. The rows are stored. / migrate | Nivaro migrations run. / promote | Configuration is copied from the development database. / schema | Business tables, indexes and procedures are brought in line. / convert | The data conversions run. / verify | Every check runs its current query and is compared with the baseline.
The whole run happens under maintenance mode, and scheduled jobs hold while it is on: a partner poll or an auto-sweep writing into the half-converted copy would otherwise move a record between capture and verify and show up as a false mismatch. Jobs resume when the run ends; an admin’s Run now is never held.

Colour | Meaning / Green | Every compared row is equal. / Amber | Rows differ, and every difference is expected. / Red | At least one difference is not expected. Look at it. / Error | The check could not run or ran out of its time budget. It says why.
The Staging quality checks page lists the checks of the latest run by area. Open a check to see its clusters (mismatches grouped by the dimensions the check declares, such as state or zone) and the mismatch rows. A row links to the record in production when the deployment configures a legacy link.

Some differences are deliberate. Use Mark as expected on a mismatch row, or on a whole cluster, and give a reason. The difference then reads amber instead of red in every later run.
• A known difference belongs to one check and matches rows by their key or cluster. A key pattern may use * for any run of characters, up to four times. Mark as expected on a row names that row's key exactly, * included. • The Known differences tab lists them with the reason, who added it and how many rows it matched last time. • A known difference that matches nothing for 3 runs in a row is marked stale. It is kept until someone removes it. • Known differences are configuration. They are copied with the rest of the configuration.

Re-run checks starts the read-only check runbook on the host without rebuilding anything. It runs the verify phase again against the current database, using the baseline of the latest run. It skips the dry-run gate that other host runbooks require, because it writes nothing outside the results tables. It refuses to start while a rebuild of the same database is running. The button queues only the runbook the extension that supplies the checks declares for it (quality_rerun), and only when that runbook runs on the host and declares skip_dry_gate.

Each check can be downloaded as CSV: one line per mismatch row, with the key, label, status, whether it is expected, the differing fields, the baseline and current values, and the reason. Cells that begin with a formula character are neutralised so the file is safe to open in a spreadsheet.
Red never fails a rebuild. The checks report. They do not block a phase, stop a chain or change data. A check that fails to run is recorded as an error and the rest continue.

Four tables, created by migration 404, in the application database:
• nivaro_quality_runs — one row per capture and verify cycle for a target, with status, times and totals. • nivaro_quality_rows — per check and side (baseline, current, diff) the row list, compressed. • nivaro_quality_results — per check verdict, counts, clusters and up to 500 sample rows. • nivaro_quality_known — the known differences.
Runs, rows and results are per database and are not promoted between environments. Old runs are pruned. The results database must not be the production database or the target itself; the runner refuses both.

The /ask page answers natural-language questions about your business data. Claude runs a tool-use loop against the CMS — every tool call executes as the requesting user, so RBAC, field allow-lists and row-level security apply exactly as on the REST API.
POST /api/ai/chat
{ "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "How many workflows per payment status?" }] }

→ { "data": { "reply": "…markdown…", "trace": [
    { "tool": "aggregate", "input": {…}, "summary": "count by payment_status: 3 gro…
• Tools: list_collections, query_items (items service — RLS applies), aggregate (refuses when the user is row-filtered), semantic_search (hits intersected with the permission-checked read), integration_status (the obligation ledger for a record), record_event_path (the newest integration events naming a record and the path each set off — writes, transitions, flows, partner calls, where it failed), explain_access (why the asker — or, for administrators, another user — can or cannot see a record), record_integrity (a record's live integrity findings, or a collection's newest sweep totals) run_custom_query (a saved SQL query from the catalogue the assistant is given — only queries whose access admits the asker, User-Scope params injected, 200 rows at most) and queue_summary (a queue the asker may read, by name or id from the queue catalogue in the prompt: totals, by-state counts, SLA breaches with hours over and owners, the oldest and unowned records as friendly ids with links, and the at-risk rules firing most — read as the asker through the queue service, so scopes apply), waiting_on_me (the asker's own My Work “Waiting on you” list — records whose current pipeline step they own, SLA-breached first, plus approval steps naming them; no person parameter, narrowed to records the asker may read; an empty list is said as “nothing waiting”, never replaced by another list). • Ask about a queue from its page: the queue toolbar's "Ask about this queue" opens /ask with the question seeded (/ask?q=… seeds and sends one question, then drops the parameter). • Reads are direct; mutations only ever happen through the proposal gate (see AI Actions & Dashboards) — the model can never write without your approval. • Every answer shows the tool trace: exactly which queries produced it. • A breakdown or a series (per state, per month, per vendor) comes with a chart: the model attaches a fenced chart block ({type, title, data:[{label, value}]}) that renders as a bar, line or pie under the prose. • The same standalone question by the same person inside the answer-cache window (Settings → AI Features, default 15 minutes) answers from cache — the page says when it was first answered and offers "Ask again". Answers that propose an action are never cached; fresh: true in the request skips the cache. • An answer written only from the in-app docs (search_docs and no other tool, no page context, no remembered notes) is also kept for everyone: the next person asking the same question in the same language, with the same docs audience (administrators see more sections), gets it from cache. Any data tool keeps an answer private, and a new docs index never serves an answer quoting the old one. • Within one conversation, a read the assistant already made (same tool, same arguments, same person) is reused instead of queried again, as long as nothing in that collection changed since — the steps say "reused". A write in between, a configuration change, or 30 minutes passing makes it read again. • Tool results reach the model as compact tables (column names once, each link label once); Show the steps and exports keep the readable rows. • When an administrator switches on "Start cheap" for Ask AI (AI Quality → Cost savings), a quick answer from the smaller model says so and offers "Try harder", which asks the main model. • Under a single number (an ungrouped count, sum, average, minimum or maximum) the page offers "Tell me when this goes over…": pick a threshold (goes over, reaches, drops under, falls to) or a trend watch (alerts when the series changes direction or moves outside its recent range, using the anomaly engine statistics), and how often to check (daily or hourly). The watch is re-read hourly AS YOU, so permissions and row-level security apply; you get an in-app notification when it crosses (once per crossing, not every check). "Numbers you watch" at the top of /ask lists each with its current value, change today, threshold and last alert — edit the threshold, pause or stop watching. Watches live in your own account preferences (20 at most) via GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE /api/ai/watches (POST /:id/check reads one now), and appear in your daily summary with the change since yesterday and whether they are close to the threshold. Ask "what am I watching" to have the assistant list them (my_watches). • The past_state tool reads revision and pipeline history under the same read gates as the revision API: "what did this record look like on March 1" (as_of), "when did the amount change and who changed it" (changes), "how long was it in Finance Review" (time_in_state). • Uses the chat model from Settings → AI Features → Model per feature; a model the gateway refuses falls back to the default model. • Answers stream as they are written: send stream: true and the route answers 202 {data: {stream_id}} at once, then emits ai:delta (text, with its round), ai:status (the tool running), ai:done (the full normal body — proposals, trace, request_id) and ai:error to your Socket.io user room; add Accept: text/event-stream to get the same events as SSE instead (widgets, hosts without the socket). A caller with neither gets the plain reply. POST /api/ai/chat/:stream_id/stop halts a running answer. /summarize and /generate take the same stream option with text deltas only. The /ask page streams by default, shows what the model is doing while tools run, and has a Stop button.
Admin page /ai/quality (Insights → AI → Quality). Review poor answers, set optional daily spend caps, watch provider health, and try another model before switching.

Every thumbs-down Ask AI answer lands here with the question, tool calls, answer and the person's comment, sorted by an automatic cause (wrong tool, wrong filter, missing data, permission, misunderstood question). Reassign the cause, delete the learned playbook, add a hint to the data guide, or mark it handled.

• Caps are off by default (no limit). Each cap is a daily dollar amount per person, per role or for everyone, optionally for one feature, per person or as a shared pool. The day is UTC. • Past a cap the feature switches to the cap's cheaper model if one is set, otherwise it stops with a message naming the cap and when it resets. • People see what is left today under the Ask AI box, only when a cap applies to them. • A fallback model (same provider) is tried when a call fails; the answer says a fallback wrote it. With none set, AI features say AI is unavailable.

• Start cheap (off by default): pick a small model and the features that may start on it — Ask AI, record review, record summaries and field generation. The first call goes to the small model; it moves up to the feature's main model when a tool call fails, before any proposal or plan (always the main model), when the reply is not the JSON the feature asked for, or when the small model says it cannot answer. Streamed summaries and field drafts stay on the main model. • "Try harder" under a quick Ask AI answer asks the main model straight away. • What starting cheap saved: every call is logged with its model and cost; the figure is what the small model's useful calls would have cost on the main model, minus what they cost, minus any cheap calls thrown away (a question asked again on the main model, or replaced by Try harder). This month or the last 30 days. • Tool results sent to the model: per tool, the readable size and the compact size actually sent (about four characters per token), and how many results were reused from earlier in the conversation. • The figures need migration 469 (nivaro_ai_calls.meta); until it has run the switches work and the figures say so.

Compare runs one prompt on two models; Replay re-runs up to 50 recent Ask AI questions as their askers (read-only, no proposals) on a candidate model. Both show a cost estimate you confirm first, are logged as admin activity and count against budgets. Live calls streams each finished AI call (feature, model, person, cost, status) while the tab is open.

• Spend shows this month so far and a projected month end per model, feature and person, with last month beside it. The projection adds the last seven finished days’ pace to what is already spent. • Admins get one notice a month when the projection passes a daily budget (counted over the whole month) or last month by a percentage you set. The same figures ride the Monday operations summary. • Last month survives the 30-day call log because a nightly job rolls the log up per day. • Log against the bill: enter or import (CSV lines month,model,usd) what the provider charged. A gap means calls that never reached the log, or prices that drifted; set the billed price per million tokens and new calls are costed with it.

Tokens each part of a request carried (tool definitions, system rules, data guides, glossary, collection lists, playbooks, attachments, history, the question), counted from what was actually sent and scaled to the provider’s own count. Per feature you see the biggest parts and how much was served from cache (only the stable start of a prompt can be); a table by release shows bloat as it ships.

Per Ask AI tool: calls, error rate, empty results, retries after an error (and how many worked, each a wasted round), answers where zero rows were read as “none”, rounds per answer and time. Open a row for its recent failing calls and slowest runs.

A nightly check asks the provider which models it offers (its list where it has one, otherwise a one-token probe per known model). New and retired models are listed. A new model automatically runs Compare and a small replay of saved questions so the side-by-side is waiting; a model still named in the settings that was retired raises a readiness warning and tells admins. Nothing ever switches a model by itself.
Extension tools lists the tools extensions give Ask AI (ctx.ai.registerTool): the extension each comes from, whether answers that used it may be shared (only a read-only tool its extension declared replayable), and its calls and failures since the server started. A tool whose name a built-in already uses is marked and never offered.
GET  /api/ai/spend/forecast     admin: month so far, projection, last month, alerts
GET  /api/ai/spend/reconcile    admin: logged vs billed per month and model
PUT  /api/ai/spend/settings     admin: prices, alert percentage, catalogue switc…

Press ⌘J (Ctrl+J on Windows) on any page, or type a question in the command palette (⌘K) and choose “Ask…”, and the Ask AI panel slides in over the page. What the page shows rides along as chips under the box: the open record, the list or queue with its filters and the rows on screen, or the report with its date range and filters. “Which of these are late?” then means the rows you are looking at. Remove a chip to ask without it. The panel keeps its questions as one conversation in your Ask AI history; “Open in Ask AI” continues it on the full page.
A chip sends ids and filters only. The server reads every record, row, report and file again with your access before the model sees it, so a record you cannot open is simply left out. An answer that used page context stays yours: it is never shown to people a conversation is shared with.
While the panel is open, drag rows from a collection list or a queue onto it. Each becomes a chip, and “what do these have in common” means exactly those records (up to 20).

Drop a PDF, Word, Excel, CSV or text file on the panel (or use the paperclip) and ask about it together with the data: “does this quote match the PO on PO-1042?”. The file is read with the same text extractor as document autofill; only its text is kept, for a day, and only you can use it. The file itself is not stored in Files. A scanned PDF without a text layer cannot be read. Up to five files per conversation share the 60,000-character reading budget; a longer document is read from the start and the answer says it was cut short.
On a record, the files already attached to it are offered under the box (“Attachments on this record — use as sources”). Pick the ones to read; they are only offered and read when you can open the record.

On a Report Studio report, questions like “why did March dip” or “which zone drives the overrun” are answered from the widgets’ own queries, re-run with your access and the date range and filters on screen. For one widget the answer can read its whole series, the biggest movers and the rows behind the current and previous periods.

• “Which rules, flows and layouts use workflows.amount?” — the field impact scan plus flows that name the field. • “Why does this field lock?” — field settings, layout lock conditions, role-locked sections, lock rules and locking pipeline states. • “Who approves inventory requests over $50k in Zone 3?” — the owner matrix for the state, matched against the values you give, with the people in the winning group and the roles each transition needs. • “What fires on this collection?” — rules, flows, webhooks, SLA rules, alerts, field watches and code hooks.

A manager can ask about their own direct reports — workload per person, stuck records, who is out and who covers, overdue tasks, the last week. It follows the team pages’ rule: only people whose manager you are, and records you cannot open are counted, never named.

Key | What it does / ⌘J | Open or close the panel on any page / Enter | Ask (Shift+Enter for a new line) / ↑ in an empty box | Bring back the last question to edit / Esc | Stop the answer while it streams; close the panel otherwise / ⌘↵ | Ask the last question again, fresh (skips the answer cache)

Every Ask AI conversation is kept for the person who started it: each question, the answer, the tool calls behind it and any action it proposed (with that proposal’s outcome, read live). The History list beside the chat shows them newest first, pinned ones on top, and searches titles and text. Opening one resumes it — the next question goes to the model with the whole thread. The AI call log stays the administrator’s record; this history is the person’s own, and administrators get no view into it.

• Pin a conversation from the list or the page header; pins sort first and are never pruned. • Delete removes the conversation and everything in it. Someone it was shared with can remove it from their own list instead. Deleting a single message deletes your own; the owner removing someone else’s message only empties it — it stays a withheld turn, so later answers that may repeat it stay withheld too. • Settings → AI Features → Ask AI conversation history: how many days an untouched conversation is kept (blank = 180, 0 = forever). The nightly retention job prunes the rest, except conversations any participant has pinned.

Each person can turn Ask AI history off — Profile → Ask AI history, or the switch at the top of the History list on the Ask page. From then on nothing they ask is stored as a conversation: answers still work live (the thread lives in the open page only), but there is no History entry, and Share, Post to chat, Branch, export and saved plan cards are unavailable because they need a saved conversation. A saved conversation opened while history is off is read-only. Turning it on offers a separate “Also delete my saved conversations” — it deletes only the conversations that person started (with their shares to other people); conversations others shared with them stay.
Still kept while history is off | What and for how long / Ask AI memory notes | Only the notes the person explicitly saved; they edit or delete them on Profile. / Thumbs up/down | Only when the person chooses to give one: the rating and any comment they type, kept in the AI feedback table. / AI call log (administrators) | One row per model call with tokens, cost, latency and capped copies of the request and response — which include the question — pruned after 30 days. Visible to administrators in AI analytics. Unchanged by this switch. / Activity log | An ai-chat entry per question with the number of tool calls — no question text. / Answer cache | The same standalone question by the same person answers from a per-person Redis cache for the configured window (default 15 minutes), then expires. / Not kept | The conversation itself, and the shared playbook of worked examples (a question asked with history off never becomes one).

Say “remember that amounts are in thousands” (or “remember: I work Zone 3 inventory requests”) and Ask AI keeps the note instead of answering. Notes ride every later question as context about you. Profile → Ask AI memory lists them for editing or deleting. At most 20 notes of 300 characters; when the list is full a new note is refused — nothing is ever dropped to make room — and the answer links to Profile → Ask AI memory to remove one first. Notes are stored in your preferences and never grant access to anything. Nobody else writes them — administrators included: they are left out of user reads, lists and revisions, and an administrator’s edit of your preferences keeps your notes as they were.
Remember this? When a question shows a lasting preference (“by my zone I mean Zone 3”, “show amounts in thousands”), Ask AI may offer a note under its answer. Nothing is kept unless you click Remember; “Not now” hides the offer. Offers are only ever shown to the person who asked — never to someone a conversation is shared with — and are never offered for one-off facts, record values, other people or anything that reads as an instruction to Ask AI (“call…”, “ignore…”, “always run…”). The offer says plainly that the note is added to every future question. With Ask AI history off, offers still appear and Remember keeps only the note. At most two per answer, none once your memory is full (a click on a full list is refused the same way, with a link to Profile).
Administrators can view and clear a person’s notes for a support or compliance request: People → the person → Admin tools → Ask AI memory. The notes stay hidden until Show notes; each view and each clear (one note or all) is written to the activity log as ai-memory-view / ai-memory-clear with counts only. Administrators can remove notes but never add or reword them.

The owner shares a conversation with colleagues (Share in the header). They are notified, see it in their History, can read it and can ask follow-ups in the same thread; a new question or answer appears for everyone who has it open. Each person’s questions run with their own permissions.
An answer is shown to someone other than the person it was asked for only when it is safe to: it made at least one data call, every call is a plain read (not saved SQL, not an action proposal) that did not error, re-running each one with the reader’s access returns exactly what the model saw, and every earlier answer in the thread is readable by the reader too (the model saw those answers and may repeat them). Otherwise — including an answer with no data calls, or data that has changed since — the answer is withheld from that reader with an “Ask it with my access” button. Opening a thread re-checks at most 10 calls; anything past that is withheld until asked again. A follow-up asked by the reader is built only from the turns they may read.
Live sessions: while one person’s answer streams, everyone else with the thread open follows it — each finished step, then the answer text — but only once every step so far has been re-run with their own access and returned exactly what the model saw, and every earlier answer is readable by them. Text written before any data call, a step that is not a plain read, or a result that differs for them stops the stream for that person: they see that someone is asking, then the answer when it is stored, under the rule above.

The clock button next to Send asks the question in the background: a longer run with a bigger budget of data calls, shown in the Jobs tray while it works. It reads with your access, and it can only read — it cannot draft changes or plans (ask on the page for those). The answer is saved to the conversation in your Ask history and you get an inbox notification; Cancel in the tray or under the question stops it and keeps whatever had arrived. It needs your Ask history on, and at most two run at once.

Hover an earlier question and choose Edit to ask a different version of it. The answer continues in a new conversation (a branch) that holds everything before the edited question as you could read it — an answer withheld from you is copied as an empty placeholder that still counts as withheld; the original thread stays as it was. History nests branches under their source, and the conversation page links between them.

The owner can Post to chat: it sends the conversation to a channel, direct message or record room as a card: the question, a short answer and an Open link. The card is built for each reader — the short answer appears only when the sharing rule above admits them; otherwise it says the answer was given with the poster’s access. Anyone who can read the room can open the conversation and ask follow-ups with their own access.

• An answer built from a query offers CSV and Excel. The download re-runs the query with your access today — it never copies the answer’s text — and is named after the question and the time. • A table, chart or “label: value” list in an answer has a Table · Chart · List switch. The other formats are drawn from the same rows, with no new question and no model call. A chart needs a column of numbers. • Add to dashboard (under a chart answer) keeps the chart on one of your dashboards, or a new one. The widget stores the query behind the chart — the grouped count or total, or the saved query — not the answer, and re-runs it with the access of whoever views the dashboard. Hover its title to see the question it came from. • Copy as code (administrators, and people with an API token or key) turns the reads an answer made into an SDK call, a REST request and a curl command. Anything naming data you cannot see — a filter on a hidden field, a grouping, a saved query you may not run — is left out and counted.

Route | What it does / POST /api/ai/chat { messages, save: true } | Ask and start a stored conversation. The answer carries conversation_id. / POST /api/ai/chat { messages, conversation_id } | Ask inside a conversation. The server builds the history from the turns the caller may read; only the newest question in messages is used. / POST /api/ai/memory { text } | Keep a note the answer offered (memory_suggestions on the answer) in the caller’s own memory. 409 when the memory is full. / GET /api/users/:id/ai-memory | Administrators: a person’s notes. Logged as ai-memory-view. / DELETE /api/users/:id/ai-memory[/:noteId] | Administrators: clear all notes, or one. Logged as ai-memory-clear. / GET /api/ai/conversations?q=&pinned=1 | Mine and shared with me, newest first. / GET /api/ai/conversations/:id | The thread as the caller may read it (visible: false = withheld), shares (owner only), branches, parent. / PATCH /api/ai/conversations/:id { title?, pinned? } | Rename (owner) or pin (each person their own). / DELETE /api/ai/conversations/:id | Owner: delete. Shared: remove from my list. / DELETE /api/ai/conversations/mine | Delete every conversation the caller started (with its shares). PATCH /api/users/me/preferences { ai_history_off: true | null } is the opt-out; with it on, save is ignored and conversation_id answers 409. / POST /api/ai/conversations/:id/shares { user_ids } | Owner shares with people (notifies them). / DELETE /api/ai/conversations/:id/shares/:shareId | Owner stops sharing. / POST /api/ai/conversations/:id/branch { message_id, question } | New conversation holding the turns before that question; ask question in it next. / POST /api/ai/conversations/:id/post { room, note? } | Owner only: post to a chat room they can see. / GET /api/ai/conversations/:id/messages/:mid/export?format=csv|xlsx&step= | The rows behind an answer, re-run as the caller. / DELETE /api/ai/conversations/:id/messages/:mid | Remove one message (owner, or your own). / POST /api/ai/research { question, conversation_id? } | Ask in the background (202 {run_id, conversation_id, question_message_id}); 409 with history off, 429 past two running. / POST /api/ai/research/:run/cancel | Stop a background question (its asker, or an admin). / GET /api/ai/answer-code?conversation_id=&message_id= | An answer’s reads as {snippets: [{title, sdk, rest, curl, omitted}], skipped} for the caller; GET /api/ai/answer-code/access says whether they may.
Live updates: participants receive ai:conversation {conversation_id, by, message_id, state: asking|answered|failed} on their user room — ids only; the client refetches and the server filters the answer per reader. A live answer arrives as ai:live {conversation_id, message_id, by: {id, name}, kind: working|step|delta|end, tool?, summary?, text?, round?} — steps and text only for readers the checks above admit.

Everything here runs as you: starter questions name only what you can open, saved views are the ones you can see, and every figure or row is read with your own permissions, row rules and scopes. None of it adds a model call beyond the answer itself.

The empty chat offers two or three questions fitted to the page it was opened from — “Why is workflows #12 late?” on a record you can open, “Which records in queue 7 breach their SLA today?” on a queue, “What changed since last month?” on a report — plus the examples an administrator wrote into the collection’s data guide. After each answer, three short next questions drawn from what the tools found appear under it; one click asks one. They are written in the same call as the answer.

Type / in the Ask box to list the commands, then Tab or Enter to pick one.
Command | What it does / /chart <question> | Answers with a chart (bar, line or pie) built from the numbers the tools return. / /table <question> | Answers as a table. / /explain | Explains how the last answer was reached: what was read, how the figure was computed, access limits. / /steps <question> | Answers as a short numbered list of steps. / /export [xlsx] | Downloads the last answer’s rows as CSV (or Excel), re-run with your access.

When a question is genuinely ambiguous (“which zone?”, “this year or the funding year?”) and no sensible default exists, the answer asks with clickable options instead of guessing: the distinct values of a column, matching records you can read, or short interpretations. Picking one continues the same conversation. Answers that ask a question are never cached or shared as replayable.

Say “my late IRs view” and Ask AI resolves it to a saved view you can see — your own, ones shared with everyone, and ones shared with your role. The view’s filter is checked against the fields you may read (a view that filters on a hidden field is refused, not trimmed) and its rows are read as you. The filter can then be extended or grouped by a follow-up question.

Ask for “Q1 vs Q2 spend by zone”, “this year vs last year” or “compare these two requests”. The compare tool runs the same guarded aggregate over both sets and returns values with deltas (B minus A, and percent), or lays two to four records side by side with the differing fields first. Fields you cannot read are never shown.

Click a bar, point or slice of a chart answer to open the rows behind it in a sheet. The grouping is re-run as you and matched to the point you clicked; Open as list takes you to the collection filtered to exactly those records (up to 500).

A number or chart answer that was built only from counts and sums stays current while you leave it open: when records in its collection change, the same aggregate is re-run as you (debounced, no model call) and the fresh figure appears under the answer, marked “updated …”. Updates stop while the tab is hidden and when you pause or close the answer. Only the newest two such answers refresh.

GET  /api/ai/starters?page=&collection=&id=     (signed in) starter questions for a screen
POST /api/ai/chat                               body.command = chart | table | explain | steps
POST /api/ai/chart-drill {collection, group_by, filter…

What Ask AI knows beyond the data itself: the in-app docs, a shared glossary of business terms and a data guide per collection. Admins manage it all on /ai/knowledge (Insights → AI → Knowledge); everyone else sees the glossary there.

Ask AI has a search_docs tool over these Docs pages. For "how do I…" questions it quotes the passage and links the section (/docs?section=<id> opens this page there), next to the help-video search. Sections outside the Overview, User Guide and Collaboration groups are administrator material and are left out for people who are not administrators (a section can set its own audience). The search reads api/src/services/docs-index.json, regenerated by pnpm docs:ai-index and by pnpm sync-docs.

• A term has a definition, other spellings, an optional collection it belongs to, an optional rule ("is_on_hold = 1") and an optional saved query that computes the figure. • Ask AI uses the definitions and the same words in answers. A short glossary rides every prompt; a long one sends only the terms named in the question. A term scoped to a collection the asker cannot read is left out. • The app marks terms with a dotted underline and shows the definition on hover: on form field labels (terms scoped to another collection are skipped) and in Ask AI answers, where the first use of each term links to its entry. • Draft entries from the data: Suggestions → "Draft glossary from the data" proposes terms from choice lists, field help text and the docs. Nothing is added until an admin accepts (optionally edited) or dismisses it.

Hints and example questions for one collection ("forecasts are one row per workflow and year"), edited on the collection's Settings tab in the Data Model or on the Data guides tab. A guide is sent to Ask AI only when a question names the collection (or its display name, singular or plural) or closely matches one of its example questions, and rides list_collections for that collection — so the global guide in Settings → AI Features no longer has to hold everything.
Suggestions → "Draft guide lines from corrections" reads thumbs-down reasons (and any correction source an extension registers) and proposes guide lines, per collection or global, for an admin to accept, edit or dismiss.

Every docs search that finds no section answering the question is logged. The Docs gaps tab groups those questions by topic with counts, people and examples — a list of docs to write. A topic drops off by itself once a docs section answers it; Dismiss removes it by hand. The "try" box runs the same search Ask AI uses.

The Conflicts tab lists glossary terms and data guides that work against each other: the same word defined two different ways, near-duplicate terms with different meanings, and terms or guides that name a collection, field or saved query that no longer exists. The check runs when you save a term or guide and every night at 03:45 (the nightly run also asks the AI to read the definitions for contradictions a word match cannot see). Each finding links to both sides. A finding resolves by itself when you fix the cause; Dismiss hides one you have decided to keep.

The Topic map groups recent Ask AI questions by meaning and shows each topic by role: how many questions, how many went unanswered, how many got a thumbs-down and what they cost on average. A topic marked Gap goes wrong often and nothing in the glossary, data guides or playbooks matches its questions: write one. Topics have generated names; the questions themselves stay hidden unless you tick "Show sample questions", which is written to the activity log. Admins only.

Search by meaning only finds records that have been embedded. The Search index tab shows, per collection, how many records have no embedding yet or changed since their last one, how long the oldest of those has waited, and whether the embedding provider changed since the vectors were written (vectors from different providers cannot be compared, so the collection needs a reindex). Reindex embeds what is missing; after a provider switch it rebuilds every vector. A collection is flagged when a twentieth of its records are behind or a change has waited more than a day.

On the First week tab pick a role and choose Draft with AI. The draft is built from what the role touches: its forms, the queues it can read, videos required of it and views shared with it, and every step points at something the role really has. Edit the steps, then Publish. Nothing reaches people until you do. A person whose role was set in the last two weeks sees the published list at the top of My Work; a step ticks itself when they open its link, finish its video or save a record in its collection, and they can hide the list. Redrafting never touches the published version.
GET    /api/ai-knowledge/glossary                 (everyone)
POST   /api/ai-knowledge/glossary                 (admin) {term, definition, aliases[], collection?, query_slug?, query_note?}
PATCH  /api/ai-knowledge/glossary/:id             (a…
Ask AI can propose mutations — never execute them directly. Every proposal is stored, previewed in an approval card, and only runs when the proposing user clicks Approve within one hour.

• bulk_update — a filter plus field changes; affected records resolve through the permission-checked read path (RLS applies), capped at 200. • create_record — a single new record from field values. • create_dashboard — a named dashboard with up to 12 widgets (count, sum, avg, latest, bar_chart, line_chart); widget collections need read permission and fields validate against the registry.
POST /api/ai/proposals/:id/approve   → executes as the proposer
POST /api/ai/proposals/:id/reject    → discards

Execution goes through the items service per row — hooks, validation,
row security, computed fields and activity logging all ru…
Proposals expire after one hour and can only be approved by the user who asked. Dashboards are created private to the proposer.

A request that needs several changes together — "close out the lines on these 12 POs and tell their owners" — comes back from Ask AI as one numbered plan instead of separate proposals. Each step carries its own preview, built as you when the plan is proposed; nothing runs until you approve.
• Approve & run all runs every step in order; Run next step runs one and pauses, so you can approve step by step. Every step runs as you through the normal services — permissions, row security, validation, hooks and activity all apply. • Step kinds: update records (bulk_update), create a record, create a task, create a dashboard, send a message (an in-app notification to named people and/or the current owners of records — owners are resolved again when the step runs), post to a chat room you can see, and run an active manual flow (administrators only). • A refused step stops the plan with the reason; the steps after it stay pending. A bulk step where some records refuse reports how many and which. • Conditions: a step can say "only if still in Finance Review" (a filter the records must still match) or "only if the amount is unchanged" (fields that must still hold the value they had when the plan was made). A step whose condition fails is skipped and named in the result; on a bulk update only the records that fail are left out and the rest run. • While a plan runs, the card shows each step start, finish, fail or skip as it happens, with a running count of records changed. • Retry: after fixing the cause, Re-check and retry rebuilds the failed step and the ones after it as you now — a bulk step re-reads its filter and, after a partial run, keeps only the records that refused — shows which steps changed, then runs from where the plan stopped. • While an answer is being built, each tool step is listed as a plain line ("Reading workflows… 42 found") above the answer and folds away once the answer starts. • A plan nobody started expires after an hour, like a single proposal.

GET  /api/ai/plans/step-kinds     the step kinds the model may use
GET  /api/ai/plans/:id            the plan with each step's state (owner or administrator)
POST /api/ai/plans/:id/run        {mode: "all" | "next"} → 202; steps run in the b…
The chat answer carries proposed plans in plans next to proposals. Progress is pushed to your Socket.io user room as ai:plan ({plan_id, status, records_changed, step, plan}); ai:status events of a streamed answer now also arrive with done: true and a short result when each tool returns. Plans are stored in nivaro_ai_proposals with action_type plan.

Every plan card leads with its impact, read off the step previews: "Touches 34 records in 3 collections, messages 12 people, moves 5 records to Approved". "What changes" opens the change report — every field the plan would change (or, for steps that ran, did change), per record, old value → new value — with an Excel download. The report is built for whoever looks at it: a record you cannot read shows as #id with no values, a field you cannot read as (hidden).

"Run later…" approves the plan for a set time. Each minute the ai-plans-scheduled job picks up the due plans; before running, every pending step is rebuilt as you at that moment. If the records a step would act on changed, or a step no longer builds, nothing runs: the plan comes back to you for approval with the new previews and the reason, and you get a notification. Cancel the schedule from the card to approve it again by hand.
When a plan finishes, the person who approved it gets a notification (in-app, plus push or Teams by their own notification rules) with the outcome, the failed step if any, and a link to the plan.

• /ai-plans (Home → AI Plans) lists plans with who approved them and when, their steps, impact and outcome. Everyone sees their own; administrators see every plan. • Undo (administrators): a step that wrote records can be reverted record by record, but only where nothing has changed the record since — its newest revision is still the plan's write and every field still holds the value the plan wrote. Records changed since are named and left alone. Messages, chat posts, flows and tasks cannot be undone. • Make a draft flow (administrators, plans that ran to the end): the steps become flow operations, chained in order, with the records as the same ids, the original filter, or whichever record fired an update event. The flow is created switched off and opens in the tester. Record updates and creates use the new Write Records flow operation, which runs as whoever triggered the flow through the normal record rules. When nobody triggers it (a webhook, a schedule, a system event) it runs only as a 'Run as' person named on the operation — never as the flow's author — and refuses without one; that person must be active, and the collection must be named, not templated. • Templates: ready-made plans for common chores (close out a record's open lines, reassign a leaver's open records, move old drafts to a status, tell the owners of matching records). Fill in the blanks and the usual plan preview appears; nothing runs until you approve. Administrators add their own (blanks + steps as JSON). • Data Integrity: on a run's field + rule filter, "Fix as a plan…" builds the confident fixes for that cluster as a plan, previewed record by record in the change report before approval.
GET  /api/ai/plans?scope=mine|all&status=
GET  /api/ai/plans/:id/changes          (+ /changes.xlsx)
POST /api/ai/plans/:id/schedule         {"run_at": "2026-10-16T21:00:00Z"}
POST /api/ai/plans/:id/unschedule
GET  /api/ai/plans/:id/undo    …

blocks.h: Let AI do this — tasks and support tickets
blocks.t:
The person a task or a support ticket is assigned to can ask AI to do it for them.
