To reach a whole group at once, use @channel in a channel room — it notifies up to 300 members and is limited to the channel’s creator or an admin. Regular @mentions are per-person.

blocks.h: Polls, slash commands and search by meaning
blocks.t:
Type /poll in the composer to ask a room a question: 2–10 options, single or several answers, anonymous votes, and an optional close time. Results update live; when the poll closes (by its author or an admin, or at the close time) a summary line is posted in the room. Anonymous polls show counts only, never who voted.
Typing / lists the commands: /task (on the room’s record or for a person), /remind, /poll and /note (on the record) each open a small form above the box. Extensions add their own with ctx.chat.registerCommand({ name, description, run }); they run as the person typing.
Extensions can also add items to a message’s ⋯ menu (for example “Log to record”) with ctx.chat.registerMessageAction. The menu appears on hover only when an action fits the room and the message; it runs as the person clicking, and anything it posts goes into the room as them.
Chat search also finds messages by meaning, listed after the exact matches and limited to rooms you can see. The room info drawer’s Files and Links tabs are searchable and each link has a Show jump. The @mention picker lists people who are online first.

• Custom emoji: an admin adds images (PNG, GIF, JPEG or WebP, up to 256 KB) under the picker’s Workspace tab and gives each a shortcode. :shortcode: in a message and in a reaction shows the image. A removed emoji shows as its text again. The image files are private to the emoji list, they never appear in the file library for other people. • Drafts: unsent text in a room is saved about a second and a half after you stop typing and appears in another browser or device. Rooms with a draft show a pencil in the list. Sending or emptying the box removes it, and drafts untouched for 30 days are deleted. Attachments and thread replies are not synced. • @channel and @here: in a channel’s settings, choose whether the owner and admins, every member, or only admins may use them. @here still notifies only members who are online, up to 300. • DM time hint: the DM header shows the other person’s local time, from their profile time zone or else the zone their browser reported. While you type outside their working hours (08:00 to 18:00 on weekdays unless they set working_hours in preferences) a quiet note says what time it is for them. • Quiet channels: a channel with no posts for 90 days (Admin > Chat analytics > Channels sets the number, 0 turns it off) sends its owner one notification. The owner sees Archive or Keep open at the top of the channel. Keep restarts the clock. Archived channels stay searchable and can be reopened in their settings. Admins see the waiting and archived lists in the same tab. • Membership history: owners and admins see who joined, left, was added or removed, and by whom, under the members panel. Admins see every channel’s changes in Chat analytics > Channels. GET /api/chat/channels/:id/membership-history and GET /api/chat/admin/membership-history return the same events.

blocks.h: Link cards, request ids, offline sending and long rooms
blocks.t: • Links to dashboards, queues, reports, saved views and custom queries show as a card with the page’s title, what kind of page it is and its description — never its data. The card is built for each reader: someone who cannot open the page sees the plain link. Custom queries are an administrator page, so only administrators get their card. • Paste a request id (the id an error message shows) or a trace id and it shows as a card. Administrators see the route, status, duration, who made it, when, and a link to the request on the Traffic Map (GET /api/chat/request-card?id=). Everyone else only sees that the id names a logged request. An id that names no request stays plain text. • Messages written while you are offline, or while the connection is coming back, wait in your browser and send by themselves when it returns, one at a time and in the order you wrote them. Each carries its own id, so a resend never posts twice. A waiting message can be edited or cancelled; while you edit it, the messages after it in that room wait too. A message that waited more than a day is not sent on its own: it shows Not sent with Retry, Edit and Remove. Signing out clears what is waiting. • Long rooms only draw the messages near the screen once more than 150 are loaded, and load earlier history as you scroll up. Your place is kept when history loads above you or when an image or card above you finishes loading. Link cards load as their message comes near the screen. Jumping to unread messages, a pinned message or a search result still lands on that message.

When Settings names a chat assistant (chat_bot_name), mentioning it in any room asks it a question. It answers with the same permission-checked tools as Ask AI, run as the person who asked.
• The answer is written into the room as it arrives. The person who asked gets a Stop button; what arrived before Stop is posted, marked "(stopped)". The socket event is chat:bot-stream (phases start, delta, status, private, end, error), and POST /api/chat/bot/streams/:id/stop stops it. Only the person who asked can stop it. • In a record’s room the assistant already knows the record. It reads it as the person asking, and if they cannot read it there is no record context. Its record tools default to that record, so "@assistant what’s blocking this?" needs no id. • In a channel, the channel’s name, topic, description and pinned messages are part of the question, so a channel about one program or vendor gets answers about that program or vendor. The assistant treats this text as background, not as instructions. Pinned ops posts are included only in an admin-only ops room. • Who sees the answer is decided before any of it is written. The answer is posted in the room only when everyone who can read the room could read everything it used. In a DM, a private channel or a small role channel (up to 20 other people), every tool call is re-run as each reader and must return the same result. In General, open channels, big role channels and record rooms, only reads of the room’s own record can be checked this way: one reader from every role that can read the collection re-runs each read. Anything else, such as lists, totals, saved queries, your own tasks or extension tools, goes privately to the person who asked. That answer is saved in their conversation with the assistant, the bubble in the room shows "Only you can see this", and the room gets a short notice with no data in it.
To keep answers in the room, ask about the record or name the fields you need. A read of a few fields that every role can see passes the check. A read of every field usually does not.

A huddle is a voice call inside a channel, General or a record’s room, started from the headphones button in the room header. While one runs, the header shows who is in it with a Join button. Once you are in, a strip under the header holds the call: one row of controls (timer, microphone, camera, screen, reactions, hand, notes, add people, a ⋯ menu and Leave), then the people, and any shared screen or cameras. In a narrow chat panel or on a phone, Add people and Raise hand move into the ⋯ menu. The room gets a line when a huddle starts and when it ends. You can open other rooms while you talk — the huddle keeps going and the header says so. You are in a huddle once: joining it from another window, tab or app moves you there, and the window you were in hangs up and says so. Screen sharing offers the tab you are on as well as other tabs, windows and screens. Huddles are not recorded.

• Starting a huddle in a direct message (or a group conversation) calls the other people: each of them gets a call card at the top of the screen with Accept and Decline, a ring with their own notification sound, and a notification through the normal path (category "Huddles & calls" in Profile → Notification rules), so a closed tab still learns of it through push. Under do not disturb the card and the ring are held. Nobody answers in 30 seconds and the room reads "No answer from …"; a Decline reads "… declined the call". The caller sees "Ringing …" in the strip under the header, with a way to stop ringing. Joining the huddle any other way (the Join button, another window) counts as accepting, and answering in one window closes the card in the others. • Add people from the strip while you talk: the picker lists only people who can see that room (the server checks each one), and whoever you pick is called the same way. An invitation never grants access to a room. • While you are in a huddle your presence reads "In a huddle" wherever people are listed (beside any status you set, never instead of it), and notification toasts and sounds are held: the strip shows how many are waiting, and when you leave they are released as one summary with one sound. Turn that off under Profile → Notification rules → "Hold notifications during huddles". The inbox and the badges move either way; a critical notification still breaks through. • Schedule a huddle from the room header’s ⋯ menu: a title, a start, how long, and who to invite (in a direct message the other person is already in). The room gets a card showing the time and the people, with Join while it is on, a calendar file (.ics) and an "Outlook" link that opens a pre-filled event — nothing is written to anyone’s calendar. Five minutes before the start everyone invited gets a reminder; at the start the invitees are called. The organizer or an administrator can cancel it from the card. • Calls have limits so nobody can be flooded: after someone declines, misses or is hung up on, you can call them again after 30 seconds; you can ring the same person at most 5 times in 10 minutes and start at most 6 calls a minute. A call that is not placed tells you who and how long to wait. Leaving and rejoining a huddle within 20 seconds continues the same huddle (no new started or ended line; in a direct message the others are still rung, within the limits above), and a room gets at most 6 started/ended lines in 10 minutes. • One person can have at most 20 upcoming scheduled huddles and schedule at most 10 an hour (cancelled ones count); past that the form says so.
• Audio goes browser to browser (WebRTC). The server only relays the handshake over the chat socket, and checks that you can still see the room on every message of it — lose access mid-call and you drop out. • Share your screen with the screen button in the controls; only one share shows at a time (the first). The browser’s own "Stop sharing" ends it. Browsers without screen capture do not show the button. • Administrators set the STUN/TURN servers under Settings → Huddles, per instance. Nothing configured means no outside server is contacted and people on the same network reach each other directly; add a STUN/TURN server for people on different networks — behind strict firewalls that means a TURN relay (a self-hosted coturn with use-auth-secret is the recommended setup — each person then gets a short-lived credential and the secret never leaves the server). The same page turns huddles off and caps how many people one can hold (default 8). TURN credentials are handed out only for a room the person can see and only while huddles are on; on the coturn side, deny every peer (denied-peer-ip=0.0.0.0-255.255.255.255), allow back only the ranges people connect from (allowed-peer-ip), and set no-tcp-relay, so the relay can never be used to reach internal hosts. After saving, **Test connection** asks the saved servers for a relay from your own browser (nobody is called): "The relay works" proves the server answered, accepted the credential and handed out a relay port from your network. • Hosts that mount no realtime adapter, or browsers without WebRTC, simply never show the button. • A headset badge with a head count appears beside any room that has a huddle running: in the room list, on the Chat button of a record whose room has one, and as "In a huddle in Ops" on a person’s card. You only ever see badges for rooms you can see; a room you cannot open never shows up. • Administrators get a Huddles tab in Chat Analytics: huddles per day, time talking, median length, how many call links ran through the TURN relay, connection failures, average packet loss, the busiest channels and records, and how many huddles are live now. Each browser reports its own call quality when someone leaves, and the server keeps totals per huddle. Nothing records audio or screens. Direct and group huddles are counted but never name a room or a person. Records are kept 180 days. • Under Settings → Huddles, **Server health** shows whether the TURN server is answering. Every 5 minutes the server asks each saved TURN server for a real relay with the credential a browser would get (and each STUN server for its address); the page shows the last result and a day of history, and three failures in a row raise an issue. With a shared secret the credential carries an expiry, so keep its lifetime longer than your longest huddle, because coturn re-checks it when it renews a relay and a long call on the relay can drop after it passes.

Peer to peer, every person in a huddle uploads one audio stream per listener, which stops working past a handful of people. An administrator can add a self-hosted LiveKit media server under Settings → Huddles → Large huddles (address, API key, API secret). Huddles still start peer to peer; the join that takes one past "Move to the media server above" (default 5 people) moves everyone over — each browser then uploads once and the server fans it out. The move takes a moment and nobody hears a gap: the old links stay open for up to three seconds while the new ones come up. A huddle that moved stays on the media server until it ends. With a media server the cap on people per huddle defaults to 25 (up to 100); without one it stays 8 (up to 16).
• Who is in a huddle, mute and share state, and the "started / ended" lines never move: they stay with this instance. The media server carries sound, cameras and shared screens only, and sees rooms by an opaque name (a hash of the room key), never the channel or record name. • Each person gets a five-minute join token minted here, only for a room they can see, only while the huddle is on the media server, and only once they are listed in its huddle. Leaving, dropping out of the roster or losing access to the room also removes the person from the media server straight away, and the media room is closed when the huddle ends — a later huddle in the same room is a new one. The API secret signs those tokens and never leaves the server (it shows masked under Settings). • **Test media server** on the same page lists the server’s rooms with the saved key and secret: a pass proves the address is reachable from this instance and the pair matches. The deploy/livekit folder in the repository holds a compose file, a livekit.yaml template that points LiveKit at the same TURN server as the huddles, and the ports to open (TCP 7880/7881, UDP 50000–60000). • The LiveKit client library downloads only when a huddle first goes large; mesh-only instances never fetch it. • Everything a small huddle does works in a large one: cameras (still the first four live), point and draw on a shared screen, reactions, raised hands, notes, Follow me, mute, switching microphone or speaker, speaking rings, picture-in-picture, ringing and scheduled huddles, and the connection bars with the "your connection is poor" banner. On the media server the marks you draw travel through this instance to the others in the huddle (never stored), and the bars and the banner judge your own link to the media server, since one upload serves everyone. • The media server address must start with wss:// (ws:// only to the same computer) and no address may carry a user name or password; the server never follows a redirect from the media server. In cloud mode the STUN, TURN and media servers are set by the platform (HUDDLE_STUN_URLS, HUDDLE_TURN_URLS, HUDDLE_LIVEKIT_URL): Settings → Huddles shows them but cannot change them, and with none set the server health and media server tests answer that they are not available here.

• Whoever is talking gets a green ring around their picture in the huddle strip, and the strip moves the most recent speaker to the front (at most every 2 seconds, so it does not jump around). With reduced motion turned on in your system, the ring stays still instead of pulsing. When you talk into a muted microphone, the strip says so. • The small arrow beside the microphone button picks your microphone and, in browsers that allow it (Chrome, Edge), your speaker. The bar under the microphone moves as you talk; **Test speaker** plays a short chime. Noise suppression, echo cancellation and automatic volume can be turned off there. Changes apply straight away without dropping the call, and your choices are remembered in this browser. • To check your microphone before joining, use the small arrow next to the huddle button: it shows the same choices and level bar with a **Join huddle** button. The huddle button itself still joins in one click. • Plug in a headset during a huddle and the call moves onto it ("Switched to …"); unplug the microphone you are using and it falls back to the default one. • Each person in the strip has four connection bars; hover them for the delay, packet loss, jitter, whether the connection is direct or goes through the relay, and the bitrate. When your own connection has been poor for 10 seconds (more than 5 % loss or over 400 ms delay to everyone), the strip says "Your connection is poor". While you share your screen, a poor link to someone gets a lighter version of your screen until it recovers, so your voice stays clear.
Shortcut (while in a huddle) | Action / Hold Space | Talk while muted (push to talk); letting go mutes again / M | Mute or unmute / Shift+S | Share your screen, or stop sharing / L | Leave the huddle (press it twice while you are sharing) / ? | Show the shortcut list next to the controls
Shortcuts never fire while you are typing in a field. Space on another button presses that button as usual; on the huddle controls it is push to talk. Switching to another window or tab while holding Space mutes you again.

blocks.h: Reactions, raised hands, camera, marks and the mini-player
blocks.t: • Reactions: the smiley button in the huddle strip opens six emoji. The one you pick floats up over the strip for everyone in the huddle, with your name under it. You can send one a second. • Raise hand: the hand button puts you in the queue, which the strip shows in the order hands went up. Click it again (or the × on your name) to lower yours. Anyone in the huddle can use **Lower all** — there is no host. • Camera: the camera button in the controls turns your camera on (it is off when you join). People with their camera on show as tiles in the strip — one, two side by side or a 2×2 grid, and a sideways strip on a narrow screen; your own tile is mirrored. Only the first four cameras turned on are sent: a fifth sees "Video paused to keep the call smooth" on their own tile, and their video starts by itself when someone turns theirs off. • Point and draw: over a screen someone shares, the small tool strip lets you point, draw or drop an arrow; everyone in the huddle sees your marks in your own colour, and the person sharing sees them on their preview with "2 people are pointing". Marks fade after four seconds; the eraser clears every mark on that screen. Press Esc or click the tool again to stop. Marks go browser to browser and never through the server. • Mini-player: in Chrome and Edge **Pop out a mini-player** in the strip’s ⋯ menu opens a small window that stays on top of other windows and apps, with who is here (and who is speaking), the timer, mute, leave and a thumbnail of a shared screen. It keeps going when you close the chat panel or open another room; closing it changes nothing, and leaving the huddle closes it. The first time you switch away from the tab during a huddle, coming back offers it once — **Every time** makes the browser pop it out by itself whenever you leave the tab. Other browsers do not show the menu item.

While you are in a huddle, the notes button in the huddle strip opens one shared note for everyone in the call. Anyone in the huddle can type in it; changes reach the others about half a second after you stop typing, and if two people type at once the last change wins. **Preview** shows it with the same formatting as chat messages (bold, italic, lists, code). Notes are written by hand — nothing is transcribed.
• When the huddle ends, a note that is not empty is posted to the room as one message headed "Huddle notes · 24 min · written by Ana and Ben" — sent as the person who edited it last, under the room’s normal posting rules, and only when everyone who wrote in it may post in that room. Then the room gets the end line with how long it ran and everyone who joined ("Huddle ended after 24 min · Ana, Ben and Chris"). • If any writer may not post in the room (an announcement channel, for example), the notes are not posted: the end line says why, and the last person to leave gets a **Copy notes** offer. The notes stay available for about two minutes, only to the people who were in that huddle; a new huddle in the room starts with an empty note. • A note holds up to 20 KB. It lives only as long as the huddle; if every browser drops out without leaving, it is gone with the huddle. • Only people in the huddle receive the note, and the server checks on every change that you can still see the room.

In a huddle in a record’s room, **Follow me** (in the strip’s ⋯ menu) makes everyone else’s page follow yours on that record: they are taken to the record, and when you change tab or scroll to another section their page does the same. A chip at the bottom of their screen says "Following Ana" with **Stop**; going to another page or picking another tab themselves also stops following, and **Follow** on the chip picks it up again.
• Only one person presents at a time. While someone does, the menu item reads **Ask to present**: the presenter sees the request on their chip and can **Hand over** or **Keep presenting**. The presenter leaving the huddle ends it for everyone. • Following is only navigation. Each person sees the record with their own permissions — someone who cannot read it gets the usual not-found page — and only the record the room is about can be followed (the server names it, not the presenter’s browser). • Follow me stays on the one record and its tabs; it does not follow into related records or other pages.
A screen clip is a short recording — up to 60 seconds of your screen and microphone — made from the clapperboard button in the composer and sent like any other attachment. The button becomes the clock while it records; Stop, the 60 s mark or the browser’s "Stop sharing" ends it. The clip arrives with a poster frame and plays inline in the message. It is an ordinary file in the file manager (tagged chat-clip), not a help video.

Prevent simultaneous editing conflicts with soft item locks. When a user opens a record for editing, a 5-minute TTL lock is acquired. Other users attempting to edit see an amber banner and the form switches to read-only. Locks auto-release after 5 minutes without activity, preventing stale locks from crashed tabs.

The record form keeps a copy of your unsaved work in the browser (IndexedDB, per record and per user): the fields you changed, staged grid rows, edits and removals, and staged relation links — written about a second after each change and removed the moment the form is clean, saved, or you discard it. If the tab crashes, the session expires or you navigate away, the next time you open that record (or the new-record form for that collection) a banner offers "Restore your unsaved changes from N min ago" with the diff (field: was → will be) and staged counts; nothing is applied until you choose Restore. A draft whose values now match the saved record is dropped silently, and the banner flags when the record changed underneath the draft. On a new-record form only the fields you actually touched are kept — layout defaults and prefills are not treated as your work.

• User opens item editor → client POSTs to acquire lock • Lock created in nivaro_item_locks with 5-minute TTL • Client heartbeat endpoint called every 2.5 minutes to refresh TTL • On close/navigate away, lock is deleted via DELETE • If lock already held, acquiring user gets 409 Conflict with holder info • After 5 minutes of no heartbeat, lock auto-expires

Locking can be enabled/disabled per collection in Data Model → (collection) → Settings → "Item locking". Default is ON.
GET /api/item-locks/config/:collection
  # { item_locking_enabled: boolean }

PATCH /api/item-locks/config/:collection
  # { item_locking_enabled: false } — admin only
  # Disabling immediately releases all active locks

• Amber banner: "Being edited by Sarah Chen (expires in 4 min 30 sec)" • Form switches to read-only when locked by someone else • Admin sees "Take over" button in banner to force-acquire lock • Heartbeat interval: 2.5 minutes; TTL: 5 minutes (prevents stale locks) • If disabled returns true, all lock UI is suppressed silently

The presence feature tracks all users currently viewing a record (not just editing). It is powered by Socket.io room subscriptions and appears as a list of avatars in the item header.
GET /api/presence/:collection/:item
  # Returns list of users currently viewing

{
  "viewers": [
    {
      "user_id": "user-123",
      "name": "Sarah Chen",
      "avatar_url": "...",
      "viewing_since": "2026-06-15T10:15:00Z",
     …
Presence uses Socket.io — updates are real-time. Presence data is NOT persisted; it reflects active connections only.

An open record keeps up with what other people and automations do to it, without a reload. The server only says THAT something changed (record id and field names, never values); each panel then re-reads through its own permission-checked request, so nobody sees a value they could not already open.

When | What you see / Someone else moves the record | The state badge, pipeline panel and transition buttons refresh, and a toast says who moved it where ("Kim moved this to Finance Review"). / Owners change (owner matrix, delegation, out of office, team membership) | The owners chip and approval chain refresh. / Someone else deletes the record | A banner says the record was deleted and saving is turned off. Administrators, and whoever deleted it, also see who and when, and get a Restore button when they have create permission. / Your access changes (role, policy, row filter, User Scope, subtree grant) | The page re-reads the record as you. If you can no longer see it, the form is cleared — its values, history, comments and any unsaved edits leave the screen and the page’s cache — and only "You no longer have access to this record" with a Back button remains. / An addendum is created, submitted, approved or rejected | The record’s addendum view refreshes, and list/queue addendum badges follow. / Comments or tasks are added or closed | The record’s comments and tasks refresh; open-task counts on collection lists and queues, and comment counts on grid rows, update in place. / A partner push lands, fails or is acknowledged | The Integrations chip and its dialog refresh. / The after-save integrity check finishes | The integrity banner (or the Summary-mode field marks) refresh at once. / Fields change while you are in Summary mode | The values refresh and the ones that moved briefly highlight. / The history panel is open | New changes appear at the top, marked New. / A flow run is working on the record | A banner names the flow ("Automation is updating this record") until the run ends. / The same record is open with unsaved changes in another tab of your browser | A banner warns you before you edit here too, with a button that asks the other tab to come forward (browsers may only flag its title).
Your own saves never echo back as "someone else": writes this tab sent are recognised for a few seconds and skipped.

Event | Room | Payload / collection:update | collection:<name> | {collection, item, action?, changed_fields?}. A notice with no action whose fields are all $ names ($state, $addendums, $comments, $tasks, $integrations) says a related surface moved, not the record’s columns. / record:integrity | record:<collection>:<id> | {collection, item} / record:automation | record:<collection>:<id> | {collection, item, flow_id, flow_name, state: start|end} / owners:changed | the tenant (cloud: t:<tenant>:all; self-hosted: every socket) — coalesced 5 s, at most one per 15 s | {at} / access:changed | the tenant for an administrator’s access write; only the person’s own sockets for their own scope pick — coalesced | {at}
GET /api/trash/record?collection=&item= answers the latest deletion of one record (deleted_at, deleted_by_name, can_restore, and trash_id only when you may restore it) — to an unrestricted administrator or to the person who deleted it. Everyone else gets { "data": null }, the same answer as "not deleted": the trash snapshot cannot be checked against your row filter or User Scopes.

blocks.h: Queries that say what they read

blocks.t:
Readiness, the Issue log, the Support desk, Team pages and the person page team-load card, My Work, the Delegation console and Broadcast receipts refresh on their own when what they show changes. The server sends one small ops:changed {topic} event to a topic room; the page re-reads through its normal permission-checked route. A poke never names a row, a person or a value, and a burst of writes is one poke.
Topic | Who may join | What moves it / readiness | Administrators | A finished run of the checks (the report rides the event, so other open pages show it without re-running) and a fix finishing / issues | Signed-in users | Any write to the issue log: new issues appear at the top, occurrence counts tick / issue:<id> | Administrators | Each new occurrence of that issue: the person (id), route and build, streamed into the open issue / support | Signed-in users | Tickets, claims, replies and status moves / team | Signed-in users | Owner changes, tasks, SLA acknowledgements and escalations / my-work | Signed-in users | Owner changes, tasks, approvals; new notifications arrive on your own room. New rows highlight briefly / delegation | Signed-in users | Out-of-office, delegate and owner-seat changes / broadcasts | Administrators | Deliveries, acknowledgements and notifications being read
import { useLiveOps, useFreshIds } from '@nivaro/shared'

// Refetch when the topic pokes (inert without a host realtime adapter):
useLiveOps('support', () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['support-tickets'] }))

// A short hig…
Writes are noticed at the database driver (the same seam that signals "who owns what changed"), so raw SQL, procedures and imports poke the pages too. Pages keep a slow safety poll in case an event is missed.

A dashboard or report widget on screen asks the server to watch it. When someone saves a record in a collection the widget reads, the server works the widget out again — at most once every 10 seconds per widget — as YOU, with your role, row filters and User Scopes, and sends the new figure to your screen only. Nobody else’s figure ever reaches you, and yours never reaches them.
Widget | How it refreshes / Report: KPI, charts, tables, pivots, heatmaps, movers, KPI groups, …; dashboard: count, sum, average, latest rows, charts, saved view | Pushed when its data changes. Its own refresh interval drops to a 5-minute safety net. / Query widgets (raw SQL), AI insight, narrative, calc formulas, metric catalog, queue stats | Unchanged: the widget keeps its refresh interval.
• You must still be able to open the dashboard or report AND read every collection the widget reads; when that stops being true the push ends and the widget goes back to its normal refresh. • Every widget — pushed or polled, on a dashboard, a report, a public dashboard link or a record page — reads as the person viewing it: their read permission on each collection, their row filters and User Scopes, and only fields their role can read. A widget built on a field you cannot read shows "Forbidden" instead of a figure; a public dashboard link shows what its creator can see. A "latest rows" widget reads only its configured columns (Columns on the widget; without them it shows the record title, and nothing on a public link). On record-page rollups and review lists, values and labels from related records you cannot open stay blank. • After a lost connection the widget refreshes once when it is back, then pushing resumes. • Recomputes are capped per server (WIDGET_LIVE_MAX_PER_MIN, default 300 a minute); a widget over the cap catches up in the next minute.
socket → widgets:watch   { watches: [{ key, kind: 'report'|'dashboard', widget, report?, params? }] }
server → widget:watching { accepted: [key], refused: [{ key, reason }] }   reason: not-live | forbidden | not-found | busy
server → widget…
Hosts built on @nivaro/shared get this from useLiveWidget({ kind, widget, report, params, onData }), which returns whether the push is on; liveWidgetInterval(live, ms) gives the poll to keep meanwhile.

Long actions you start show their progress where you are, and pages that other people keep open hear about changes that matter to them. Every notice carries ids, counts and field names only — never values — and the page re-reads through its own permission-checked request.

Bulk runs, backfills, staged imports, background exports and PDFs you started appear in a tray at the bottom of every page: a progress line while they run, then the result with a link to the details or a Download chip for the file. The tray follows you across pages and browser tabs until you dismiss an entry (Clear finished dismisses them all). It is yours alone — nobody else sees what you started, and an administrator’s tray shows their own work; the Jobs console is the place for everyone’s.
Action | How it gets into the tray / Bulk write (async) | POST /items/:collection/bulk?async=1 — a job run with live done/total. / Staged import | Queued → "3rd in line, about 4 minutes" (moves up as the runs ahead finish) → running with its stage → result. / Export | Export menu → a preset’s Background button (POST /export-presets/:id/run-async). The finished file is a Download chip. / PDF | POST /pdf-templates/:id/render-async — renders as the caller (record and child rows read with their access) and saves the PDF to the file library. / Slow query or widget | "Run in background" on a custom query, report widget, page widget or dashboard widget that is known to be slow — see below. / Anything else started with a user | Any job run started with a user and not by the scheduler.

When a custom query, report widget, page widget or dashboard widget has been loading for a few seconds and is known to be slow (its usual run is 4 seconds or more; anything still loading after 8 seconds counts too), the loading area offers "Run in background". The server then runs the same request as you, on its background connection pool, so your permissions and User Scopes apply exactly as they would on the page, and a cached query or widget stores the result under its usual key. The page shows how long it has been running against how long it usually takes; you can leave, and the Jobs tray says when it is ready and links back. Back on the page, the result appears without asking again. Anyone can use it, not only administrators; each person may have 3 runs going at once, and asking the same question twice joins the first run.
GET  /api/background-runs/estimate?method=POST&url=/custom-queries/:slug/execute
POST /api/background-runs   {method, url, body?, label?, href?}  → 202 {data: run}
GET  /api/background-runs/:id          → your run (another person's id is 40…

A queued staged import waits for the running import of its lock group (its staging table) and for the runs queued before it. The estimate adds each run ahead’s typical time — the median of that definition’s last 10 completed runs; a running one counts what is left. GET /staged-imports/queue returns it (administrators see all queued runs, anyone else the ones they queued); the Import Console shows it in the Status column and the live banner.

blocks.h: Import in progress on a record
blocks.t: While a staged import writes a record through the items service, its change events carry source: "import". A form open on that record shows "An import is updating this record" and refreshes the changed fields; the notice lapses 8 seconds after the last import write. Imports that run a stored procedure write outside the items service and are announced when they finish instead.

The bulk bar, registry bulk actions and queue bulk actions send ?progress=<id>; each selected row shows a spinner while the run is on it, then a tick, a dash (already there) or the reason it was refused — in the list and in queues — instead of one toast at the end. The events go only to the person who ran the action.

• **Announcements** — a banner or broadcast that goes live, is edited, ends or is deleted reaches open tabs at once (announcements:changed); the viewer’s audience rules are still applied when the tab re-reads /announcements/active. The 1-minute poll remains the fallback while the socket is down (and catches a window that simply elapsed). • **Feature flags** — toggling a flag sends flags:changed; open tabs re-read /feature-flags/mine immediately, so a flag turned off for a misbehaving feature takes effect within seconds. • **Form definitions** — editing a layout, field, field rule or pipeline sends config:update (naming the collection when the edit does). An open record form on that collection says "This form was changed. Reload to see the new version"; what was typed is kept by the draft store and offered back after the reload. • **Stored roll-ups** — recalculating a stored roll-up announces the parent record’s changed field, so open forms, lists and queues refresh the figure.

A flow step (refresh-pages) that announces records changed — collection, ids, changed field names — after the flow wrote them raw or through a partner. It uses the same broadcast as items-service writes (coalesced; over 100 ids become one "some records changed" event). Options: collection, items (comma list or {{ids}}; blank = some records changed), changed_fields, action. System collections are refused.
Hosts that mount the shared components wire the socket in with relayLiveEvent(event, payload) for job:progress, bulk:rows, announcements:changed and flags:changed (admin does this in lib/socket.ts) and mount <JobsTray /> once inside a client + navigation provider.

blocks.h: Saving while the network is down
blocks.t:
When you press Save on a record and the request never reaches the server (no connection, or the gateway says the server is unreachable), the change is kept in an outbox on this browser and the record shows "Will save when you are back online". When the connection returns it is sent against the version of the record you were editing. A refusal from the server (a validation error, missing permission) is never queued — it shows as it always does.
Situation | What happens / Nobody else changed those fields meanwhile | The change saves on its own and a toast says so. Other tabs showing the record refresh. / Someone else changed one of the same fields | Nothing is overwritten. The record opens the merge dialog (their value or yours, per field); if the record was closed, a toast offers Review and the dialog opens when you open the record. / The record form is still open | It sends the whole save again — lines and links included — when the connection returns. / You sign out | Every pending offline save on the browser is cleared. / Someone else signs in on the same browser | Every pending offline save that is not theirs is deleted at once — a shared device never keeps your values for the next person, and nobody else ever sees or sends them. / A save waits more than a week | It is dropped, and you get a one-time note: "an unsaved change from <date> was discarded". / You are in a "View as" tab | Nothing is queued: a save that cannot reach the server shows the normal error. Leaving View as also clears anything stored under the person being viewed.
New records are not queued: if the answer to a create was lost the record may already exist, and sending it again would create a second one.

The pop-out button in a record’s header tools opens the record in its own window, without the navigation sidebar, for side-by-side work on two screens. Popping the same record out again brings its window forward. The window is an ordinary signed-in page: nothing secret is put in its address.
• It stays live like any open record: who else is viewing, other people’s changes, moves, comments and the edit lock. • It stays in step with your main window: a save in either one refreshes the other, and unsaved edits in one are flagged in the other. • The edit lock follows you: closing the record in one window does not leave the other editing unlocked — it takes the lock straight back. • From a "View as" tab, the pop-out opens as the same person being viewed; your own tabs are never mixed with it.
Headless hosts: openRecordPopout(href, collection, id) and isRecordPopout() from @nivaro/shared (the URL gains ?popout=1 so the host can hide its chrome), and <RecordOutboxHost userId onOpenRecord /> mounted once so offline saves replay from any page. Call clearRecordOutbox() on sign-out.

Collection lists, queues and their calendar, Gantt, map and kanban views keep up with what other people do. The server only says THAT a record changed (its id, the field names and who wrote it, never values); every list then re-reads through its own permission-checked request, so nobody sees a record or value they could not already open.

When | What happens / Someone else changes a row on your page | The row briefly highlights (no highlight if you have reduced motion on). Hover it for "Changed by Beth just now". / A record is created, or edited so that it now matches your filters | It slides in at the top of page 1, marked with a cyan dot. The server decides whether it belongs, as you — a record you cannot see never appears. / A visible record stops matching your filters, or is deleted | The row is removed and the total drops. Changes on other pages count into the "N updates · Refresh" pill instead. / Someone is editing a record | A lock icon appears on its row with their name on hover, from the same edit locks as the record page. Only locks on records you can read are shown. / Queue totals, SLA breaches and at-risk counts | The stat tiles re-count shortly after records move, instead of on the next refresh. Queue rows that changed refresh and flash; the table does not reshuffle while rows are selected or a card is being dragged. / Kanban cards (queues) | Cards move to their new state column when anyone moves a record or its state changes. / Saved view pills | Each pill shows how many records match the view right now, counted as you, and re-counts as records change. / Calendar, Gantt and map views | Records others add, move or reschedule appear in place without a flash.

The focus button in a list or queue toolbar holds live updates back. While it is on, changes collect and are applied together every 1, 3, 5 or 10 minutes (click the interval to change it); a "12 updates" pill applies them at once, and switching focus mode off applies them immediately. The setting is kept in this browser. Notifications are not part of the list feed and still arrive at once.

• collection:update now also carries by (the writer’s user id) when a person made the change; system writes omit it. Clients still ignore their own writes. • POST /api/item-locks/:collection/active {ids} (signed in) returns [{item, locked_by, locked_by_name, is_mine}] for the records in ids that are locked and that the caller can read through the items service. Collections with locking off, and system tables, return nothing. • A lock taken or released sends a payload-free $lock notice on the collection feed (LIVE_ASPECTS.lock). • In @nivaro/shared: useRowChanges, useRowLocks / useRowLocksByCollection, viewerMatches, useLiveQueryRefresh (query-backed views) and FocusModeToggle / deliverLive for focus mode. useLiveCollection(…, { focusable: true }) holds its batches while focus mode is on.

The operations screens, and help videos, follow what is happening without a reload. As with live records, the server only says THAT something moved (ids, counts and field names — never values); each screen re-reads through its own permission-checked request. A slow poll stays underneath as the safety net, so a screen is never worse off when the socket is down.
Screen | What moves on its own / Data Integrity — Form conformance | A running sweep shows a progress bar per collection (records checked of the table’s size, issues so far) and its findings appear in the run as the sweep goes. Sweeps started by someone else or by the nightly schedule appear too. / Jobs | Running jobs, next-run countdowns and each job’s last outcome update as jobs start and finish. Open the arrow on a run to see its log lines and progress as the job writes them (kept for a day). / Header (administrators) | While a heavy job, bulk run, render or import is running, a pill reads "System busy: nightly reforecast running, about 12 minutes left". The estimate is the median of that job’s last completed runs; with no history it only says "running". Click it to open Jobs. / Help videos | A video that was "getting ready" starts playing by itself when its render completes. While you watch, a newer published version is offered with a Switch button that keeps your place in the recording where the new cut allows. The Videos button’s required count follows publishes and requirement changes. A viewer’s question shows the author’s reply as soon as it is posted, and authors see new questions arrive.

blocks.h: Live surfaces and the socket inspector
blocks.t: • Notes: comment edits, deletes and reactions (on comments and on recorded notes), plus machine entries (transitions, partner events, import runs, change reasons), refresh in an open record as they happen. The notice carries the $comments aspect only; each viewer re-reads the thread as themselves. • Tasks: assigning, claiming, editing, completing and deleting a task refresh the record's Tasks section ($tasks). • Record chips in chat and linked record tokens update their state pill when the record moves. No state name travels in the notice; each viewer re-reads the pill with their own access. • Queue item sheets follow their record (state, comments) the way the full record page does; drill sheets rendered by the record form already did. • A record open in a drill-down sheet counts as open: the sheet joins the record room, so the people on that record see the viewer, and its strip shows who else has it open. • Realtime console, Sockets and rooms, Inspect: pick a connected client to see its rooms and the last 100 events sent to it (name, room, size, time, never the payload). Recording is off until an administrator opens the panel and stops when it closes or after 10 minutes unread. Routes (administrators only, caller's tenant only): GET|POST|DELETE /realtime/sockets/:id/inspect. • The inspector also lists the events the client sent, with how long the server took to handle each one, and how many bytes are waiting to reach that client.

Realtime console → Socket health shows every API server at once (each one reports through Redis every 10 seconds): bytes waiting to be sent, the clients with the most waiting, the biggest rooms, waiting bytes over the last 10 minutes, how long each socket event handler takes (p50, p95, slowest, and the longest stretch one call kept the server busy), and how often a connected client caught up a room after missing an event. Route: GET /realtime/health (administrators only, your tenant only).
• Slow clients: once more than SOCKET_BUFFER_SOFT_BYTES (default 1 MB) is waiting to reach a client, it stops getting each room event. When it has caught up it gets one realtime:stale {rooms} and reloads what those rooms show. • Past SOCKET_BUFFER_HARD_BYTES (default 8 MB) the client is disconnected and its queued events dropped, so one slow client cannot hold server memory. When that tab reconnects it reloads its lists and records instead of replaying (catchup:full {reason: "slow-consumer"}). • Missed events while connected: journaled events carry the room they went to (_room) and that room’s own counter (_rseq). A client that sees the counter skip asks for that room alone (catchup:room {room, cursor, missed} → catchup:room:events {room, full, events}) instead of reloading everything. The admin app and createSocketRealtime both do this.
Binary socket frames (msgpack) were measured against JSON with per-message compression on the realtime message mix and not adopted: compressed, msgpack sent about 5% more bytes, and encoding and decoding took about twice as long.

blocks.h: Turning live updates down for one collection
blocks.t: Table Editor → Settings → Collection Browser → Live updates (browser_config.live_events): Every change (default), Batched (changes gathered for 2 seconds and sent as one list of ids) or Off (no live record events, no journal entry, no cross-server stream; lists on the collection refresh every 30 seconds instead). Use Off for import staging tables and other high-churn rows nobody watches live. Other API servers pick up a change within 30 seconds.

sections.label: Presence, Do Not Disturb & Tab Sync

blocks.h: Presence, Do Not Disturb & Tab Sync
blocks.t: Small live signals tell you who else is on the thing you are working on, and your own state follows you across tabs and devices. They carry names only, never content, and only reach people who could already open the same record, ticket or page.

You see | Where | Who sees it / "Beth is writing a note" | Under the Notes thread while someone has an unsent note | Everyone viewing that record (the record read gate, row filters and User Scopes included) / "Kim is approving" | A pill on the pipeline panel while someone has a transition confirm or requirements dialog open | Everyone viewing that record. The repeat-transition guard still refuses a second move; this warns before it happens. / "Kim is looking at this" | A support ticket sheet, and an issue row in the Issue log | People who can open the ticket (requester, assignee, its team, administrators); anyone signed in for an issue / "Kim is replying" | Above a support ticket reply box while someone is typing a reply | People who can open the ticket / Online, idle or away, and the page | A person’s page header and their user card | The same people the chat Online list shows: a person restricted to other zones or regions does not see presence outside their own scopes, and the page follows the Presence display setting
A signal is a heartbeat: the sender repeats it every four seconds while it is true and receivers let it lapse after seven, so a closed tab never leaves a stale "is typing". Typing relays through the record room (record:signal), ticket and issue pages through a topic room (ops:ticket:<id>, ops:issue-view:<id>) whose join is gated like the page and re-checked when access changes.
Event | Room | Payload / record:signal | record:<collection>:<id> (sender must already be in it) | {collection, item, kind: note|transition, state: start|stop, user: {id, name}} / ops:changed with viewers | ops:ticket:<id>, ops:issue-view:<id> | {topic, viewers: [{id, name}]} / ops:changed with signal | ops:ticket:<id> | {topic, signal: {kind: reply, state, user}}, sent from the client with ops:signal

Turn it on from the avatar menu or the chat Online tab, for 30 minutes, an hour, four hours, until tomorrow morning, or until you switch it off. While it is on, toasts and sounds are held on every tab and device, and a red mark shows on your avatar (colleagues see it on your people page while you are online). Notifications still land in your inbox and the badge still counts them. Critical notifications (the Critical lane) still break through with their toast and sound. It is stored as preferences.dnd = {until} through PATCH /users/me/preferences (null turns it off) and syncs live, so ending it in one tab ends it everywhere.

Under a note that mentions someone, a line says whether they have seen it. A mention counts as seen once the person opens the record or reads the mention’s notification after the note was written; both come from watermarks the app already keeps (nivaro_record_views, nivaro_notifications.read_at), so nothing new is tracked. GET /api/comments adds seen_at to each mention, only for readers who can open that very record. Open thread views update the moment the person opens the record.

blocks.h: Your tabs and devices stay in step

blocks.t: List rows in the collection browser and in queues show who else has that record open right now: up to three small avatars where the unseen dot usually sits (the browser) or after the label (queues), "+N" when more people are there, and the names in the tooltip. It arrives live through the presence room — a list tells the server which rows it shows (presence:watch) and hears presence:rows whenever a record's viewers change — instead of the old 30 second count poll, which remains the fallback for a host without a realtime adapter. Your own tabs are never counted. Only people you may see as people (the same rule as the Online tab) get a face and a name; the rest count towards the number.

With several tabs open, one browser used to hold one live connection per tab (plus one per open record page). Now every tab of an app attaches to one SharedWorker, served by the API at /api/realtime/worker.js, which owns the single connection: it signs in once, keeps the union of every tab's rooms (a room is joined when the first tab needs it and left when the last one goes), runs one catch-up after a reconnect, routes each collection, record and chat room's events to the tabs that hold it, and reports the tab you used last as your current page. Tabs talk to it through createWorkerSocket (@nivaro/react), which looks like a socket.io socket, so chat, presence and every live surface work unchanged.
• Fallbacks are automatic: no SharedWorker (Safari before 16), a "View as" tab, an API on another origin, a worker that does not answer, speaks another protocol version or goes silent, or a worker whose socket cannot connect while the API answers HTTP — the tab opens its own socket and the older leader-tab relay (one tab carries the noisy rooms over a BroadcastChannel) takes over. • Off switches: REALTIME_SHARED_WORKER=off on the server (the script answers 404), or localStorage.setItem('nvr-realtime-worker', 'off') in one browser. /realtime lists shared-worker connections with the shared_worker flag in their hello. • A new release is picked up by the next worker start; a running worker lives until its last tab closes, and a tab meeting a worker from another protocol version simply uses its own socket.
Everything here is best effort and per server node, like the viewer avatars: with several API replicas a viewer list may show only the people connected to the same node.

Beyond the bell dropdown, the /notifications page is a full paginated inbox of every notification — filter by status, jump to the related record, and mark all as read in one click.
• Paginated list with sender, subject, message, and relative timestamp. • Click a notification to open its collection/item; it is marked read automatically. • "Mark all read" clears the unread counter everywhere (bell included).

Every notification sits in one of three lanes. Critical (SLA escalations, maintenance, failing monitors — they bypass every mute and quiet hour), Needs you (something asks THIS person to act: a task, an approval, an access request, a mention, an SLA clock, a record they currently own moving state, any row with an inline action), and FYI (everything else). The bell badge counts only the first two — FYI rows sit in the inbox without pulling the eye; the badge turns red while a Critical row is unread. The bell offers Needs you / FYI / All tabs, the Notifications page a lane strip (Critical / Needs you / FYI) beside the unread/read/snoozed filters. Lanes are stamped at write time (ownership resolved once, per recipient); rows from before lanes existed were backfilled from their subject and kind.
GET /api/notifications/unread-count
→ { "unread": 7, "attention": 3, "lanes": { "critical": 1, "needs_you": 2, "fyi": 4 } }

GET /api/notifications?lane=attention|critical|needs_you|fyi&category=workflow

blocks.h: Delivery status — where did this go?
blocks.t: Each inbox row shows small chips per channel: In-app (landed / skipped and why), Push (sent · time / no browser registered / held by quiet hours or the matrix / failed), Email (sent · time / held for your daily summary / off for the category / dropped by mail test mode / no address / failed with the SMTP reason) and SMS. The email chip links to the mail-log row that recorded the send. Hover any chip for the reason — the same reason the test bench simulator would give. The record is written by notifyUser as each channel reports back (delivery on GET /notifications); rows from older writers carry only the in-app chip.

A chat mention offers Reply — an inline box that posts straight back into the room. A mention in a record note offers Reply onto the record's thread. A workflow-transition notification offers "Comment on this", which adds a note to the record (the row stays unread; commenting is not acknowledging). Reply actions are server-declared like every inline action (actions[].input names the field the box fills) so hosts stay domain-blind; the normal permissions apply — posting on a record needs create rights on its collection.

A flow "Send notification" step (Needs acknowledgement), or an extension passing ack_required: true to notifyUser, marks a notice as needing an explicit Acknowledge. It shows an Acknowledge button in the bell and the notification center, stays pinned above the lists until acknowledged (reading it does not count), reminds by push after 4 hours and tells the recipient's manager after 24 hours. The sender sees who has and has not acknowledged in the Sent view.

In the notification center: select rows (or everything matching a filter) to mark read, snooze, archive or open their records in tabs; "Archive everything read and older than N days" in one action, or turn on automatic clean-up. Archived notifications stay searchable under the Archived filter. In Profile > Notification rules: pick a sound per category (or none) on top of the global sound; a card suggests muting categories you mostly never open, with undo; and every rule change shows what last week would have looked like (in-app, push and email counts) replayed through the same delivery decision the sender uses.

blocks.h: Channel fallback chain (if it stays unread)
blocks.t:
Snooze: a notification can sleep for an hour, until tomorrow 8am, until next week — or, when it is about a record, until the record changes. "Until the record changes" wakes it the moment someone else writes a field on that record or moves it to another pipeline state (your own edits do not wake it); it returns unread in the inbox and the bell. POST /api/notifications/:id/snooze with { "until": "<iso>" }, { "until_change": true }, or { "until": null } to wake it now.
Profile → Notification rules → "If it stays unread": per category, how long an in-app notification may sit unread before it climbs to a browser push, then to an email — one notification escalating channels, stopping the moment it is read or snoozed. Each step fires once, and a channel that already delivered the row at send time is not repeated (an email sent immediately is never re-sent as an escalation). Only rows from the last 7 days are considered, so switching the rule on does not replay an old inbox. Runs every 5 minutes (notification-escalation cron); the escalation shows as an extra chip on the row.
PATCH /api/users/me/preferences
{ "notification_prefs": { "escalation": { "workflow": { "push_after_min": 60, "email_after_min": 240 } } } }

Profile → Notification rules is one matrix over the notification categories (mentions, workflow & approvals, SLA & escalations, field watches, alerts, anomaly detections, reports, system & digests, everything else) with three channels per row: In-app (the bell inbox row), Push (browser push to your registered devices), and Email. The "?" badge on each column header explains that channel, and the one beside each category name lists what that category covers.
• Email per category is Individual email (sent as it happens, deferred only during your quiet hours), Daily summary (held and delivered once in the daily action summary), or No email (dropped — the in-app row still lands). • Precedence with a subscription's own delivery setting: the subscription is the more specific one and wins. A subscription set to Instantly emails as it happens even when its category is on Daily summary (No email and quiet hours still apply); a subscription on Daily or Weekly summary rides the daily action summary at your delivery hour (weekly on Mondays), and items from a category set to No email are left out of it. There is one morning email — the old separate "daily digest" is folded into the action summary. • The Daily action summary block on the same card sets the delivery hour (Eastern time), a compact layout, and a "send me a test summary now" button. Anyone with at least one category on Daily summary receives the digest. • Critical subjects (SLA escalations, maintenance notices, failing monitors) always email immediately regardless of the matrix. • The legacy Profile → Email delivery card is gone; its instant/daily toggle maps onto the "All email" quick buttons. • Notifications & alerts (the sources list below the rules) shows, under every source, whether it fires on an event or on a schedule — and the schedule in words ("Scheduled · At 08:00 AM, only on Monday"), read from the live cron roster so an overridden schedule reads correctly. • Every email leaves through the same sender, so cron-driven mail (scheduled reports, report and view digests, alert checks, anomaly sweeps, SLA escalations, coverage notices, flow mail ops) follows the same rules. Senders pass an explicit category; a flow mail op can set category in its options.
PATCH /api/users/me/preferences
{ "notification_prefs": { "matrix": { "workflow": { "inapp": true, "push": false, "email": "daily" } } } }

Unread rows that name the same record fold into one bell entry — "3 things on REQ-1042" — with the categories as chips and the most urgent lane colouring the row. The chevron expands the rows (each keeps its own actions), clicking the bundle opens the record, and the check marks the whole bundle read in one call. The Notifications page does the same behind "Group by record" (on by default). GET /api/notifications?bundle=record returns bundles ([{collection, item, label, count, unread, lane, categories, newest, url, ids, rows}]) beside data, which then holds only the rows that stayed single; a lone row about a record is never bundled. total, /count and /unread-count are unchanged — a bundle presents rows, it does not reduce them. The label is never a bare id: the friendly id, else the display label, else — for a record deleted since — its trash snapshot's label with a "deleted" chip (deleted: true, no Open link), else "<Singular> #<id>"; collection_label carries the singular name for the chip beside it. Collection-wide subscription rows name the record the same way ("updated PRB1 (regions)").

blocks.h: As it was — what they saw when notified
blocks.t: A notification about a record remembers the record's revision current at send time (revision_id, stamped by notifyUser). "As it was" on a bell or inbox row opens a sheet with the record as it stood then beside the record now; fields that changed since are marked with an amber dot and listed first. Older rows (or a purged revision) fall back to the newest revision written before the notification; a record with no revision from that time says "No snapshot from that time" and shows the current values. GET /api/notifications/:id/as-it-was answers {snapshot, current, changed_fields, fields, labels, revision_id, at} for the caller's own row; current is read as the caller, so a record they can no longer open answers 403/404 and the snapshot is never shown without it. Scalar and link fields only — related sets are not compared.

Any authenticated user can send an in-app notification to another active user — built for chat @mentions and similar frontend features. The sender is always the authenticated caller, and delivery rides the full channel stack: the inbox row, a live Socket.io notification:new event, and browser push for users with a registered subscription.
POST /api/notifications
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "recipient": "<user uuid>",
  "subject": "Jane mentioned you in General chat",
  "message": "optional body, max 500 chars",
  "collection": "orders", …

An "Activity" button in the user editor and profile page header opens a right sidebar with a full chronological timeline of everything that user has done: item mutations, workflow transitions, logins, lock acquire/release — including the IP address for each event.
• Entries are grouped by calendar date with a sticky date separator and a vertical connector line. • Action-type chips at the top (create, update, delete, login…) act as one-click filters. • Filter bar: action select, collection text input, sort toggle (newest/oldest first). Chip count badge shows active filters. • Collection and item values link directly to the record; clicking navigates and closes the sidebar. • Load-more pagination — 50 entries per page, infinite scroll. • Visible to admins on the user editor; visible to the own user on their profile page.
GET /api/user-activity/:userId
  ?page=1&limit=50
  &action=create        # filter by action type
  &collection=orders    # filter by collection name
  &date_from=2025-01-01 # ISO date lower bound
  &date_to=2025-12-31   # ISO date upper bo…
Both endpoints require admin access. The summary endpoint drives the clickable action chips — it is fetched once when the panel opens and is not re-fetched on filter changes.

The admin UI is fully keyboard-navigable. Press ? anywhere to open the shortcut overlay. Navigation uses two-key sequences (press g, then a letter). All bindings are rebindable from the overlay and persisted in localStorage.
Shortcut | Action / ? | Show / hide the shortcut overlay / Cmd+K / Ctrl+K | Global search palette / g then c | Go to Collections / g then d | Go to Dashboard / g then n | Go to Notifications
Custom bindings are stored per browser in localStorage — use the overlay's "Reset to defaults" to restore.

Notifications can be delivered over SMS (and push) in addition to in-app and email. SMS uses Twilio, configured entirely through environment variables; the shared notifyUser service routes a notification to every channel the recipient has enabled.
# .env
TWILIO_ACCOUNT_SID=AC...
TWILIO_AUTH_TOKEN=...
TWILIO_FROM=+15551234567
• Users opt into channels per notification type in their profile. • notifyUser() in the services layer fans out to in-app, email, SMS, and push based on those preferences — extensions can call it too. • When TWILIO_* is unset, the SMS channel is a silent no-op.

Short screen recordings that show people how a screen works. Authors record in the browser, cut and annotate in a visual editor, and publish; everyone else watches them in the Videos library, from the Videos button on the screen a video explains, and — when a video is required for their role — from My Work until they have watched it.

Administrators always can. Videos → Who can record adds roles whose members may record and edit too. Everyone else can only watch, and only the videos whose visibility includes them ("Everyone" or the chosen roles). A video limited to roles with none chosen (or whose last chosen role was deleted) is visible to authors only.

Record a video (or "Record one for this screen" from a Videos button) asks for a screen, window or tab and, optionally, a microphone. A three-second countdown starts it; a small bar shows the time and stops it. Recording follows you from page to page — the bar stays up while you navigate, so you can record a walk-through across screens — and inside a dialog or sheet the bar and setup open inside it. The recording uploads in five-second parts while it runs and keeps unsent parts in the browser, so a dropped connection or a closed tab loses nothing — the next time you open the recorder it offers to finish the upload. A recording that finished uploading but was never saved as a video (the tab closed during the save) is offered there too, ready to save or discard; one left unsaved for a week is deleted. Recordings are limited to 30 minutes.
Clean screen while recording (on by default, remembered per browser) keeps the author's own things out of the video: from the countdown until you stop, notification counts, the chat button and panel, toasts, banners (announcements, update and reload notices, View as) and floating chips are hidden, notification sounds stay silent, and your name, email and photo in the app's menus read Demo User. Pausing keeps the screen clean; stopping, cancelling or closing the recorder brings everything back at once. Other people's names and photos on the page are not changed — check the screen before you start, or blur in the editor.
The recording controls (time, pause, mute, stop, the script) are kept out of the video when you record this tab in Chrome 132 or later: the capture is limited to the page itself, so dialogs, menus and toasts are recorded and the controls are not. In other browsers, or when you record a window or the whole screen, the controls show in the video as before; trim or blur them in the editor. The View as bar is never recorded, whether clean screen is on or off.
Recording as someone else: an administrator who can author videos may View as another person and record from there. The video shows that person's screen (their navigation, their data, their permissions), while the video, its upload and every edit belong to the administrator. The help-video library and editor work as the administrator; the per-screen Videos button and required videos still show what the other person sees.
Script (optional): write the steps before you record, one per line (up to 60 steps of 200 characters). While you record they show above the recording bar as a teleprompter — the current step large, the next one dimmed, "Step 2 of 5" — and Next (the button, or Alt+Shift+N / ⌥⇧N, which works even while you are typing in a field and is never typed into it) moves on and marks the moment. The new draft opens with a chapter per step you reached, titled with the step's text, the first at 0:00; a step you never marked makes no chapter, and you can move or rename them in the editor as usual. The script is kept with the version, so Re-record offers it again, pre-filled; an uploaded file has no script.
Recording window: Open a recording window (under the script, with a size: 1280 × 800, 1440 × 900 or 1920 × 1080, remembered per browser) opens the same page again in a separate window of exactly that size and records that window, so every video has the same frame and readable text. The recorder opens in the new window with your settings carried over (microphone, clicks, clean screen, script); press Start there and, if the browser asks what to share, choose that window. This tab shows only how it is going (starting, recording with the time, saving) and warns when the browser could not make the window the size asked for (the bar in the window shows its real size too); when the recording is saved, this tab opens the editor on the new draft and the window closes itself. Clean screen applies inside the window, a recording window never opens another, and if pop-ups are blocked the recorder says so and records in this tab as before.

Upload a video (beside Record a video, or "Upload a video" from a Videos button, which pre-fills that screen) takes an MP4, WebM or MOV made elsewhere — up to 30 minutes and 1.2 GB, the same limits as a recording. It goes through the same upload as a recording and opens the editor on a new draft. The server judges the file by its contents, never its name: it reads the streams, keeps an H.264 MP4 or a VP8/VP9 WebM as it is (an MP4 is rewritten so playback starts before the whole file loads), converts only the sound when a browser cannot play it (for example the PCM audio of many MOV files), and converts anything else — HEVC from a phone, ProRes, AV1, 10-bit video — to H.264 with AAC sound, at most 2560 pixels on the long side. Converting runs in the background at low priority and takes a few minutes for a long video; the dialog shows its progress and Cancel stops it. A file that is not a video, has no picture or cannot be read is refused with the reason. An uploaded file has no recorded clicks or microphone levels, so the editor offers no automatic click ripples or pause suggestions for it (add ripples by hand with the Ripple tool). If the connection drops, picking the same file again carries on where the upload stopped.

• Cut: split at the playhead (S) and delete the piece; trim the ends by dragging. You cannot cut everything — at least one second stays. • Suggested edits (the toolbar button beside the drawing tools): long pauses in the narration (3 seconds or more of quiet microphone), and on a recording of your own tab also stretches where nothing happens (no mouse, scroll or key for 3 seconds or more) and typing in a text field. Pauses and still stretches are suggested as cuts, typing as 4× so viewers still see what was entered; each row offers both, or dismiss it for this session. The recorder notes only that you typed, never what or which keys, and nothing inside an area marked .nvr-no-record. Stretches where you speak are never suggested, a cut wins where a cut and a speed-up overlap, and a stretch you have already cut or sped up leaves the list. An uploaded file, and a recording of another window or the screen, has no typing or stillness to suggest. • One author at a time: opening a video in the editor takes its edit lock (the lock icon in the header — add a note for others, or release it). Anyone else who opens it sees who is editing and a read-only editor, and can ask them to wrap up, ask to be next (the lock comes to them when it frees) or, as an administrator or a role allowed to take over locks, take over. Closing the editor releases the lock, and an editor left idle past the lock idle limit lets it go. When the lock comes back to you the editor loads the latest draft; if two people still save the same draft, the save that arrives second is told and offered a reload. • Speed: play a piece at 0.5× (slow motion, for a fast menu or drag), 1×, 1.5×, 2× or 4×. Narration under a slowed or sped-up piece keeps its pitch. • Hold a frame: Hold (or H) freezes the frame at the playhead for 3 seconds so viewers can read a callout; select the hold on its timeline lane to set 0.2 to 10 seconds or move it. The video and its sound wait on that frame — like slow motion, a hold adds its own time and skips nothing — and every callout, zoom, blur and caption on screen at that moment stays up for the hold; chapters, captions, banners and links to a moment land where they should afterwards. A hold has to sit on a part viewers see (one left inside a cut is dropped). The preview and a viewer watching the original recording get the hold from the player (the video waits on the frame while the clock runs on); the finished render has it baked in. • Selecting several pieces: Shift-click (or ⌘-click) bars on any lanes to add them to the selection, or drag across empty timeline space to select everything the rectangle touches (hold Shift to add). The side panel then shows how many are selected with the group actions: nudge them a frame (arrow keys; Shift: a second), align their starts or ends to the playhead ([ and ]), duplicate them right after themselves (Ctrl/⌘+D) and remove them (Delete). Dragging one bar of the selection moves them all, stopping where the first reaches the start or the last reaches the end of the recording. Each action is one undo step; a move that would land a zoom on another zoom or a hold inside a cut is refused with a note. • Chapters and poster: add a chapter at the playhead; choose the frame the library shows. Use this frame while the preview shows the title card or end card makes that card the poster. The library shows a new poster once the video is published and rendered. • Callouts, arrows, boxes and click ripples: draw on the preview, then set the text and how long it shows. Callouts, boxes and arrows fade in and out over a fifth of a second (half their length when shorter), in the published video and in the preview while it plays; paused, they show solid so what you just drew is easy to see. "Add click ripples" places one at every click the recorder saw; a ripple from a recorded click says what was clicked (hover its bar, or select it). Each ripple makes a soft tick as it plays (one tick for ripples less than 0.08 s apart): the render mixes it into the finished sound, and the live preview plays it at the video’s volume. • Jumping from the side panel (a chapter, a caption, Jump to it, Show it) offers Back to the spot you were at, with the selection you had, until you use it, close it or move the playhead on the timeline. • Steps: the Step tool draws a numbered badge, alone or with text beside it in a callout. Steps number themselves 1, 2, 3 in the order they appear and renumber when you move one; a step inside a cut has no number. Select a step to set the badge Shape (Circle, Square) and Size (Small, Medium, Large) for every step in the video. • Spotlight: draw the one area to keep lit; the rest of the frame dims while it shows. Spotlights sit under every other drawing, so a callout on the dimmed part stays readable. • Length from text: a new callout, step or typed-along caption stays up as long as its text takes to read (about 3 words a second, never under 2 seconds), and keeps following its text while you type, until you set its length by hand. When anything with text is shorter than that, the side panel says "Short for its text" with a one-click fix. • Zoom: draw the area to zoom into; the video eases in and out. A zoom can move: with it selected, put the playhead somewhere inside the zoom and drag or resize its area — that adds a stop there (a diamond on its bar), and the picture pans and resizes in a straight line from one stop to the next, holding the first before it and the last after it. The side panel lists the stops (press one to go there, the bin removes it); down to one stop the zoom stands still again.
