Each widget runs its default bound values (when every binding has a default) and its 3 most-seen recorded bound sets (the render route records them for cached widgets). Defaults run first, most-used first. Every run takes a heavy-read slot under the same single-flight key the viewer’s request uses, so a viewer who misses meanwhile joins the warm’s run. Only cached queries (cache TTL above 0) are ever run by usage. Extension warmers (ctx.cache.registerWarm) run last, each with its own timeout inside what is left of the budget. The viewer phase and extension warmers run on the boot and 06:30 warms only, never in cloud mode. A "Warm daily" query with no cache TTL still runs (that warms the database) and its rows are dropped; the 06:00 query-cache-warmers job runs every "Warm daily" query, always overwriting its entry, with no overall budget. The boot warm runs once per cluster per version and takes the heavy-job slot; a run stops starting queries when its time budget (CACHE_WARM_BUDGET_MS, 4 minutes) is spent, and each query has a 90-second timeout. CACHE_WARM=off turns the boot and 06:30 warms off; on forces them on a process that does not tick scheduled jobs. Ops Console lists the job as cache-warm, with Run now and Dry run.
Queue worklists warm in the same run, after the viewer phase and inside the same budget. The warm replays the first pages people actually opened in the last 7 days: GET /api/queues/:id/items requests with no page or page=1, from the request log, development instances not counted. People are grouped per queue by what their read costs, which is their access (administrator, or role plus restrict-mode User Scopes), not their tab, sort or filters. Each group gets one read, made as the person who sent the group’s most-used request, through the route’s own query parser and queue access check. Up to 12 reads run, most-used first, one at a time, each source taking its own heavy-read slot. Nothing the warm reads is stored or shown to anyone: queues have no result cache. The read only leaves the database pages, query plans and in-process caches it touched warm, the same ones the person’s own request would fill. It never writes: it skips the materialization promotion a large live queue would queue, and it calls the service directly, so it adds no request-log row and no last-access time. Every process also warms what a queue read pays once per process: the source collections’ metadata and the predictive-SLA percentiles. Owner groups already warm at boot. Like the viewer phase, the queue phase runs on the boot and 06:30 warms only, and never in cloud mode. Dry run lists it under queues.

The process panel reports the connection pool over the last five minutes, not at the instant you looked: p50 / p95 / max time a request WAITED for a connection, and the share of the window with every connection busy. Identical 80ms statements once read 2.2s because that wait was invisible — no query timing shows it. The pool-monitor job raises an issue when the p95 wait passes 500ms or the pool sits full for a quarter of the window.

Background work has its own connection pool, so a person never waits for a connection a background job is holding. Background work here means scheduled jobs (including dry runs and catch-up runs), staged and CSV imports, queue rebuilds, the cache warm after boot and other boot-time warms, and anything that holds the heavy-job slot, such as help-video renders. Requests use the main pool (DB_POOL_MAX, default 60). Background work uses DB_POOL_BACKGROUND_MAX (default 10). Both pools connect to the same server and database, so one process can open up to DB_POOL_MAX + DB_POOL_BACKGROUND_MAX connections; budget that against the server's connection limit for each replica. The background pool opens connections only when it needs them and closes idle ones, so a process with no background work holds none. Set DB_POOL_BACKGROUND_MAX=0 to turn the separate pool off; background work then shares the main pool, as it did before.
No code changes are needed to use it: the db handle checks, on every call, whether the current work is background work and picks the pool to match. Everything a job awaits uses that pool too, including timers it sets and promises it starts. A transaction stays on the one connection it opened. Long-running statements (runLongSql / withLongConnection) take their connection from the same pool. An admin's "Run now" runs the job on the background pool, while the request that asked for it, and the job-run record, use the main pool. Before a heavy job starts, it waits until the background pool has room. In cloud mode, a tenant's work always uses that tenant's own pool, and no background pool is created.
DB & Runtime Health shows both pools: "Pool · requests" and "Pool · background jobs", with in-use count, waiting count, p95 wait and the most connections this process can open. Held connections are listed with the pool that holds them. GET /api/ops-db/pool keeps the main pool at the top level (as before) and adds background (null when the pool is off) and total_max. GET /api/ops/runtime adds background_pool, and /api/metrics adds nivaro_db_background_pool_used, _pending and _max. The heavy-read gate is still sized from the main pool (HEAVY_READ_CONCURRENCY, default max(4, DB_POOL_MAX/3)).
Storage runway needs at least 7 nightly snapshots before it projects a growth rate — until then it reports how many snapshots it has collected. Snapshots are written by the storage-snapshot job at 03:45 daily.

Database tuning, the Tuning tab of the Database page (/database/tuning, Operations → Database), is a propose-only tuning loop over the platform’s own workload. Each night it reads what the database and the API already record, turns what it finds into candidate changes, proves every candidate before listing it, and ranks the proposals by the time each would save per day. Nothing changes until an administrator clicks Apply. An applied change is watched (7 days by default) and rolled back on its own when it regresses. Admins only; index and procedure changes need SQL Server.
The page lists proposals in tabs: Proposed, Watching, Applied, Rolled back (failed ones too), Rejected by proof, Dismissed and Stale. Each proposal shows its evidence, its proof and the method that produced it, the exact change and its undo. The Database page’s Overview tab shows a strip linking here while proposals are waiting.

Kind | Found from | The change / Index (create) | SQL Server’s missing-index DMVs, the index advisor (foreign keys, queue filters, row filters, state mirrors) and the missing-index groups in slow-run plans captured for saved queries. One or two key columns; a candidate whose keys equal or lead an existing index’s keys is declined. | CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX; the undo drops it. / Index (drop) | Index usage since the server started: a plain nonclustered index with no reads and more than 100 writes, or whose keys are a strict prefix of a live index’s. Nothing before 30 days of uptime. | DROP INDEX; the undo recreates the exact definition recorded at proposal time. / Procedure rewrite | Procedures averaging 2 s or more and run at least 20 times a week, with a body the twin proof can run and recorded parameter sets. Rewritten by mechanical transformers first (a filter-only junction join becomes EXISTS; a correlated "last success" MAX becomes a grouped temp table), else by one AI call. | CREATE OR ALTER PROCEDURE with the new body; the undo restores the old body. / Store a rollup | Virtual rollup fields read at least 200 times a day (list reads in the request log over 7 days), against the writes to their source collections. | Turns on computed_store the way the Table Editor’s Store toggle does (column, flag, backfill); the undo turns it off and keeps the column. / Cache a query | Saved queries that run uncached, take 1 s or more and run at least 10 times a day. | Sets cache_ttl, and warm_daily when its slowest run is more than twice its average; the undo restores both.
• A query cache TTL comes from measured write gaps: the activity log’s create, update and delete rows on each source table over the last 7 days. A source is nightly-fed when gaps of 6 h or more cover 80% of the week and 80% of the last day, and one gap lasts 20 h or more; it gets 6 h. Otherwise the TTL is half the median gap, between 1 minute and 24 hours. • A source with no activity rows (a table nothing writes through the API) cannot be measured: the proposal says gap_assumed and its TTL is capped at 5 minutes. A query whose sources cannot be resolved is never proposed. • Recursive (tree) rollups and rollups on nivaro_* collections are never proposed for storing: a stored total recalculates on a direct child’s write only, so descendant writes would leave a tree total stale. • A drop is never proposed for a unique, primary-key or foreign-key-backing index, anything that is not nonclustered, an index named anywhere in a module definition (an index hint fails with error 308 once the index is gone), or an index this ledger created in the last 60 days. • The temp-table guard transformer is never applied to a stored-procedure body: a guard inside a callee would drop the caller’s same-named #temp table.

Every candidate is proven by the method its kind allows before it is listed. A passed proof lists it as Proposed; a failed one lists it under Rejected by proof with the proof kept, so the reason is visible. Proofs never change a real object; the twin and hypothetical index are temporary.
Kind | Proof | Rolls back when / Index (create) | Hypothetical index: the top statements that touch the leading column are planned without and with it (estimated plans only; the index is built STATISTICS_ONLY inside a transaction that is rolled back). Passes when one statement is at least 20% cheaper and none is more than 1% dearer. When that path is unavailable, dmv-estimate: SQL Server’s improvement measure is at least 10, or, for a candidate SQL Server never asked for, the column has observed read traffic (live reads that filter or sort by it, or a captured slow plan that wanted it). A candidate from configuration alone fails with "no observed traffic". | 20 of the trailing 24 hourly samples (average elapsed time of the statements that touch the column) are over the regression threshold / Index (drop) | Usage stats, read live when the proof runs: zero reads over at least 30 days of uptime, or a strict prefix of an index that still exists. | The same statements regress, by the same rule / Procedure rewrite | Twin: the rewrite is deployed as <proc>__tune_<8 hex>, a name of its own per proof, and both bodies run with every recorded parameter set in A B B A order (old, new, new, old). Rows must be identical (canonicalised, compared as a multiset), the new median at most 75% of the old, and no set slower (every new run of a set slower than every old run of it). When the old body’s two runs disagree, the procedure is nondeterministic and the proof refuses. proc_timeout_minutes bounds the whole proof. | 20 of the trailing 24 samples of the procedure’s average elapsed time are over the threshold, or the nightly re-diff finds different rows / Store a rollup | Cost model: reading costs at least 3× the upkeep (reads a day × a list page’s recompute, against child writes a day × one recalc, timed on a 20-row sample). | Any of 20 sampled rows drifts from the live formula, at once / Cache a query | Freshness: its source tables resolve and it saves at least 5 s a day. | 20 of the trailing 24 samples of its average execution time are over the threshold
The regression threshold is the baseline × (1 + regression_pct / 100). The baseline is read just before the change runs; fewer than 20 measured samples never count as a regression, so one bad hour never rolls a change back.

• A body, the current one or the rewrite, that writes a real table (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, TRUNCATE, BULK INSERT or SELECT INTO anything but a #temp table or table variable), runs DDL on anything but a #temp table, or runs GRANT, DENY, REVOKE, DBCC, BACKUP, RESTORE, KILL, SHUTDOWN or RECONFIGURE. • Dynamic SQL (sp_executesql, EXEC(@sql), EXEC @proc), a call to itself, a linked server (four-part names, OPENQUERY, OPENROWSET, OPENDATASOURCE), an EXEC into another database, or a call to an sp_ / xp_ system procedure. • Each procedure either body EXECs is read from sys.sql_modules and judged by the same rules, one level deep: a callee that calls further is refused, not followed. A real procedure already holding the twin’s name is refused too. • Every EXEC in a proof runs inside BEGIN TRAN … ROLLBACK, a backstop for a write the rules missed. The twin is dropped when the proof ends. A process killed mid-proof leaves it behind for the boot sweep, which drops twins (…__tune and …__tune_<hex>) older than max(30, proof timeout + 5) minutes; a younger one may belong to a proof running on another process. The readiness check fails on a twin older than a day. • A proof that could not run (a catalog read threw, or it ran out of its time budget) judged nothing: a standing proposal stays Proposed. A refusal on policy rejects it.
The hypothetical-index path uses DBCC AUTOPILOT, which is undocumented and may need sysadmin. Where the database login cannot run it, dmv-estimate is the expected path, and the proposal says which method it used.

• Apply is two clicks and sends only the proposal id; the change itself comes from the proposal row. Only a Proposed row applies. A Stale or Rejected-by-proof row needs Re-prove first, and a procedure rewrite needs a passed twin proof whatever its status says. Re-prove reads the live object first: one that changed since the proposal keeps the row Stale (409 TUNING_STALE) and is not proved; the nightly run proposes against what is live. • Before anything runs, Apply re-reads the live object: an index that now exists or whose definition changed, a procedure body edited since the proof, a query whose cache settings changed. Any of these moves the row to Stale. An index drop is refused (409 TUNING_NOT_APPLICABLE) when the live index is unique or backs a primary key, a unique constraint or a foreign key. • Every index statement is parsed into a fixed shape, its names re-checked against sys.*, and run as the canonical rendering, never as stored. A created index may not be UNIQUE, filtered or on a named filegroup, and may set only ONLINE, SORT_IN_TEMPDB, DATA_COMPRESSION, FILLFACTOR and MAXDOP. An index drop’s undo may restore the full recorded definition. • The watch baseline is read before the change runs: CREATE INDEX recompiles the table’s plans and CREATE OR ALTER resets the procedure’s stats, so a figure read afterwards is mostly empty. If the change fails part-way, whatever landed is undone at once and the row ends Failed with the reason. • The hourly watch samples every watched change against its baseline. A regression rolls the change back and tells whoever applied it in their Notifications inbox. A change past its watch window becomes Applied. • A rewritten procedure is re-diffed every night at 07:55 UTC: the old body is deployed as the twin and run against the live rewrite on one recorded parameter set, a different one each night. Different rows roll the rewrite back. When the live procedure’s own two runs disagree (the data moved between them), the re-check is nondeterministic: it is listed in the watch run, never rolled back. • Roll back by hand from Watching or Applied. The undo is refused, and the row left Failed for a person, when the live object changed since the apply (a procedure edited since, an index dropped or rebuilt). • The watch also ends an apply or rollback that died with its process: a row stuck in applying for more than 30 minutes whose job run is no longer running is marked Failed, without running the undo, so a person reads the row and its undo first. • Dismiss needs a note and works on Proposed, Stale, Rejected-by-proof and Failed rows. A dismissed or rolled-back change is not proposed again for 90 days. A change rejected by proof is not proved again for 7 days. An AI rewrite counts as one attempt per procedure body, whatever the model answers. A Proposed row whose evidence has not been seen for 14 days closes as dismissed. • Apply, rollback, dismiss, re-prove and settings changes each write an activity row, which the incident timeline shows. Apply and rollback also appear in Jobs as runs of kind tuning.

A change to a replication article (a table or procedure published by SQL Server replication) forwards to every subscriber. Proposals carry replicated, and Apply checks replication again, live, at apply time, because a publication may postdate the proof. A replicated target, or a rollup whose collection is one (storing it adds a column), is refused unless the request says the DBA agreed (dba_ok). The page then shows the statements that would forward and asks for "The DBA agreed — apply".

The Settings card is on the Database tuning page itself, not under Settings. Values are stored in nivaro_settings.db_tuning; a save that holds a bad value names every bad key. A save sends only the fields changed on the card and merges them onto the stored value, so an instance override (Settings → Instance) is never copied into the shared row. Database tuning is off by default.
Setting | Default | Range | What it does / enabled | off |  | The master switch. While it is off the nightly observe and the hourly watch return at once and the readiness check passes. / ai_rewrites | on |  | Ask the AI for a procedure rewrite when no mechanical transformer applies (at most 5 a night). The answer must keep the procedure name and the exact parameter list. The calls are logged in AI calls under the feature db-tune. / min_estimate_ms_per_day | 5000 | 0–86,400,000 | Candidates estimated to save less are not proved. Procedure rewrites are exempt: their estimate is a lower bound until the proof measures it. / watch_days | 7 | 1–30 | How long an applied change is watched. / regression_pct | 25 | 5–100 | How much worse than the baseline a sample must be to count against the change. / proc_timeout_minutes | 10 | 1–30 | The time budget of one twin proof, every set and run together. A proof that runs out drops its twin and judges nothing: a standing proposal stays as it was. / ai_daily_budget_usd | 2 | 0–1000 | AI rewrites are skipped while the last 24 hours of AI spend is over this.

• db-tuning-observe, nightly at 03:35 (a heavy job): every observer reads its evidence (at most 10 minutes each, 60 minutes for the run), candidates are deduplicated, ones dismissed or rolled back lately, rejected by proof in the last 7 days, or on a target with a change in flight are skipped, and the 20 biggest estimates are proved. The rest carry over to the next night. • db-tuning-watch, hourly at :55. • Both are always registered and return at once while database tuning is off. Scheduled ticks also need a process that ticks (CRON_TICKS); Run now in Jobs always works, and both have a dry run. • Run the observer from the page: a real run starts in the background and the page follows it until it finishes. One observe run at a time per database: a run is refused (409 TUNING_RUNNING from the page) while another, on any process, has been running for less than 70 minutes. Dry run lists what it would prove and changes nothing. • The readiness check db-tuning (Operations) fails on a leftover twin older than a day, and warns on an observe run older than 48 hours, a change still watching a day past its window, an apply or rollback that died, or a failed apply or rollback.

A procedure proof replays real calls. Every saved-query execute (POST /custom-queries/:slug/execute) and every procedure execute (POST /procedures/:name/execute) records the parameters the call actually bound in nivaro_tuning_param_sets, the newest 10 per target, with values under credential-looking names masked. A procedure also gets the sets of the saved queries that EXEC it, when every name in a set is one of the procedure’s own parameters (a saved query records its own names). A procedure with no recorded sets is not proposed.

GET   /api/db-tuning                         // counts by status and kind, open estimate, last run, is_running, settings, extension observers
GET   /api/db-tuning/proposals?status=proposed,stale&kind=index_create
GET   /api/db-tuning/propos…
Admins only. A refusal answers 409 (400 for a malformed change) with a code: TUNING_STALE, TUNING_REPLICATED (with the target and the statements), TUNING_NOT_APPLICABLE, TUNING_INVALID, TUNING_DISABLED or TUNING_RUNNING.

SQL checks, the SQL checks tab of the Database page (/database/sql-checks, Operations → Database), checks the SQL that runs against the database for mistakes that corrupt or slow data. It reads every procedure, function, view and trigger definition from the database itself (sys.sql_modules), plus the SQL bodies Nivaro keeps in its own tables: import definitions’ stored procedure bodies and custom queries. Findings are tracked across runs, so a finding has a history: when it first appeared, how many runs saw it, and when it went away. Checks only read; nothing is changed by a run. Two kinds of procedure fix can be applied from a finding by a person (see Applying a fix). Admins only; SQL Server only.

Check | Severity | What it finds / MERGE on a nullable key | Critical when the key holds NULLs now, else warning | A MERGE whose ON clause compares a nullable target column with = and no NULL-safe form (ISNULL / COALESCE, an IS NULL pair, IS NOT DISTINCT FROM, INTERSECT). NULL never equals NULL, so those rows are inserted again on every run. With live counts on, the finding shows how many rows hold NULL keys and how many extra rows already sit in NULL-key groups. / MERGE source may repeat a key | Warning | A MERGE source with no ROW_NUMBER / GROUP BY / DISTINCT and no unique index on the joined columns. A repeated key stops the whole MERGE. / Write without WHERE | Critical | An UPDATE or DELETE with no top-level WHERE and no JOIN predicate. Temp tables, table variables and MERGE actions are ignored. / Transaction without XACT_ABORT | Warning | BEGIN TRAN in a module with no SET XACT_ABORT ON and no CATCH that rolls back on @@TRANCOUNT: a failed statement can leave the transaction open on a pooled connection. / Local-time clock | Info | GETDATE() / SYSDATETIME() calls (one finding per object, with the count and lines). / NOT IN over a nullable column | Warning | NOT IN (SELECT col …) where col is nullable and the subquery does not filter NULLs. / SELECT * on a wide table | Info | SELECT * from a table with max-length text or binary columns. / Import body differs from deployed | Warning (info when not deployed) | An import definition whose stored procedure body differs from the deployed procedure of the same name (comments, whitespace and the CREATE / ALTER verb are ignored), or names a procedure the database does not have. / SQLFluff rule | Info | Correctness rules from SQLFluff (ambiguous references RF01/RF02, AM01–AM07, unused CTEs ST03, subqueries in joins ST05) when a SQLFluff sidecar is configured. Layout and style rules are dropped.
The checks are pattern checks over T-SQL with comments and string literals blanked out, not a full parser: each prefers missing a case to raising a wrong one. A finding that is intended (a procedure that clears a work table on purpose) is marked as expected with a note; it stays out of the open count until someone reopens it.

• Header: open critical / warning / info counts, the last run (when, how long, whether SQLFluff ran), Run now (two clicks) and Settings. • Findings: filter by status, severity and check, or search. The detail shows the statement with line numbers, why it matters, the live figures, the suggested fix with a Copy button, the history (opened, resolved, reopened, marked as expected) and a link to the editor: /procedures for a procedure, the custom query editor, or the import definition in the Imports console (/imports?definition=<key>). • Trends: open findings per run by severity, new and resolved per run, open findings by check and the objects with the most. • Fixes: cleanups and guard indexes logged by fix scripts, and “Procedure changed” rows Nivaro logs itself when a run finds that findings went away because their procedure or query was edited. • Runs: every run with its duration, counts, SQLFluff status and errors. • The Database page’s Overview tab shows a strip linking here while critical findings are open.

Settings live on the tab (nivaro_settings.sql_checks): run nightly (off by default), count NULL keys and copies (reads the tables a MERGE writes; tables over the row cap, 5,000,000 by default, are skipped), the per-table count timeout (120 s), and whether to check import definitions and custom queries. The nightly run is the sql-checks job at 03:30 (Jobs can move it); it only ticks on deployed instances. SQL_CHECKS=on or off in the server environment forces the nightly run on or off whatever the setting says, for databases rebuilt nightly from another one (the setting would be wiped); the page then shows the switch as set by the server’s configuration. Run now always works.

SQL_LINT_URL points at a small service running SQLFluff with the T-SQL dialect; SQL_LINT_TOKEN is its bearer token (a secret: SQL_LINT_TOKEN_FILE works, and the environment viewer masks it). Each module’s text is sent on its own, never any data: POST {SQL_LINT_URL}/lint with {sql, dialect: "tsql"} answers {violations: [{code, line, description}], parse_errors}. A busy sidecar (503) is retried with a short backoff; a refused token (401), a sidecar that stays busy or does not answer marks the run’s SQLFluff as unavailable and keeps the other checks; a per-module timeout (504) skips that module only. SQLFluff findings resolve only in runs where SQLFluff answered.

Two mechanical findings can be fixed from their detail panel with Propose fix: a transaction without SET XACT_ABORT ON (the statement is added first in the procedure body, after AS / AS BEGIN and after a leading SET NOCOUNT ON), and a MERGE on a nullable key whose ON clause is a plain AND of column-to-column equalities (each pair on a nullable target column becomes (s.k = t.k OR (s.k IS NULL AND t.k IS NULL))). Anything else (functions, OR, literals, ranges in the ON clause, other checks, views and functions) says “This one needs a person” and keeps the written steps.
• The preview changes nothing: it shows the diff with old and new line numbers. The compile check is a separate POST (it holds a schema lock on the procedure for up to 5 seconds) that compiles the new definition inside a transaction that is rolled back. • Adding XACT_ABORT is marked risky when the procedure commits in a CATCH block or reads XACT_STATE() or @@ERROR to carry on after an error: with XACT_ABORT ON those paths behave differently (error 3930). A NULL-safe ON carries a note that the OR form can turn an index seek into a scan on a large table. • A NULL-safe ON is marked risky when copies already sit in NULL-key groups (one incoming row then updates all of them) or when the MERGE source may repeat a key (SQL Server would stop the whole MERGE). A risky fix needs an extra confirmation. • Apply (two clicks) sends the preview’s hash; if the definition changed since the preview it is refused (409) and the preview is rebuilt. • A procedure is changed with CREATE OR ALTER through the same path as the Procedures page, on one connection that holds an exclusive application lock on that procedure (so two servers cannot change it at once) and re-reads it first: if it changed since the preview, nothing is deployed. The deployed text always names the procedure itself (a renamed procedure, or a header without a schema, is rewritten to [schema].[name]). It is then checked again at once; if the re-check reports anything new, or the finding is still there, the previous definition is put back automatically (only while the procedure is still exactly what the fix deployed) and the panel says why. • An import definition whose stored body was identical to the procedure gets the new body too (with a version snapshot). A finding on a stored body that differs from the deployed procedure only changes the stored body; deploy it from the import definition. • Every apply, automatic put-back and revert is a “Procedure changed” row on the Fixes tab with the diff; Revert (two clicks) restores the previous definition, and is refused when the procedure changed again after the fix. When an automatic put-back itself failed, the row offers Restore previous version. Import definition bodies that were synced are put back only if nobody edited them since, with their deployed hash and time.
If your deployment keeps a procedure’s source elsewhere (a repository or deploy script), update it there too — otherwise the next deploy puts the old version back.

blocks.h: Logging a fix from a script
blocks.t:
A script that repairs data (removes copies, adds a guard index) logs what it did so the page can show it next to the findings: insert into nivaro_sql_check_fixes directly, or POST /api/sql-checks/fixes as an administrator (an admin’s API key works).
{
  "action": "cleanup",
  "check_key": "merge-null-key",
  "target_table": "workflows_files",
  "rows_affected": 273657,
  "backup_table": "zz_backup_workflows_files_20261019",
  "detail": { "kept": "newest row per key" },
  "run_by": "fix…
action is cleanup, proc_fix, guard_index or other.

Route | What it does / GET /api/sql-checks/summary | Open counts by severity and check, the last run, the trend over the last 30 runs, top objects, settings and whether a run is going. / POST /api/sql-checks/run | Starts a run in the background (202 with run_id); 409 while one is running. / GET /api/sql-checks/runs · /runs/:id | Run history (paged) and one run with its stats. / GET /api/sql-checks/findings | Findings; filters status (open, accepted, resolved, all), severity, check, object, q; page and limit. / GET /api/sql-checks/findings/:id | One finding with its statement, figures, suggested fix and event history. / PATCH /api/sql-checks/findings/:id | {status: "accepted", note} marks it as expected (a note is required); {status: "open"} reopens one marked as expected. / GET /api/sql-checks/findings/:id/proposal | The proposed fix: {proposable, class, risky, reasons, notes, diff, unified, new_definition_hash}. Changes nothing and compiles nothing. / POST /api/sql-checks/findings/:id/proposal/compile | {new_definition_hash} compiles the previewed text in a rolled-back transaction: {ok, error?}. / POST /api/sql-checks/findings/:id/apply | {new_definition_hash, confirm_risky?} applies the previewed fix; 409 when the definition changed since the preview, 422 when it does not compile. Answers {fix_id, applied, rolled_back, reason?, deployed}. / POST /api/sql-checks/fixes/:id/revert | Restores the definition a fix from the page replaced (also after a failed automatic put-back); 409 when the procedure changed after the fix. Answers {reverted, skipped_import_bodies}. / GET · POST /api/sql-checks/fixes | The fix log (paged); log a fix from a script. / GET · PATCH /api/sql-checks/settings | Read and change the settings (strict: unknown keys and bad values are refused with every problem named).

The Config Review page at /config/review (System → Config hygiene → Review) is a monthly report on the configuration itself. It runs on the 1st of each month at 04:20 and tells the administrators when it finds something; Run review now runs it on demand. Every finding says why it matters and links to the editor that owns it. Where a fix is safe, the finding offers one: you see the exact change set first, apply it with the same writes the editors make, and undo it from the Fixed list. Admins only.

Finding | Why | One-click fix / Contradicting field rules | Two active rules on the same trigger set the same field to different values. The later rule always overwrites the earlier one, so the earlier one never takes effect. | Switch off the rule that never takes effect (undo switches it back on). / Duplicate field rules | Two active rules do exactly the same thing. | Switch off the earlier one. / Empty fields on layouts | A column empty on every record (at most 250,000 rows, at least 30 days old) still takes a row on one or more layouts. | Remove it from those layouts. Each layout gets a version first; the column and its data are not touched. / Unused fields | A visible field on no layout and empty on every record. | None: check what references it before dropping it in the Table Editor. / Layouts nobody opens | Not the active layout for its type, no slug, no conditions, and nothing (grid, drill, form, PDF, addendum) names it. | None: open the Layouts tab. / Duplicate saved views | Same filters, sort and columns for the same audience. The default view, or else the oldest, is kept. | Delete the duplicate. Not offered for a default view or one somebody subscribes to. / Inactive owner groups | Every member of an owner group is suspended or redacted and no team is linked, so nobody can act on the records it covers. | None: pick replacements in the owner matrix.
The Review list also carries the owner-filter lint, pipeline lint warnings and retired columns that are still present, so the report is one list.

• **Old drafts**: form drafts not saved for N months (default 3). Shows the count and storage. Delete removes up to 500 per round and keeps a copy for undo when they hold under 2 MB. • **Idle tasks**: open tasks untouched for N months (default 3). Support requests are left out. Cancel marks them cancelled with a history line and notifies nobody; undo reopens the ones still cancelled. • **Unreferenced files** (report only): files over 30 days old that nothing names — no foreign key, file field (with or without a relation row), M2M file junction, attachment list, configuration text (pages, widgets, report and PDF/mail templates, forms, settings, layouts, comments) or rich-text field. Shows the count, storage and the 200 largest. The config review never deletes files; review them in Files. • **Unopened views**: saved views nobody opened in N days (default 90). Default and subscribed views are left out. Opens are recorded from the view pills (one row per person and view per hour), and the check waits until opens have been recorded for the whole window.
The thresholds sit in the page header (drafts and tasks 1–24 months, views 30–365 days). Changing them affects the next Run review now; **Save as defaults** stores them for the monthly run and for the page (activity-logged). Anything unsaved or out of range falls back to 3 months, 3 months and 90 days.

The label check collects every label that names a field: the field label, layout label overrides, queue column aliases, saved-view column labels and report widget columns. When one field reads differently across them ("Req Amount", "Requisition $", "Requested"), it suggests the label used most. Pick a candidate or type your own; the preview lists every place that changes. Layouts and reports get a version first. Undo puts back only labels nobody changed since.

When AI is configured, the run (on by default) asks the summarize model to re-word each reason for an administrator and to propose one label per inconsistent concept. The model sees configuration names only, never record data, and its reply is checked: only plain reason text and short labels for findings it was sent are kept. It never decides or applies a change. A re-worded reason is marked AI-worded; hover it for the check’s own words.
API: GET /api/config-review?family=review|cleanup|label&status=open|fixed|dismissed, POST /api/config-review/run (202; the page polls running), GET /api/config-review/:id/preview?label=, POST /api/config-review/:id/apply, POST /api/config-review/:id/undo, POST /api/config-review/:id/dismiss, GET|PUT /api/config-review/settings ({cleanup: {draftMonths, taskMonths, viewDays}}, 400 out of bounds). The preview returns the exact target ids and a hash; apply must send both back, re-plans from the rows as they are now, answers 409 when the hash differs and touches only targets that are in both. Fixed findings stay listed for 30 days.

The Ops Console at /ops-console (Operations → Ops Console) is the operational side of the API process: the live log, log-based alerting, environment inspection, maintenance windows, and controlled restart. Admin-only throughout.

Jobs (Operations → Jobs, /jobs) lists every cron the process registered — core schedules and extension-registered ones alike — with its effective schedule, last outcome and next run. Each row can be paused/resumed, run now, and have its schedule OVERRIDDEN from the admin: click the expression, type a new cron expression (the next fire times preview live; an invalid expression is refused with the parser message), Save. Revert puts the job back on the schedule its code registered.
• Overrides persist in settings.cron_overrides and are hydrated before extensions register, so an override binds to an extension job on every replica after a restart — no deploy needed. • Pause keeps the job registered but its ticks return immediately (settings.paused_crons); Resume is instant. • API: GET /api/cron (effective + default expression, override metadata), GET /api/cron/preview?expression=, PATCH /api/cron/:id {expression | null, note}, POST /api/cron/:id/revert, /pause, /resume, /run. Every change is activity-logged (cron-override, cron-revert, cron-pause, cron-resume, cron-run-now). • Flows have the same enable/disable from the Flows list (the Power action on a row) — an inactive flow keeps its config and its version history; the editor’s Versions panel reverts config. • Dry run (#32) — a job that registered a dry-run handler shows a "Dry run" button: it reports what a tick would do with nothing written (the rollup drift sweep lists stale rows without raising an issue; the miss detector lists missed windows; the query warmers list the queries they would run). API: POST /api/cron/:id/dry-run. • Run after (#54) — the per-row select chains a job after another one: its own schedule goes dormant (ticks are no-ops, the expression stays registered as the revert target) and it runs right after the chosen job completes, in registration order when several chain on one parent. Cycles are refused. Persisted in settings.cron_chains and hydrated at boot before any schedule registers. API: PATCH /api/cron/:id {after: id | null}. • Miss detector (#81) — cron-miss-detector runs every 30 minutes: for each job not paused or chained it derives the previous expected fire time from the schedule and, when no run has been recorded since (past a grace of 10% of the period, five minutes minimum, and never for a window before this process booted), raises one deduped issue naming the window. • Heavy jobs yield (#75) — a job marked heavy waits while the connection pool is hot (80% checked out or acquires queued), in five-second steps for up to ten minutes, before taking its serialized turn; interactive requests win the morning rush.

A job that no-ops behind a deployment flag says so on the Jobs page: a green <FLAG> on badge when the flag names it, an amber <FLAG> off · inert badge when every tick returns without doing anything. Extensions declare it with cron.annotate(id, { gate: { flag, enabled } }); a readiness check can still add up the coverage, but the per-job truth sits beside the job.

blocks.h: Log tail and log alert rules
blocks.t: • Log tail — the last 2,000 log lines from this replica, held in memory (nothing is persisted), auto-refreshing every 10 seconds with level filters and a plain-text search. It captures structured logger output; anything printed with bare console.log goes to stdout only and will not appear here. • Search the tail with a regular expression (the .* toggle, case-insensitive; an invalid pattern falls back to a plain substring match) and bound it with since / until — an ISO datetime, epoch milliseconds, or the relative forms now-15m, now-2h, now-1d (#82). • Log alert rules — a rule is a name plus a regular expression (optionally with a minimum level). When a log line matches, an issue is raised in the Issue Log; a 5-minute per-rule cooldown keeps a noisy line from raising the same issue every second. Rules apply as lines arrive, on every replica. A rule may also carry a threshold ("10 matches in 15 minutes") and its own cooldown, and a rule saved from Ask the logs can watch the request log instead — see Ops assistant. • Keep patterns simple: patterns longer than 200 characters, or ones using nested quantifiers (the shapes that can hang a regex engine), are accepted but quietly never match — if a rule seems inert, shorten and simplify its pattern. • Silent failures — a counter panel for deliberate catch-and-continue sites in the code, showing how often each has fired since this process started. A site firing 50 times in an hour raises an issue on its own.

• Incident timeline — pick a moment and build a merged timeline of everything within ±60 minutes: issues, failed or interrupted background jobs, and configuration changes. Made for "what changed around 14:00" questions. • Clock & DST — measures the clock skew between the API and the database (flagged red past 5 seconds) and lists scheduled jobs whose hour falls in the 0–3 AM band that daylight-saving transitions can skip or repeat. • Environment knobs — every configuration variable the process was started with, plus the documented raw-env switches. Values are masked two ways: any key whose name suggests a secret (secret, token, pass, key, credential, signing) shows as dots, and any value shaped like a credential-bearing URL has its password segment replaced — so connection strings are safe even under innocent key names.

The Ops Console lists what this build carries versus the migration ledger: pending migrations with their source (so the DDL a restart will run can be read first) and the newest applied ones with timestamps. Pending is normally empty — boot applies migrations — so a non-empty list means a restart is about to change the schema, or a replica is serving mid-deploy. API: GET /api/ops-runtime/migrations (#68).
Each applied migration also shows what it DID: the schema is listed before and after every run and the difference is stored beside the ledger (nivaro_migration_effects — tables, columns, indexes, foreign keys and procedures added or removed, with the duration). A migration whose row reads "no schema change" either found its objects already in place or only touched data; the ledger alone cannot tell those apart, which is why the row exists. Migrations that ran before this was tracked say so.

Maintenance mode freezes every write for non-admins while reads keep working; admins stay exempt so they can do the work. Scheduled jobs hold too — a tick that lands during the freeze is skipped and the job resumes on its next schedule once it lifts (Run now still works, and the sweep that ends a maintenance window keeps ticking). Turn it on by hand from Security Center (Operations → Security Center → Maintenance mode) or let a scheduled window flip it. People are told what the freeze means in one of two presentations: a strip above the app (Banner — browsing works, saving is paused, anything saved earlier is unaffected) or a page that replaces the app until the freeze lifts (Full page — the portal is unavailable until maintenance ends, earlier saves are safe). Admins always get the strip. The optional "Expected back" time shows on the page with a countdown, and the page checks every 30 seconds and returns people to the app on its own the moment maintenance ends. A write refused during the freeze answers 503 with code MAINTENANCE and the same explanation. A maintenance flag can also come from outside the database — a rebuild job that restores the database cannot keep a row there, so it sets the Redis key nvr:maintenance, which the platform honours above the settings row; the Security Center card says "Set by a rebuild job" when that is the source, and End maintenance clears it.
A maintenance window is a scheduled freeze with a lifecycle the platform runs for you. Create one with a title, start, end, optional message and the presentation (banner or full page); from there it is automatic:
• Pre-announce — once the start is under 24 hours away, a warning banner appears for everyone with a countdown and the local start–end times. • Start — a per-minute sweep flips maintenance mode on at the boundary, carrying the window’s presentation and its end time as the expected-back time. Non-admin writes are refused while it is on, the banner switches to a non-dismissable notice (or the full page takes over), and the alert engines (ops monitors, alert definitions, report alerts) pause — their skipped evaluations are not queued up, they simply do not run. • End — the sweep flips maintenance mode off and runs a smoke check (database, Redis, migrations, registered collections, and a self-request). Only when it passes is the "Maintenance complete" all-clear broadcast sent; a failed check raises a high-severity issue instead and holds the all-clear. • Cancel — deleting an active window turns maintenance mode off immediately. The smoke check can also be run by hand at any time from the same card.

blocks.h: Restart, follow-user, heap snapshot, CPU profile
blocks.t: • Restart — the Restart button requires a typed reason (audit-logged) and is refused while work is mid-run: running background jobs, staged imports, or processing collection imports each block it, and the refusal names what is running. The process exits cleanly and relies on the host’s restart policy to come back. • Follow a user — pick a person and their next 50 requests are traced in full detail (per-phase waterfalls), regardless of how fast they are. Traces appear on the API Analytics page; a follow expires after an hour on its own. • Heap snapshot — captures a V8 heap snapshot of this replica and downloads it for analysis in Chrome DevTools. The file lives in the process’s temp directory, so download it right away — a restart discards it. • CPU profile — POST /api/ops-runtime/cpu-profile with {"seconds": 1–30} (admins only) samples this replica’s main thread while you reproduce the slow screen, then answers with where the time went: self time by function, time by source file or package, and time by Nivaro’s own functions. The full .cpuprofile downloads from GET /api/ops-runtime/cpu-profile/<name> for Chrome DevTools; like the heap snapshot it lives in the temp directory until a restart. One profile runs at a time, no debug port is opened, each run is logged in Activity, and it is refused in cloud mode.

Administrator tools that use AI to read operations data — never to change it on its own. Ask the logs turns a question into the request list’s own filters; log alerts can be saved from a question or accepted from suggestions; in an admin-only chat channel the assistant answers from live operations data and proposes actions as approval cards; incident mode keeps a running thread in the ops channel.

On API Analytics and the Ops Console: type "errors for Beth yesterday afternoon" or "who called /items/orders most today". The question becomes the same filter object the request list uses (path, method, status class, caller, auth kind, errors, a time window, or "rank by caller / path"; or level + text over the server log). The filter shows as chips before anything runs — take any chip away. Run reads the normal admin routes (GET /api/api-analytics/requests, which now takes group=caller|path for a top-20 ranking, or GET /api/ops-logs/tail); "Open in the request list" fills the full list below. A person named in the question is matched to accounts on the server; when several match, pick one.
What reaches the AI provider: the question (scrubbed of tokens and secrets), the filter’s field names and allowed values, and the current time and your time zone. Never a log line, a path list or a list of people.
POST /api/ops-logs/ask { "question": "errors for Beth yesterday afternoon" }   (admin)
→ 200 { "data": { "filter": { "target": "requests", "errors": true, "user": "<id>", "user_label": "Beth Ng", "from": "…", "to": "…" },
                  …

blocks.h: Alerts from a question, and suggested alerts
blocks.t: • "Save as alert" stores the question’s filter as a log alert rule with a threshold, a window and a cooldown ("10 matches in 15 minutes, then quiet for 60"). A request-log rule is checked every 5 minutes (log-alert-requests job) across every server, against its own window — the question’s time words do not carry over; development instances never count. A server-log rule keeps working on each server as lines arrive. • Suggested log alerts (Ops Console) lists errors that keep coming back with no rule watching them: failing requests over the last 24 hours that happened in at least two different hours, and error lines in this server’s log seen in at least two different minutes. Each comes with the filter or pattern, a threshold (about twice the busiest quarter-hour) and a cooldown; Accept saves it as shown (origin "suggested"), Dismiss hides it in your browser. No AI is involved. • Rules: POST /api/ops-logs/rules { name, pattern?, level?, filters?, threshold?, window_minutes?, cooldown_minutes?, origin? }, PATCH /api/ops-logs/rules/:id { is_active?, threshold?, window_minutes?, cooldown_minutes? }, GET /api/ops-logs/rule-suggestions. Filters, thresholds and cooldowns need migration 442 (409 MIGRATION_PENDING before it).

blocks.h: The assistant in an ops channel
blocks.t:
In an admin-only channel — a private or admin-role channel whose every member is an active administrator, checked against the database each time a question is asked — an administrator can mention the assistant: "anything failing right now?", "why is the queue slow?". It reads request volume and errors, slow paths, circuit breakers, open issues, running / failed / paused background jobs, recent imports, failed partner pushes and readiness. In any other room, or for anyone who is not an administrator, the tools are not offered and a call is refused.
It may propose one action as an approval card: pause a background job, refuse or rate-limit a noisy caller or entity for some minutes (a circuit breaker), retry a failed partner push, or turn incident mode on or off. Nothing runs until an administrator presses Approve. Approval re-checks the approver and runs the action through the same admin route a person would use (/api/cron/:id/pause, /api/traffic-map/breakers, /api/erp-submissions/:id/retry, /api/ops-assistant/incident), as the approver; one decision per card; every proposal, approval and dismissal is logged as activity, and the outcome is posted under the card. People who are not administrators see only a link.
What reaches the AI provider from an ops channel: counts, method + path patterns (ids replaced by *), job ids and labels, issue titles, collection names and submission ids, scrubbed of tokens. Never request bodies, record values or people’s names.

• Pick the ops channel on the Ops Console (it must be admin-only; PUT /api/ops-assistant/channel { room }). If it later stops being admin-only, threads go quiet. • The ops channel, and any channel already holding assistant ops posts, only ever gains active administrators: joining, adding, bulk-adding and default-role auto-join refuse anyone else (403 OPS_CHANNEL_ADMINS_ONLY), and the channel cannot be opened to everyone or to a non-admin role. Every assistant ops post is flagged, and message lists, search, mentions, pins, saved messages and room summaries leave flagged posts out for anyone who is not an administrator. • Start incident mode from the Ops Console or an approved card (POST /api/ops-assistant/incident { on: true, title }). The assistant opens a thread in the ops channel and, every 2 minutes (ops-incident-updates job), posts what changed: new issues, server errors starting, rising, falling, recovering — plus every approved action. Ending it posts a summary: duration, the 5-minute error peak, issues seen and actions taken. • While incident mode is on, every administrator sees a slim banner across the app — "Incident in progress: <title> · started <time> · Open thread" (the ops channel). It appears and clears live: starting or ending sends a payload-free ops:incident notice to the admin-only ops watch room, and the tab re-reads GET /api/ops-assistant/incident (admin-only). Non-administrators never join the room or ask the route, and see nothing. • A critical alert (a new critical issue, or a critical integration signal with new rows) opens its own alert thread when no incident is on, feeds the incident thread when one is, and an alert thread closes with a summary after 30 quiet minutes. • Threads live in nivaro_ops_incidents (migration 442); GET /api/ops-assistant/incident returns the current one and the last ten.
The checks that tell you a deploy really landed, which versions are running where, and what changed shortly before something went wrong.

An API answering its new version is not enough: an extension mount can fail or readiness can drop while /api/version still answers. After a release, the verify stage (and the staging deploy gate) requires:
• GET /api/ready answers 200. • GET /api/preflight does not fail. • POST /api/ops-runtime/smoke?strict=1 passes. • The readiness score is no lower than a snapshot taken just before the deployments were pushed. Both reads run every check live (GET /api/readiness?fresh=1). It is read again once after a minute before the stage fails.
The Release card passes each API’s token from the Environments registry to the chain through its environment. Without a token only /api/ready is checked, and the plan says so; a token the API refuses fails the stage, so update it under Environments and resume from verify. On staging the extra checks run when the masked CI variable STAGING_GATE_TOKEN is set. A failing database or cache alone only warns, since the previous image would meet the same database.

Each release run stores how long each stage took, worked out from the run’s log. The Release card’s Stage timing table shows a trend per stage and highlights the slowest stage of each release. GET /api/release/timings returns the same.

Environments lists every environment variable the loaded extensions declare, per registered API, as set or unset. Values are never read. A variable set on one environment and missing on another is listed at the top ("EFP_OPS_TAKEOVER is set on staging, missing on production"). A component running an older build reads "older version" rather than missing.
GET /api/environments/env-presence/local   → this instance
GET /api/environments/env-presence         → every registered API, compared

Every front end reports the build it runs on each call (x-nivaro-client: build=…; api=…; tab=…; loaded=…) and in the socket’s client:hello. /realtime → Sockets & rooms lists open tabs per app and build, against the API version they first talked to. The list covers every API replica: each socket publishes its report on its own connection data, which every replica answers for; when one does not answer in time the page says only this replica’s tabs are counted. Each row names who is on that build.
Which build is current survives a rolling deploy. Admin is served by the API itself, so its current build is the one version every API replica serves (the instance roster) once a tab reports it; while replicas serve two versions, tabs on either of them are not judged and the "loaded before the API update" reason is off. Any other app takes its newest page load, but while two of its builds have loaded within 10 minutes those two read "Deploy in progress" and are not judged. Only the builds being rolled out are shielded: a tab on any older build of that app is old straight away. Force client refresh → Old versions reloads only tabs on another build, or loaded before the API update, on every replica, and leaves tabs on builds still rolling out alone (the toast says so). The Traffic Map’s Old tabs tile still counts per process over its window.
Administrators also see an "Old build" pill beside a person in the Online list (chat panel and /chat) while any of their tabs runs an old build; the tip names the app, the build and the current one. GET /presence/online sends stale_build to administrators only, and only for people with an old tab.
A custom front end reports its build with setClientBuild / installPageContextFetch({ build }). A tab that reports nothing groups as "Not reported"; builds named dev are never judged old.

blocks.h: Force refresh reaches tabs that were offline
blocks.t:
Force client refresh (on /realtime and a person’s admin tools) reaches the tabs connected at that moment, and is also remembered for 24 hours (FORCE_REFRESH_REMEMBER_HOURS, 0 = off; the newest 20 are kept, FORCE_REFRESH_REMEMBER_MAX). A tab that was asleep, offline or discarded gets it when its socket connects again — only if its page loaded before the refresh was pushed and it matches the target (everyone, one app, named people, or old versions as judged when it was pushed). A tab reloads at most once for one push: it remembers the pushes it reloaded for (per tab) and says so when it connects, and the server tells each tab at most once per page load. The Force refresh panel lists the remembered pushes with a Stop for each.
Minimum build (next to Force client refresh) is off until an administrator sets one, per app. Any tab of that app on an older build reloads after the countdown you choose (default 30 seconds, at least 5) with your optional message — the tabs open now, and every tab that connects later. Builds that read as versions compare as versions (0.3.9 is older than 0.3.12); any other build (a commit id) counts as older when it differs and the page loaded before the minimum was set. The panel shows how many open tabs a value would reload before you save it, and Turn off removes it. Every set, change and turn-off is in the activity log. A tab still on the old build after reloading twice (a cached bundle) is left alone.
One person at a time: an administrator opens anyone else's user card (their photo in chat, the Online list, a record or a list) or People → the person → Admin tools. Reload tabs pushes the same countdown banner to every tab they have open; Sign out (a second click confirms) ends every session they have on every app — the tabs go back to sign-in and their live connections close on every server. They can sign in again at once: suspend the account to keep them out. API keys and static tokens are not sessions and keep working. Each sign-out is in the activity log as sessions-revoke-user on that person.
A reload never throws away work. While the tab has unsaved changes — a record form, the layout editor, a payload template, a help-video recording, a useNivaroForm form, or saves waiting in the offline outbox — the banner reads "A reload is waiting — save or discard your changes" and reloads the moment they are saved or discarded; Reload now reloads at once. A custom front end reports its own forms with useUnsavedWork(dirty, label) or registerUnsavedWork(label, () => dirty).
POST   /api/realtime/force-refresh {user_ids, seconds?, message?}   → reload one person's tabs
POST   /api/security/users/:id/sign-out              → end every session of that person (admin; not yourself)
GET    /api/realtime/force-refresh/…

blocks.h: How fresh the readiness scorecard is
blocks.t:
A plain GET /api/readiness (the dashboard card, the Go-Live Readiness page) answers from the stored result of each check, at once. Every check carries computed_at (when it ran) and stale; the report carries computed_at (its oldest result), stale, refreshing and fresh. A result older than its window is shown as it was, flagged stale, and one background refresh re-runs it, six checks at a time (READINESS_REFRESH_CONCURRENCY) on one process per cluster (a Redis lock), and the finished scorecard reaches open pages over the live-ops socket.
• Window: 5 minutes (READINESS_TTL_MS). A heavy check — one that declares cost: 'heavy', or whose last run took 2 seconds or more — gets 30 minutes (READINESS_HEAVY_TTL_MS). A check can set its own ttlMs on registration. • Results are stored per tenant and per API version, so a deploy starts empty. A deployed instance evaluates them about 15 seconds after boot (CACHE_WARM, which follows the cron switch when unset). Until a check has run on this version it reads pending, and the score stays empty until none is pending. • ?fresh=1 (administrators) runs every check live. It is shared: a second fresh read joins one already running, and one within 10 seconds of a finished run gets that run. The page’s Re-run checks button, the release gate and the daily score snapshot use it. • A check that takes longer than two minutes reports an error rather than holding the scorecard.

blocks.h: Readiness checks for the deploy shape
blocks.t:
Check | Warns when / Every API process runs one version | The instance roster has held two API versions for longer than MIXED_VERSION_MINUTES (default 15): a rolling deploy that stalled or a replica left behind. Roster entries carry NIVARO_ROLE (web or worker), so it reads "2 web, 1 worker". / Only this deployment runs scheduled jobs on its database | Scheduled (not run-now) job runs from another instance landed in the last 24 hours, for example a laptop booted with CRON_TICKS=on against a shared database.
Every job run records the instance, process, how it was started (schedule, run now, chained, catch-up), whether its process had scheduled ticks on, and who held the scheduler lease. A scheduled run started by a process with ticks off raises one high-severity issue naming the job and the code path that started it. Shutting down or booting a process now only marks its own deployment’s running jobs as interrupted, never another instance’s.

blocks.h: Configuration changes on the incident timeline
blocks.t: Each burst of configuration writes appears once on the Ops Console incident timeline as config:change: the area (layout, pipeline, flow, schema, access, rules…), the tables, who saved it, the instance, and a link to the activity row of the save behind it. A latency shift or readiness drop can then be read against "layout 2 saved 20 minutes ago".

blocks.h: Development traffic in the shared request log
blocks.t:
When development machines share a database with a deployed instance, their requests would show as callers and failures there for 14 days. Request-log rows from development and test instances (and any named in API_LOGS_DEV_INSTANCES) are deleted after API_LOGS_DEV_TTL_HOURS (default 3, 0 = never). API Analytics shows deployed instances only by default; "Deployed instances" switches to all.
Setting | Default | What it changes / NIVARO_ROLE | unset | web or worker; shown in the roster and the version check. / MIXED_VERSION_MINUTES | 15 | How long two versions may run together before readiness warns. / API_LOGS_DEV_INSTANCES | unset | Extra instance names treated as development (comma list). / API_LOGS_DEV_TTL_HOURS | 3 | Hours development rows stay in the request log; 0 keeps them.

blocks.h: Early Hints (103) on the release image
blocks.t:
The release image can answer a page load with a 103 Early Hints response before the page itself: it names the entry script and its preloaded chunks, the stylesheet, the font origins and any font the entry stylesheet loads, so the browser starts fetching them while the HTML is still on its way. The list is read from the built index.html when the API starts, so it always names the files of the running build. The same list rides the page response as a Link header, which a CDN in front can turn into its own 103.
EARLY_HINTS | What is sent / unset / off | Nothing (the default — whether a 103 passes through depends on the proxy in front). / link | Only the Link header on the page response. / on | The 103 as well, to HTTP/1.1 and newer clients. HTTP/1.0 clients never get one.

Resting the pointer on a list row or a record link fetches that record and the form layout it opens with, so the record page paints at once. Resting on a menu link (or tabbing to it) loads that screen’s code. While the browser is idle, a list also fetches its next page (not while a search is applied: a searched page reads every searched column, and a search is rarely paged). A prefetched copy is at most a few seconds old and the page’s normal refresh replaces it. A tab makes at most 30 prefetch requests a minute, so sweeping the mouse down a long table never floods the API, and nothing is prefetched when the browser asks to save data.

When several environments share one database — a local machine and a staging server pointed at the same instance, for example — they also share the one settings row, which makes "use a local mail server in dev but keep the real relay on staging" impossible. Settings → This Instance solves that: each environment can overlay its own values on top of the shared settings, visible only to itself.

Each API process resolves its instance key from the NIVARO_INSTANCE environment variable, falling back to NODE_ENV. That fallback means a local dev process ("development") and a deployed container ("production") already read different override sets with zero setup — set NIVARO_INSTANCE explicitly only when you run two environments that would otherwise share a NODE_ENV.

• Overrides are read exactly where mail and SMS configuration is resolved — SMTP host/port/credentials/from, mail test mode and its allowlist, the environment label, and the SMS provider settings. Every other setting reads the shared row and is unaffected. • The This Instance tab offers exactly those keys. Set a value to override it for this instance; leave a value blank to clear the shared value and fall back to this instance’s environment variables. • A second layer exists for containers: the NIVARO_SETTINGS_OVERRIDES environment variable can hold a JSON object of the same keys, and it wins over anything set in the tab. It is read once at startup, so changing it requires a restart. • Saving replaces this instance’s whole override set — the tab always shows and submits the complete list.
The other Settings tabs (Email, SMS) keep showing and editing the shared row — deliberately, since that row serves every environment. So the Email tab can display SMTP values this particular instance is not actually using; check This Instance to see what is overlaid here.
Both the read (GET /api/settings/instance-overrides) and the save (PUT) are admin-only, and every save is audit-logged with the instance key and the keys it set.

Every email the instance sends is registered as a mail TYPE (Mail Templates → "Send a real one"): what it is, which Liquid template renders it, and how to build it from a real sample — a workflow transition, a changed record, a user, a recent inbox row. Pick a type, pick a sample, and you see the exact email production would send, its subject, and the people it would go to with the reason each is on the list. Send it to yourself, to any address, or (admin, logged, confirmed) to the real recipients. Mail test mode still applies to every send.

Type | Template | Sample / Workflow state change | workflow_transition | a workflow-history row — rendered THROUGH the delivering flow ("Workflows — notify owners" / "IR Approval — notify owners"), so subject and recipients are the flow's / Workflow canceled | workflow_canceled | a history row into a canceled state / Record you watch changed | record_watch | a recent activity row (record card + labelled old → new table) / Collection subscription | subscription | a recent activity row / Daily action summary | (built in code) | a user — the digest is built for them without flushing their deferred rows / Alert / Anomaly / SLA / Mention / Report / System / Workflow (generic) | notification | a recent inbox row of that category / Extension types (e.g. an extension's invoices-on-hold digest) | invoice_on_hold | registered by the extension through ctx.mail.registerType

• Record card — the record's title (display template), a link, and the fields the collection's ACTIVE grouped layout pins in its item-header strip. The card follows the layout, not a per-collection field list in code. • Approval path — every state in order: done (who, when), current (waiting on whom), upcoming (next owners). Cancel/reject branches only show once the record lands there. • What changed — labelled old → new pairs since the record entered the state it just left (transition mails) or in this write (watch mails); FK ids resolve to display labels. • The person's comment, only when a human wrote it — machine stamps (state merges, legacy syncs, imports) are never quoted back.
Flows keep owning WHEN an email goes out and to whom; a mail op's template option names the Liquid file that renders the body, with the full trigger payload (record_card, approval_chain, brief, actor_name…) as its context. Templates live in api/templates/mail (core) or <extension>/templates/mail; partials under partials/ are shared building blocks ({% render 'partials/record-card', card: record_card %}). The Templates tab edits any of them as a database override.

Every email ends with "You're getting this because …" and a link to the recipient's notification rules (in the app they use). The reason is per recipient: builders name it (assigned a task, approver for a step, watching a record, subscribed to a queue, delegate while someone is out), workflow transition mails read it off the trigger payload (owner of the new state, creator, additional contact), and anything without a stated reason falls back to the honest default — "your notification rules for <category> send you email".
• Flow mail ops: 'One email per recipient' (option split) sends each address its own copy — the footer and every link resolve for that person; 'Why-me line' (option why, templated) pins a shared reason for ops that mail one person per run. • Programmatic senders pass why to notifyUser / sendMail / sendRawMail, or put why in the template's data. • The rules link is the profile page — portal route key profile (Settings → Project → Frontend app), admin fallback /profile.

The chrome around every email — logo, accent colour, the "Sent by" name (also the From display name) and a footer line — can differ per workspace. Each workspace sets its own on the Workspaces page (Mail branding card); anything left blank keeps the instance branding from Settings → Project (project name, project colour), and with nothing set anywhere the stock chrome stands. A send resolves the workspace from an explicit workspace_id option, else the record it is about (its collection's workspace), else the recipient's current workspace. The From ADDRESS never changes — only its display name. The harness has a workspace picker beside the sample picker so every type can be previewed and sent as any workspace; the Workspaces page has a chrome-only preview of its own.

Data Tools → Notification Bench (admin). "Send me a sample of every category" delivers one real notification per category to you — through your own rules, so a category you switched off will not arrive, which is the point. The simulator takes a person + an event (category, subject, optional record, requested channels, "as of" time) and renders the exact delivery decision notifyUser would make: in-app, push, email (sent now / daily summary / off), SMS, with the reason for every kept or dropped channel (suspended, muted, matrix row, presence, quiet hours, digest mode, critical bypass, sender cadence), plus where the click lands in the portal and the admin and which inline action the row offers. Nothing is sent from the simulator.

Every notification carries a structured target (record, task, approval, access request, SLA, chat room, queue, report, alerts, issue, import, dashboard, My Work) plus the action a click should offer. Each app maps the target onto ITS routes — the admin opens /collections/:c/:id or /tasks, the portal opens /records/:c/:id or My Work — and when a host has no page for the kind, it falls back to the server-resolved URL for the recipient's preferred app (same origin = in-app, foreign = new tab). Rows can carry an inline action the server declares safe to fire from a click: Mark task done, Acknowledge SLA. Rows written before targets existed are derived from collection + item + subject.

People → Coverage → Delegation (/coverage): one page for absence coverage. Stat strip (out now, out in the next N days, people covering, expiring, uncovered, approvals at risk), a red "would go unowned" section for anyone out — or entering an OOO window within 24 hours — with no working delegate (none, expired, suspended, or out themselves) and the open items in states they cover, the out-now and coming-up rosters, who covers whom, delegations ending soon (an expired one while the person is still out is flagged), the records blocked right now (admin; the coverage-gap resolver), and your own Out-of-office card. Admins assign or change a delegate for someone inline.
GET  /api/delegation/overview?days=14
POST /api/delegation/:userId/delegate   { delegate_id, delegate_expires_at?, is_out_of_office? }   # admin

Mail Templates → In-app notifications (admin). The wording of every templatable notification event — workflow state change, record created/updated/deleted (subscriptions and watches), mention in a record note, mention in chat, task assigned — edited as Liquid over the event's tokens: the first line renders the subject, the rest the message. The preview renders against a REAL recent example pulled from this database (the newest matching transition, activity row, mention, task), or a placeholder when none exists yet, so the admin sees what people actually receive. Saving stores an override (a notification:<event> row in the mail-template table, same revert lifecycle as email templates); a template that fails to render, or renders an empty subject, is refused rather than silently falling back.
GET    /api/notification-templates            # events, tokens, override state
GET    /api/notification-templates/:key       # body (override or default) + real sample
POST   /api/notification-templates/:key/preview  { body?, data? } → { su…

Data Tools → Notification Analytics (admin). Over 7 / 30 / 90 days: notifications sent and read, the read rate and median time-to-read (read timestamps are stamped from this release on), a per-day series, and roll-ups by category, lane, kind, sender (people vs "System / automations") and collection — each with its own read rate and time-to-read — plus per-channel delivery outcomes (push sent vs no device, email sent / summary / off / failed) and the mute picture: how many people mute something, and which collections draw the most mutes against what they sent (the "stop telling me about this" rate).
Did it lead to action? A notification that points at a record counts as acted when its recipient moved that record, commented on it or finished a task on it within a window after it was sent (4, 24 or 72 hours; ?acted_hours=). The Acted column shows that share per category, kind, lane and sender, and Read, ignored shows how many were opened and still got no action, so a category people read but never act on stands out. Notifications younger than the window are left out, and ones that do not point at a record (chat, dashboards, alerts) are not counted.

Broadcasts → history → "who saw this?" now opens with a per-audience roll-up: by role and by every scope dimension (zone, region…), delivered / opened (the inbox row was read — known for the in-app message channel) / acknowledged (banner dismissed) / still unread, with the unread names. "Nudge N unread" re-sends a "Reminder: …" inbox row (+ push through the normal rules) to exactly those people and records it as a nudge delivery; a second click skips anyone already nudged unless again is set. The in-app delivery of a broadcast keeps the inbox row id it produced (notification_id on the delivery receipt), which is what makes "opened" knowable.

Broadcasts → Message → "Draft from bullets": write a few points, one per line, and AI drafts the message for the chosen audience, severity and channels — a short banner line (≤200 characters), a fuller email with a subject (also used for the in-app message), and an SMS of at most 160 characters (always cut to fit, whatever the model returns). "Use" copies a draft into the composer; you edit and send as usual — nothing is sent or saved by drafting. Anyone who may send a broadcast may draft one (POST /api/announcements/draft { bullets, audience, channels, severity }, admin). The AI provider receives your points (with secret-looking values masked) and an audience description of role names, scope-dimension labels and counts — never a recipient’s name, email or phone, nor which zone values were picked. It runs on the per-feature "generate" model; each draft is logged as broadcast-draft activity.

Mail Log → Delivery rolls the outbound log up over the last 7 / 14 / 30 days: sent / failed / dropped / deferred with the success rate (sent ÷ attempted), a per-day stacked chart, a per-template table (labelled with the mail type when one template maps to exactly one type; a row opens the log filtered to it), the busiest recipients, "Not reaching" (addresses whose LATEST attempt failed), and failure reasons grouped by the stable head of the SMTP error (addresses, ids and session tokens collapsed). Raw sends log a template name too (flow ops as flow:<op key>, the digest as daily_digest); rows older than that land in "Untemplated sends".
A red banner at the top of the board means the RELAY is failing, not the addresses: the newest 20 send attempts are judged as one, and when at least 80% failed with one normalised error class the banner names it and when the streak began. Mixed failure classes are bounces and never raise it. The readiness check mail-relay makes the same judgement (skip under 8 attempts, pass, fail); GET /api/mail-log/relay returns it as JSON.

A hard bounce — the relay refused the ADDRESS (5xx on RCPT/DATA with the address rejected, a 550/551/553/554 head, or "user unknown" / "mailbox unavailable" / "no such user" / "does not exist" in the reply) — marks the address in nivaro_mail_suppressions (address, reason, first/last seen, count). From then on every sender drops it: each dropped address gets its own mail-log row with status dropped and error "suppressed: <reason>", and a send with nothing left returns dropped without touching the relay. Soft refusals (4xx, greylisting, a dead relay) never suppress. The first time an address is marked, every administrator is told once (system category), and so is the person's manager when the address belongs to a user; a repeat bounce never pages anyone again. The person's profile header and their contact card show a rose "Email bouncing · since <date>" pill; Mail Log → Suppressed addresses lists, searches and clears the marks (activity mail-suppression-clear), and the Delivery board counts them. GET /api/mail-suppressions (admin), DELETE /api/mail-suppressions/:id (admin), GET /api/mail-suppressions/check?address= (signed in).

Links in emails resolve per recipient. Settings → Project → "Frontend app (portal)" names the headless app and its routes (record, queue, report, alerts, chat, tasks, approvals, my_work, home; a record:<collection> key gives one collection its own page). A recipient's profile choice ("Email links open in": Automatic / Portal / Admin) wins; otherwise admins get the admin console and everyone else the portal.
