A destination the portal has no route for falls back to the admin. Emails sent to a list in one go (the workflow transition flows) link the portal when one is configured. Extensions can register the portal through ctx.links.register; the Settings value wins when both exist. The harness shows the app each recipient would land in.

GET  /api/mail-types                      # every registered type
GET  /api/mail-types/:key/samples?q=      # real samples to pick from
POST /api/mail-types/:key/preview         # { sample_id } → { subject, html, recipients[] }
POST /api/ma…

Define data-quality rules per collection (nivaro_dq_rules) and run them on demand or on a schedule; each run (nivaro_dq_runs) records pass/fail counts and the offending rows. The /data-quality page shows rule health at a glance.

Type | Checks / not_null | Field has a value on every row / regex | Field matches a pattern / range | Numeric/date field within min–max / unique | No duplicate values in the field / formula | Custom expression evaluates truthy per row
• Each run lists failing rows with links straight into the item editor. • Failing rules can raise issues in the Issue Log automatically.

A central log of operational problems — failed syncs, data-quality breaches, webhook dead letters, manual reports — stored in nivaro_issues with severity and status. Triage from the /issues page.
Field | Values / severity | info | warning | error | critical / status | open | acknowledged | resolved
• Issues link back to their source (sync job, DQ run, webhook, record) where applicable. • Filter by severity, status, and source; resolve with an optional note. • Subsystems raise issues automatically; users and extensions can create them via POST /api/issues.

Server 5xx responses and admin UI render crashes are captured into the Issues log automatically — no external service required.
• Server: any unhandled error on an /api route creates an issue with route, message, and stack. • Client: the admin error boundary reports crashes via POST /api/issues/client with the component stack. • Dedupe: repeats of the same error (fingerprint of source + route + message) bump occurrence_count on the open issue instead of flooding the list. • Resolving an issue and hitting the error again opens a fresh issue — regressions surface as new rows.
Issues appear at /issues with severity high, source server or client, and a live last-seen timestamp.

Settings → Backups downloads a logical backup of the instance: a gzip stream of newline-delimited JSON, one record per row, with a meta header line describing the export.
GET /api/backups/export?include_system=true   (admin)
GET /api/backups/manifest?include_system=true  (admin — what would be exported)

// stream shape (gunzip → one JSON object per line)
{"type":"nivaro-backup","version":1,"exported_at":"…"…
• Business collections come from the schema registry (physical tables only). • include_system=true adds nivaro_* configuration tables — schema registry, roles, policies, workflows, layouts. • Volatile/derived tables are always excluded: sessions, API logs, page views, embeddings, queue caches, migrations. • Files on disk/object storage are not part of the stream — back the storage root or bucket up separately.
Export only. Restore into a live instance is intentionally not offered through the API.

Telemetry → Disaster recovery answers one question: if the database server died now, how much would be lost and how long would getting back take? It judges each source against two stated targets — the RPO (recovery point objective: the most data a disaster may lose) and the RTO (recovery time objective: how long getting back may take) — and colours each row green, amber or red with the reason in words. Administrators only.
Row | Read from | Judged / Database backup | msdb: newest full, differential and log backup of this database | Age against the RPO: amber up to 1.5×, red beyond, red when no full backup exists / Uploads backup | The monitoring store metric efp_backup_last_success_timestamp_seconds{part=~"uploads.*"} | Age against the RPO; amber "Not reported" until the uploads backup pushes it / Restore drill | The newest restore drill (below) | Red when it failed or never ran, amber when it could not run or is over 2 days old, red over 8 days / Measured restore time | The newest passed drill | Against the RTO: green up to 75 %, amber up to 100 %, red beyond / Chaos drill recovery | Chaos drills of the last 90 days (GET /api/chaos/trends → recovery) | p90 time to recover against the RTO; grey when no drill measured one
GET   /api/telemetry/recovery            the panel: targets, backups, drill, chaos, judged rows (?fresh=1 re-reads msdb)
PATCH /api/telemetry/recovery/settings   {targets:{rpo_minutes,rto_minutes}, runbook_url, restore_drill:{…}}
POST  /api…

A backup that has never been restored is not a backup. The restore-drill job (nightly 02:30, or Run restore drill) restores the newest full backup of this database — plus the differential taken on top of it — into a scratch database, checks the copy, records how long the restore took, and always drops the copy afterwards.
• Off by default. Turn it on per instance in the panel’s settings, or with RESTORE_DRILL=on (RESTORE_DRILL=off forces it off). Never on cloud instances. The scheduled run ticks only where scheduled jobs tick. • The scratch database must start with nivaro_restore_drill_ (default nivaro_restore_drill_<database>, or RESTORE_DRILL_DB). It may never be this instance’s own database, master, msdb, model, tempdb or EFP / EFP_Development / EFP_Staging. Before any RESTORE the run records an ownership claim on its job row (no claim, no restore). A database already under that name is dropped only when the newest claim on it belongs to a run that never confirmed dropping it; anything else refuses the run. A copy the drill cannot mark or drop fails the drill. • Backups must be disk files the SQL Server can open (local, mapped or UNC paths; striped sets included). Backups taken by a backup agent (virtual device — Cohesity, NetBackup, Veeam), tape or URL are reported as "not restorable by path". When the newest full went to an agent but a full backup on disk exists, the drill restores the disk one and says so. • Log backups are not applied: the copy is the full (+ differential) point, and the result says how many log backups came after it. • Smoke check: the nivaro_ key tables (plus any business tables listed in the settings) must exist in the copy and hold rows wherever they hold rows live. Row counts and CHECKSUM_AGG over small configuration tables are recorded beside the live ones; differences are expected (the copy is older) and never fail the drill. DBCC CHECKDB (physical only) is optional. • The login needs CREATE ANY DATABASE (dbcreator) and SELECT on msdb, and the SQL Server needs disk for a full copy (checked against the target volume before restoring). Each missing piece is recorded as the reason the drill could not run. • Each run’s result lives on its nivaro_job_runs row (job restore-drill, progress column) — no table of its own. Jobs shows the runs; a failed drill reads failed there.
A drill restores a full-size copy of the database on the same SQL Server: it costs disk and IO for the length of the restore. Point the data and log folders at a volume with room, and keep it off on servers that share disk with something that cannot spare it.

Targets default to RPO 24 h and RTO 4 h. Settings live under the recovery key of this instance’s settings overrides (each environment keeps its own); env variables win and survive a database rebuilt from another one.
Env variable | Effect / RESTORE_DRILL=on|off | Forces the drill on or off over the setting / RESTORE_DRILL_DB | Scratch database name (must start with nivaro_restore_drill_) / RECOVERY_RPO_MINUTES / RECOVERY_RTO_MINUTES | The stated targets / DR_RUNBOOK_URL | The disaster-recovery runbook link on the panel (hidden when unset)
Ask AI on the Telemetry page (and the ops assistant) has a recovery_status tool with the same judged rows, so "could we recover right now?" and "did last night’s restore drill pass?" answer from the same facts. The Database page’s Overview tab shows a red strip while any recovery row is red.

Move records between instances (staging → production) with a diff preview. Export a bundle on the source, load it on the target, review per-collection create/update/unchanged counts, then apply.
POST /api/promotion/export  { "collections": ["projects", "regions"] }
POST /api/promotion/preview { "bundle": { … } }   // diff only, no writes
POST /api/promotion/apply   { "bundle": { … } }   // id-keyed upsert
• Upserts by primary key: changed rows update, missing rows insert (identity PKs handled), matching rows skip. • Never deletes target data, and only writes columns that exist on the target table. • Business collections only, capped at 10,000 rows per collection per bundle. • Admin-only; exports and applies are activity-logged.
Apply is a write operation on production data — always read the preview table first. The admin page (System → Content Promotion) enforces this order.

Answers "where is this file referenced, and can I safely delete it?". Discovery is foreign-key driven: every column with a FK into nivaro_files counts as a usage site.
GET /api/files/:id/usage        → { usages: [{ table, column, count }], total }
GET /api/files/usage/orphans    → files referenced by nothing (admin)
• Files page: the link icon on each row shows referencing tables and counts; "Not referenced anywhere" means safe to delete. • The All / Unused toggle in the header lists orphaned files — deletion candidates. • Columns holding file ids without a real FK constraint are invisible to the scan — add the constraint rather than special-casing.

Roles → Simulator answers "what would a user with this role see?" by running the same checks the API enforces: policy match, field allow-list, row-level security, tree permissions, and hidden admin pages.
POST /api/roles/:id/simulate   (admin)
{ "collection": "projects", "action": "read", "item_id": "42" }

→ { "allowed": true,
    "reason": "Allowed by the 'projects' 'read' policy",
    "fields": null,                 // null = all fields
 …
• Every verdict carries a reason — which policy matched (exact vs wildcard) or why access is denied. • Pass item_id to evaluate subtree rules for a specific record. • Admin-access roles short-circuit: all checks bypass.

Data Model → ERD renders the whole schema as an interactive entity-relationship diagram: every registered collection as a node, every relation as an edge.
• M2M junction pairs collapse into a single dashed edge labeled with the junction table. • Hover a table to highlight its relations and neighbors; the FK field name appears on each highlighted edge. • Scroll to zoom, drag to pan, search to highlight, click a table to open it in the Table Editor. • Layout groups connected tables near each other automatically.

The Infrastructure page at /infrastructure (Operations → Health) shows the Docker hosts this instance runs on: stacks and containers, rolling updates, healthchecks, the swarm itself and its secrets. It is read-only and for administrators. Nivaro never mounts the Docker socket: a deployment runs a socket proxy that allows GET requests only, on an internal network, and names it in DOCKER_HOSTS (name=url pairs, comma-separated) or DOCKER_API_URL. Each host is read separately, so a host that does not answer shows its error and the others still render. In cloud mode the page is off.
The tabs are grouped: Overview; Workloads (Stacks, Containers, Updates, Health); Swarm (Swarm, Secrets); Hosts (Hosts, Resources, Reboot, Logs); Images and storage (Volumes, Images, Provenance); Proxy and build (Proxy, GitLab). On a wide screen they sit in one strip with a thin rule between groups, and the strip scrolls when it does not fit. On a narrow screen a single button shows the current view and opens the grouped list, which you can also type into. Every Docker-backed tab shows one section per host with the host name and its status on the right; a host that does not answer says so in that place. Long lists (a host with hundreds of containers, many images) show the first rows with a button for the rest. This section covers Stacks, Updates, Health, Swarm and Secrets, and how to ask about all of it in plain words. Containers, Volumes, Images and Provenance are in “Containers, volumes and images”; Proxy, Resources and GitLab are in “Proxy, resources and GitLab”; Hosts, Reboot and Logs are in “Host health, reboot and logs”.
Tabs that read swarm services, tasks, nodes or secrets need the matching sections switched on in the proxy (INFO, CONTAINERS, SERVICES, TASKS, NODES, SECRETS). Keep SWARM and CONFIGS off: Nivaro never reads them, because the swarm section returns the join tokens and the configs section returns config contents. A section the proxy refuses is reported on the tab; everything else still shows. Whatever the Engine answers, environment variables, join and unlock keys, credential-looking label values and secret command-line arguments are removed on the server before anything is cached or sent to the page.

The Stacks tab lists, per host, every swarm stack with its services, and every compose project with its containers. A counts strip at the top gives services, running against desired replicas, failing services and containers. The filter box matches stack, service, image and error text; Failing only hides everything that is fine.
• Each service shows running / desired replicas, its image with a short digest, its update state, published ports and when it last changed. A service is failing when fewer tasks run than it wants, when its update is paused or rolling back, or when a slot has nothing running and its newest task failed or cannot be scheduled. The reason is written under the name, with the engine’s own message (for example “no suitable node” or “No such container”). • Expand a service to see its tasks: the newest four per slot, failed history included, with the node, image, state (and the state the swarm wants), error and times. • On a swarm worker only that node’s own task containers are visible; services and other nodes’ tasks are read from a manager. A host outside a swarm shows its compose projects and standalone containers.

The Updates tab follows rolling updates. Services with an update in flight come first, with the update policy in words (order, parallelism, delay, monitor window, failure action) and the rollback policy. While any update is in flight the tab refreshes every 5 seconds, otherwise every minute.
• Latest rollout, slot by slot: the old task and the new one that replaced it, how long the new task took to reach running and to pass its healthcheck, retries, and with start-first ordering how long old and new ran side by side. • When the failure action fires the service says so (paused after a failure, rolling back, rolled back). Services set to roll back on failure carry an auto-rollback tag. • Rollouts in the task history: past updates read back from the tasks the swarm still remembers, grouped by the image (and forced-update counter) they ran. A rollback to an earlier image counts as its own rollout. History is as long as the swarm’s task history limit, five tasks per slot by default. A duration marked “at least” is a lower bound because some of its tasks have since stopped. • Time to healthy is only known for containers on the host being read that have a healthcheck.

The Health tab lists every container with a healthcheck: its health now, how many times it turned unhealthy in the last 24 hours, and when its health last changed. Click a container for its detail: the last probes with exit code, duration and output (trimmed), the failing streak, restarts, how long it took from start to healthy, and its recent changes.
Docker keeps only the last five probes, so Nivaro keeps the changes itself: every time the tab is read, and every 2 minutes by the infra-health-sample background job, each container’s health is compared with the last one recorded and a change is stored in Redis for 3 days. A flap shorter than the sampling gap can be missed. The job only runs on deployed instances, like every scheduled job. Containers whose image carries the org.opencontainers.image.version label are also grouped by that version, so a release that flaps more than the last one stands out.

The Swarm tab shows the managers and whether each is reachable and which one leads, every node with its role, state, availability, engine version, size and labels, and the cluster settings: node certificate lifetime, task history kept, autolock, external CA, Raft snapshot and tick settings, dispatcher heartbeat, data path port and address pool.
• Warnings appear when managers are unreachable (and whether quorum is lost), when there are exactly two managers (they tolerate no failure), when no manager leads, when a node is not ready, and during a root CA rotation. • The node certificate expiry date comes from the host-facts collector (metric nivaro_host_swarm_node_cert_expiry_seconds in the telemetry store). It warns under 14 days. Without the collector the tab says host facts are not collected. • Autolock is shown for information only. Keeping it off lets hosts restart unattended. • The cluster settings come from the manager’s system info, never the swarm section (which carries the join tokens). A setting the engine does not report there shows as unknown.

The Secrets tab maps swarm secrets and configs to the services that use them. Versions named with a suffix such as _v1, _v2 are grouped under one name with the newest first. Flags mark secrets no service uses and services still on an older version while a newer one exists. Configs are listed only by the names service specs reference: their contents are never read, so a config no service uses does not appear.
Only names and dates are shown. Docker never returns secret values, and Nivaro never reads configs (their contents can hold credentials).

Administrators can ask about the infrastructure in plain words. The Ask box on the Telemetry page and the admin-only operations chat channel have twelve read-only infrastructure tools beside the telemetry ones: they read the same Docker hosts, swarm, proxy and host facts as the tabs above, cut down to counts and the top rows. Nothing they do changes anything, and they never return secret values or config contents: the secrets tool gives names and which services use them. A tool whose source is not set up says so instead of guessing.
Question | What the answer reads / What restarted today and why? | infra_containers (started in the last 24 hours, exit status, flapping health), then infra_stacks (failed tasks and engine errors) and infra_updates (rollouts that paused or rolled back). / What is eating /var? | infra_logs (log growth, days until full, containers with no rotation), then infra_storage (volumes, images, what a prune would free). / Would anything stay down after a reboot? | infra_reboot, with infra_hosts for pending kernels and hung IO. / Which routers have no healthy backend? | infra_proxy. / Which containers are throttled? | infra_resources (CPU throttling, memory headroom, out-of-memory kills). / When do swarm certificates expire? Is any secret unused? | infra_swarm and infra_secrets. / Is CI healthy? | infra_gitlab. / Did anyone change a running service by hand? | infra_drift (see Stack drift).
The same figures are offered to connected apps (Claude, ChatGPT, Codex) as MCP tools with the same names, for administrators only. Each one reads GET /api/infrastructure/summary/<tool>, which accepts host, limit and (for infra_resources) window = 24h or 7d. A connection that is not an administrator does not see the tools, and the API refuses the route to anyone else.

Four tabs on the Infrastructure page list what runs on each Docker host: Containers, Volumes, Images and Provenance. They read through the same read-only Docker proxy as the rest of the page, set up as described in the Infrastructure overview, and nothing on them changes a host.

Every container on the host with its owner (swarm stack, compose project and service, or none), state, restart policy, age and image. Three things are flagged and sorted to the top. A container with no owner was started by hand with docker run and nothing redeploys it. A container stopped for more than 7 days still holds its volumes. A container in a compose project but started from a different working directory than the rest of that project is the dangerous case: running docker compose up --remove-orphans from the project directory would remove it.

Named volumes and bind mounts with size, owning stack or project, the containers using each, and last write time when the host facts collector reports it. Orphaned volumes (used by no container) are listed first, largest first, with the total space they would free. A volume counts as backed up when its name or path matches INFRA_BACKED_UP_VOLUMES (a comma list of names or globs) or it carries the label nivaro.backup=true. A volume in use that is not covered is flagged.

Images split into in use, unused and dangling, with size, shared size, how many containers use each, and the build cache total and reclaimable part. A preview lists what docker system prune would remove: the stopped containers by name (a prune during a deploy deletes stopped containers mid-task), dangling images, unused networks and unused build cache, and with -a the images no container uses. The preview only reads.

For each running container whose image carries OCI labels, or whose repository starts with an entry in INFRA_OWN_IMAGES, the tag, digest, git revision (linked when the image source label is a web URL), build date and age. For the Nivaro image the version label is compared with this API and shown as how many releases behind. Your own images running :latest, running untagged, or with no revision label are flagged as not from the release pipeline.
Setting | Meaning / INFRA_BACKED_UP_VOLUMES | Comma list of volume names or globs that have a backup. / INFRA_OWN_IMAGES | Comma list of repository prefixes that are your own images.
Three tabs on the Infrastructure page read from sources other than the Docker hosts: Proxy, Resources and GitLab. Like the rest of the page they are for administrators and only read.

Set TRAEFIK_API_URL to the Traefik API on an internal network (add TRAEFIK_API_TOKEN, or TRAEFIK_API_USER and TRAEFIK_API_PASSWORD, if it is protected). The tab lists every router with its rule, entrypoints, priority, middleware chain, TLS and target service, with each backend server marked up or down. A router whose servers are all down is flagged. Traefik v2 and v3 both work.
When two routers share an entrypoint and one has a broader PathPrefix with a higher priority, the tab says so in plain words, for example "Requests for /api/x go to router A, not router B". When no priority is set, Traefik uses the rule length, and the tab shows that. Request rate and 5xx rate per router appear when Traefik metrics reach the telemetry store.

Per container CPU, share of CPU periods throttled, memory against its limit, out-of-memory kills, network and disk, from cAdvisor metrics in the telemetry store. Switch between 24 hours and 7 days, and sort by any column. A container is flagged when more than 10 percent of its CPU periods were throttled or its memory is over 85 percent of its limit. A limit of 0 shows as "no limit".

Uses the GitLab URL and token of a GitLab component on the Environments page; the token is never shown. The tab shows readiness and liveness, the version, runners (online, offline, stale after a day without contact, or never contacted), the number of pending jobs and how long the oldest has waited, and the GitLab container CPU and memory. Health checks only answer to GitLab’s monitoring allowlist, so add this server there or set GITLAB_HEALTH_TOKEN. Set GITLAB_CONTAINER to a name pattern if the container is not called gitlab. Each part reports on its own if it cannot be read.
Without an administrator token, runners and pending jobs fall back to what the token can see and to the projects mapped on Environments.

Three tabs on the Infrastructure page look at the Docker hosts themselves: Hosts (patches, reboot and IO health), Reboot (which containers come back after a reboot) and Logs (container log size and rotation). They are read-only and for administrators.

Some facts can only be read on the host: the kernel, pending updates, processes stuck on IO, NFS messages, remote mounts in /etc/fstab and container log sizes. deploy/host-facts/nivaro-host-facts.sh collects them every minute (the slow parts every 30 minutes) and writes them as node_exporter textfile metrics named nivaro_host_*. The telemetry store collects them and the Infrastructure page reads them from there. Nivaro never runs anything on a host.
• Install the script and its systemd timer as the README beside it describes, or, without sudo on the host, run it as a container (Dockerfile and compose.example.yml in the same folder) with no extra capability and only the host paths it reads mounted read-only. • Set NIVARO_HOST_NAME to the name the host has in DOCKER_HOSTS, so its facts line up with its containers. • Point node_exporter (or Alloy) at the textfile folder. Until the first figures arrive the tabs say "Host facts are not collected".

For each host: the running and newest installed kernel, whether a reboot is needed, days since the last boot, free space on /boot (under 100 MB is flagged, because the next kernel update may fail), pending security updates and how long ago the facts were collected.
It also tells you when a host is stuck waiting on IO: processes in D state, kernel hung-task messages, NFS servers that stopped answering, and a high load while the CPU is mostly idle — for example "Load 22 while the CPU is 90% idle — processes are waiting on IO, likely the mount /mnt/data". The readiness check host-hung-io warns when any host shows these signs.

Every running container gets a verdict for what happens when its host reboots:
Verdict | When / Comes back | A swarm task (swarm reschedules it unless the service restart condition is none), or restart policy always / unless-stopped. / Stays down | Restart policy no or on-failure outside swarm, or a swarm service with restart condition none. / May come back broken | It uses a remote mount (NFS, CIFS…) that docker.service does not wait for at boot, so it can start against the empty mount point.
Each host also lists remote mounts without nofail in /etc/fstab: if their server is down while the host boots, the host can stop in emergency mode. The readiness check reboot-survivability warns when any container would stay down.
Temporary containers are not judged and are listed under the table instead: a container started with docker run --rm, and a GitLab CI job container (labels com.gitlab.gitlab-runner.*). Neither is meant to come back, and a CI build running on the host while a deploy gate looked used to turn the check to warn.

For each container: its log driver, its rotation (max-size and max-file), the size of its log file and how much it grew in the last day. A json-file log without max-size is flagged, because it grows until the disk is full. Each host shows the total, the daily growth and, from the free space on the filesystem that holds the Docker root, about how many days until it fills.

Someone runs docker service update by hand on a server to fix something quickly. The next deploy quietly undoes it, or quietly keeps it, and nobody decided which. Stack drift catches this: after every deploy the deploy script stores what each service looked like (the baseline), and every night Nivaro compares the running services with it. Differences show on the Environments page and administrators get one notification per new difference.

• Image: repository and digest. A different tag on the same digest is the same image. • Environment variables, one by one. Only a short list of settings that never hold a secret keeps its value in clear (NODE_ENV, NIVARO_ROLE, LOG_LEVEL, CRON_TICKS, PUBLIC_URL, ADMIN_URL and the like, plus number-only sizing settings such as DB_POOL_MAX or WEB_REPLICAS); every other value, and any value carrying password=, token=, key=, secret=, sig= or user:password@ in a URL, is kept only as a keyed hash. The page says “Value changed (not shown)” for those, never the value. • Mounts (type, source, target, read-only), secrets and configs (name and target), mode and replicas, CPU and memory limits and reservations, placement constraints and preferences. • User, read-only root filesystem, added and dropped capabilities, healthcheck, command and arguments, update, rollback and restart settings (values equal to the swarm default are ignored, so a docker service inspect and a plain Engine read compare equal). • Service and container labels, traefik labels included. Only the labels a stack deploy writes itself (com.docker.stack.namespace, com.docker.stack.image) and swarm labels are ignored. • A service in the baseline that is not running is "missing"; a service in the stack that is not in the baseline is "extra".
Version numbers, timestamps, the update status and assigned ports are never compared. When the service spec version moved after the baseline, the difference is marked "Hand-run update" (and, when swarm kept the deployed spec as the previous one, "one docker service update after the deploy"). A new service id is marked "Recreated".

The deploy script calls this after a deploy has converged, with an administrator token. It answers 200 with what it stored; the deploy must not fail if it does not.
POST /api/infrastructure/drift/baseline
{
  "stack": "efp",
  "environment": "production",
  "version": "0.3.4",
  "release": "efp-2026.10.22-1",
  "services": [ …docker service inspect output… ]
}
• services is the array docker service inspect prints for the stack's services (at most 200, 8 MB). Services of another stack are left out and listed in the answer as ignored. Only the compared fields are stored. • Leave services out and Nivaro reads the stack itself from the Docker host named like the environment in DOCKER_HOSTS (or the only host, or the one named in "host"). • A new baseline replaces the previous one for that stack and environment (the last 10 are kept) and closes its open differences.

The infra-drift-check job runs at 03:15 on instances that tick scheduled jobs and have a Docker host configured. It reads each stack through the read-only Docker proxy, never the Docker socket. Check now on the Environments card runs it at once (POST /api/infrastructure/drift/check, optionally with stack and environment).
Without a Docker host the card says "No live source — set DOCKER_HOSTS" instead of claiming there is no drift: nothing was compared. The hashes are keyed with the instance's SESSION_SECRET: without one, baselines are refused (503) and checks fail rather than hash with a fixed key; if it changes, hashed values can no longer be compared until the next baseline, and the check says so. One check per stack and environment runs at a time across replicas (a Redis lease), so the nightly job and Check now never record or alert the same difference twice.

• Environments → Stack drift: one row per environment and stack with the baseline (version, release, when), the last check and the number of drifted fields. Open a row for deployed versus running values per field. • Infrastructure → Stacks: a one-line summary that links to Environments. • Ask AI and connected apps: the infra_drift tool (GET /api/infrastructure/summary/infra_drift) lists drifted fields; it names environment variables but never returns their values. • Notifications: administrators are told once per new difference, with a link to the row. A difference nobody could be told about is offered again on the next check.
Administrators only, and not available in cloud mode. GET /api/infrastructure/drift returns the stored status for the page.

Nivaro ships as one Docker image that holds the API and the admin app: nodeworks/nivaro:<version>. A second, smaller image, nodeworks/nivaro:<version>-slim, leaves out Chromium and ffmpeg. Both are built from Dockerfile.release for amd64 and arm64, and both are signed.
Image | Build target | What it has / nodeworks/nivaro:<v> (and latest) | runner (the default) | Everything. Makes PDFs and help videos itself. / nodeworks/nivaro:<v>-slim (and latest-slim) | runner-slim | No Chromium, no ffmpeg, no fonts (about 800 MB smaller). Sends that work to a render server, see below.

The API, Chromium and ffmpeg run as the node user (uid 1000, gid 1000). The container starts as root, like the postgres and redis images: the entrypoint hands /app/work to uid 1000 (and /app/uploads when it is empty), then switches to node with su-exec. tini stays process 1. The image owns /app/uploads and /app/work as uid 1000, so a new named volume gets the right owner the first time.
Situation | What happens / New or empty volume on /app/uploads | Handed to uid 1000; the API runs as node. / Volume with files uid 1000 cannot write (made by an image older than 0.3.5, or NFS with root_squash) | Nothing is changed and the API keeps running as root, so uploads keep working. One line in the log names the fix. / The switch is refused (cap_drop: ALL removes CAP_SETUID and CAP_SETGID) | The API keeps running as root with one warning line. TMPDIR and HOME move under /tmp when root may not write uid 1000's folders. / The deployment sets user: (for example user: 1000:1000) | That user is used as is; the entrypoint only creates TMPDIR and HOME and warns when /app/uploads is not writable. / NIVARO_RUN_AS=root | Stays root on purpose.
To finish the move to uid 1000 on an old volume, change its owner once, for example docker run --rm -v nivaro_uploads:/app/uploads alpine chown -R 1000:1000 /app/uploads. The entrypoint never runs chown -R itself: on a large share it can take hours, and NFS with root_squash refuses it. It decides from the top folder and its first 50 entries.

The process writes only to the three paths below, so you can run it with a read-only root filesystem (read_only: true, docker run --read-only).
Path | What goes there | Mount / /app/uploads | Stored files (local storage driver). | A volume. Keep it. / /app/work | TMPDIR=/app/work/tmp: scratch files, help-video uploads in progress, renders and the music cache (VIDEO_WORK_DIR defaults here), heap snapshots, Chromium profiles, render-server inputs. HOME=/app/work/home: font and browser caches. | A volume, or a tmpfs owned by uid 1000 (--tmpfs /app/work:uid=1000,gid=1000). The entrypoint creates tmp and home when they are missing. / /tmp | Anything a library writes there directly. | A tmpfs.
Installing, enabling or disabling an extension from the admin writes to /app/api/extensions. On a read-only root that fails unless the extensions folder is mounted writable. Deployments that mount their extensions read-only manage them outside the app.

The entrypoint is ["/sbin/tini", "--", "/app/docker-entrypoint.sh"] and the command is node api/dist/index.js. tini passes SIGTERM to the API, so docker stop runs the API drain, and it cleans up Chromium and ffmpeg processes left behind by a crash. If you override the command (for example sh -c "...; exec node api/dist/index.js"), the entrypoint still runs first.

The image has a HEALTHCHECK, so plain docker run and Compose show a health status too. It checks liveness only: /app/healthcheck.sh calls GET /api/version with busybox wget every 30 seconds (5 second timeout, 3 retries). The 150 second start period covers migrations at boot. In cloud mode it calls /api/ready, which needs no tenant. NIVARO_HEALTHCHECK_PATH changes the path. Readiness for traffic is a separate question; use /api/ready for that.

blocks.h: Node heap from the memory limit
blocks.t:
Node 22 sets its heap to about half of the container memory limit (measured: 524 MB at 1 GB, 1328 MB at 2.5 GB) and cannot change it after it starts. At start, the entrypoint reads the limit (cgroup v2 /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max, otherwise cgroup v1 /sys/fs/cgroup/memory/memory.limit_in_bytes) and adds --max-old-space-size=<75% of the limit in MB> to NODE_OPTIONS. For example, a 2560 MB limit gives 1920 and a 1536 MB limit gives 1152.
• Nothing is added when there is no limit (max, the cgroup v1 "unlimited" value, or more than the host has), when the limit is under 256 MB, or when NODE_OPTIONS already sets --max-old-space-size. • NIVARO_HEAP_FROM_CGROUP=off turns it off. • NODE_OPTIONS is exported, so a node process started by a wrapper command gets the flag too.

blocks.h: The slim image and the render server
blocks.t:
A slim process has no Chromium and no ffmpeg. When RENDER_URL is set, it sends PDFs, video probes, recording remuxes, uploaded-video conversions and music conversions to that process. The answers are the same as when the work runs locally. Without RENDER_URL, that work fails with a 503 that says what is missing.
Setting | Where | What it does / RENDER_URL | Slim processes | Address of a full process, with no path, for example http://nivaro_worker:3055. Plain http: is accepted only for loopback, a single-label name, a swarm tasks.<service> name, a name with _, or a private address (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x, IPv6 fc00::/7). Anything else must be https:. No user or password in the URL. / RENDER_TOKEN | Both sides | Shared secret, at least 32 characters (for example openssl rand -hex 32), sent as Authorization: Bearer <token>. On the full process it turns on the render routes; without it, or when it is shorter, they do not exist (the log says why). RENDER_TOKEN_FILE and /run/secrets work as for every secret. / RENDER_PEER_CLOUD=on | Full process, cloud mode | In cloud mode the render routes stay off unless this is also set. The render server is tenant-agnostic: it renders for anyone holding the token, and each job's private scratch folder (mode 0700, deleted afterwards) is the only separation between jobs. / RENDER_PEER_PDF_CONCURRENCY / RENDER_PEER_FILE_CONCURRENCY | Full process | How many PDFs and how many file jobs run at once (default 2 each). Up to 16 more wait, for at most a minute; after that the caller gets 503 RENDER_BUSY. / RENDER_PEER_SCRATCH_MB | Full process | Disk the file jobs may use at once in TMPDIR (default 6144). Past it: 503 RENDER_BUSY. / NIVARO_IMAGE_VARIANT | Set by the image | slim or full. A slim process never takes help-video renders, clips or other media jobs. / MEDIA_WORKER | Full process | on makes this process the media worker, off never. Unset: a full process that ticks crons and is not NIVARO_ROLE=web.

Every feature works on a slim process. Work a request waits on goes to the render server (RENDER_URL). Work that ends in a stored file or result, made in the background, goes to the media worker: the slim process saves the job (the clip row, the caption job, the upload, the export request) and puts its id on a Redis list; the media worker picks it up within seconds, makes it exactly as it would for its own request, and the author sees it finish in the same place as always. Nothing large crosses between them: the worker reads the same storage and database.
Feature | Needs | On a slim process / PDFs (layouts, dossiers, scheduled reports, Report Studio) | Chromium | Render server / Help-video upload checks, recording remux, picked-file conversion | ffmpeg | Render server / Background music conversion, music folder and package import probes | ffmpeg | Render server / Encoder report on the help-video settings page | ffmpeg | Render server (GET /api/internal/render/encoders) / Help-video renders, with cards, annotations and music | Chromium + ffmpeg | Render queue owner (VIDEO_RENDER=on); a slim publish kicks it at once / Clips and GIFs | ffmpeg | Media worker / Generated captions (reading the sound) | ffmpeg | Media worker / Upload thumbnails and waveform | ffmpeg | Media worker / Session-replay video (WebM) export | Chromium + ffmpeg | Media worker / Session-replay HTML export | nothing | Here
The media worker is a full process that ticks crons and is not NIVARO_ROLE=web (the worker of a web + worker stack), or any full process with MEDIA_WORKER=on; MEDIA_WORKER=off keeps a process out. It checks in every 30 seconds (Redis key nvr:media-worker:<database>, 90 s) and drains one job of each kind at a time on the background database pool. Keys carry the database name (and REDIS_CHANNEL_PREFIX in front), so two instances on one Redis never take jobs meant for the other. A slim process hands work off only while a worker has checked in; with none, the request is refused at once with a 503 that says so. Queued jobs wait on nvr:media-handoff:<database>:<kind> while the worker restarts; at most 500 of a kind wait (past that, 503 RENDER_BUSY), and at most 5 replay videos per person (429). A queued replay video is recorded until it has run: if it is dropped (older than a day, unreadable, lost in a crash, or it could not start), the requester gets a notification and Jobs shows a failed run. When it runs, the worker checks again that the requester is still an active administrator and that the recording still exists. Cloud mode never hands off: run the full image there. A full process always does its own work, even when RENDER_URL is set.
A slim process with nowhere to send its work is a configuration error, and the deploy gate catches it: /api/preflight answers 503 and the readiness checks fail when there is no RENDER_URL, the render server does not answer, refuses the token or lacks a binary (check render, readiness render-peer), or no media worker has checked in (check media-worker, readiness media-worker). Start or update the worker before the slim web tasks. A deploy canary (NIVARO_ROLE=canary, its own Redis, no worker) only warns: it serves nobody, and the preflight on a real web task after the roll is the gate. Until it is fixed, the features themselves answer a readable 503 (RENDER_UNAVAILABLE) instead of failing in the background.

When Chromium renders a PDF, locally or on the render server, every request the document makes is checked. Allowed: inline data (data:, blob:, about:blank), this instance's own addresses (PUBLIC_URL and ADMIN_URL; a slim process sends its own along), and public http(s) addresses, such as a logo on a CDN. Refused: file: and every other scheme, loopback, private networks, .local/.internal names and the cloud metadata address 169.254.169.254. The log names the refused origins, never the full URL.

Every release image is signed with cosign keyless signing (GitHub OIDC, Sigstore) by its digest, both the multi-arch index the tag points to and each platform image. Verify the digest you deploy:
cosign verify nodeworks/nivaro@sha256:<digest> \
--certificate - identity - regexp
;('^https://github.com/nodeworks/nivaro/.github/workflows/docker-hub.yml@refs/tags/')
\
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.c…
The signing certificate names the workflow file and the release tag (refs/tags/@app-<version>). Every build is pushed first as sha-<commit> (and sha-<commit>-slim) and signed. Only a release tag build then passes this check and gets the version and latest tags, on the same digest. A manual workflow run gets only the sha- tags, signed for its branch, and fails this check.

A process started with NIVARO_ROLE=realtime holds the live connections and nothing else: Socket.io, GraphQL subscriptions and the server-sent event streams. Connections then scale apart from request handling, and delivery never waits behind a request thread that is busy. The web processes turn sockets off with SOCKETS=off; what they emit still reaches people, through Redis (the Socket.io Redis adapter and the record-event stream). With nothing set, one process does everything, sockets included.
Self-hosted only. A realtime process refuses to start in cloud mode, and cloud mode ignores SOCKETS.

Setting | Values | What it does / NIVARO_ROLE | web, worker, realtime (also canary) | realtime starts the realtime server: no REST routes, scheduled jobs, hooks, extensions, migrations or media work. The role shows on the instance roster and in the version check ("4 web, 2 realtime, 1 worker"). / SOCKETS | on (default) or off | off on a web or worker process: it serves no /socket.io. Its emits reach the realtime processes through Redis. Ignored on a realtime process (always on) and in cloud mode.
A realtime process needs the same REDIS_URL, REDIS_CHANNEL_PREFIX, SESSION_SECRET, cookie settings, CORS_ORIGINS and database settings as web. Sockets sign in exactly as before: the browser gets a one-time token from a web process (GET /api/auth/ws-token), which lives in Redis, and any process redeems it. Streams take the session cookie, a Bearer token or a one-time stream ticket. Give it DB_POOL_MAX=20 and DB_POOL_BACKGROUND_MAX=0: after a restart moves every socket to the surviving process, sign-ins, room checks, presence writes and live re-runs all land at once. GraphQL live re-runs share the heavy-read gate there.

Path | What / /socket.io/ | Socket.io: websocket, and the long-polling fallback / /api/graphql-ws | GraphQL subscriptions over websocket / GET/POST /api/graphql/stream | GraphQL subscriptions and live queries over SSE / GET /api/events/stream | Record changes over SSE / GET /api/events/views/:id/stream | A saved view’s change stream over SSE / GET /api/events/ticket | One-time stream ticket (web answers it too) / GET /api/version, /api/ready, /api/health, /api/metrics | Health; /api/ready checks boot, database and Redis
Anything else answers 404 with a message that says to route it to the web processes. The admin /api/stream and MCP live sessions (/api/mcp?live=1) stay on web: the first reports the writes of the process it runs on, the second calls the API in-process.
Change on every deployment with several processes: /api/events/stream now also hears record changes written on other processes (read from the record-event stream); before, a stream heard only the writes of the process it connected to. A collection set to batched live updates arrives as one event per record when its window closes.

Send the five realtime paths to the realtime service with a higher priority than the web catch-all. Traefik v3:
Host(`nivaro.example.com`) && (PathPrefix(`/socket.io/`) || Path(`/api/graphql-ws`)
  || Path(`/api/graphql/stream`) || Path(`/api/events/stream`)
  || PathRegexp(`^/api/events/views/[^/]+/stream$`))
Socket.io’s long-polling fallback sends one session as many HTTP requests, and each must reach the realtime process that holds the session. Put a sticky cookie on the realtime service (Traefik: loadbalancer.sticky.cookie=true, any cookie name, httponly, secure, samesite=lax); on nginx open source use ip_hash on the realtime upstream. Websockets and SSE streams are one connection each and need no stickiness; with SOCKET_POLLING=off none is needed at all. Turn off read timeouts on the paths that stay open.
deploy/realtime/ in the repository has a compose example (web ×4, realtime ×2, worker ×1 behind Traefik) and a README with the same rules.

• Preflight check realtime and readiness check realtime-tier: a process with SOCKETS=off fails when its deployment slot has no realtime process that checked in within 45 seconds, when REALTIME_EVENT_STREAM=off, or when PUBLIC_URL/api/events/stream is not answered by a realtime process (the proxy route is missing; a realtime process marks every answer X-Nivaro-Role: realtime). It warns with one realtime process (a restart drops every connection until it is back) and passes with two or more. A deploy canary only warns. • /api/ready on web does not depend on the realtime tier, so a realtime restart never takes the REST tier out of the proxy. On a realtime process it requires Redis; the database only warns. • Roster entries carry sockets: false on a process with SOCKETS=off; the Database page’s instance roster shows the role. • /api/metrics reports nivaro_sockets_connected on every process.

About 400 sockets with extra tabs. Run two realtime processes, about 200 sockets each, so either can carry all of them through a restart; four web and one worker. Give each realtime process one core and a 1 GB limit with --max-old-space-size=512. Measured with every socket signed in and events flowing: one process held 374 sockets in 367 MB (heap 145 MB), about 0.4 MB per socket with SOCKET_COMPRESSION on (half of it compression state outside the heap) and 0.2 MB with it off; two processes sharing about 400 sockets used about 310 MB each. All 400 on one process during a restart is about 380 MB. Roll realtime processes one at a time, the new one started first: recreating both at once drops every connection. Keep event-loop lag p99 under 100 ms and the delivery target (95% under 2 s) green.

Several answers come from the sockets themselves: who is viewing a record (the viewing chip, now-editing, skipping an in-app notification for someone looking at the record), who is on a page, the socket list and room sizes (Realtime console, Traffic Map), the concurrency sample, and whether anyone is watching before the traffic feed, AI call feed or flow firehose sends. A process that serves sockets answers from its own, as before. Every process that serves sockets publishes its share to Redis every second (the realtime board; the socket list every 10 s) and lists itself in a small registry, and reads the others’ back into memory; a process with SOCKETS=off only reads. Each process merges the others with its own sockets, so those answers cover every process (the other processes’ part at most about 2 seconds old) and no request waits on another process. This applies to several replicas that all serve sockets too, not only to the realtime tier. A lone process only registers itself every 5 seconds and publishes nothing. The admin /api/stream hears the writes of every process the same way. A notification is skipped only on a board entry younger than 3 seconds, and a realtime process takes its entries off the board when it stops. Viewer counts are given only for records the asker may read; the socket inspector answers 409 for a socket held by a realtime process.
A process with SOCKETS=off only publishes through the Redis adapter: it decodes no broadcasts and is never part of another process’s socket query. When a reconnecting browser rejoins its rooms and asks to catch up in the same breath, the server waits (up to 3 seconds) for the joins before it replays, so events written during the reconnect are not lost. GraphQL over the subscription transports only reads: a mutation there is refused with “Send mutations to POST /api/graphql”.

A realtime process loads no extensions, so an extension that listens for socket connections (app.io.on('connection'), on any namespace) would never hear one on a deployment with SOCKETS=off. Rather than fail silently, a web or worker process with SOCKETS=off refuses to start when an extension registers such a handler, and the error names the setting. Move that work to an event the API emits, or keep sockets on.

• The GraphQL schema is built when a process starts; a realtime process picks up a schema change at its next restart, as every web process does today. • The Traffic Map’s room and socket detail panels show the sockets of the process that answers the request.

The Chaos page at /chaos (Operations → Health, administrators) runs controlled fault drills: arm one fault for a few minutes, state what should stay true, watch the live figures, and stop everything with one button. Every fault is time-boxed and heals itself when its window ends. A run records what happened and ends with a verdict — held, broke or aborted — so a claim like “Redis fails open” is proven by a dated drill, not asserted.
Chaos is dangerous by design. It never runs in cloud mode, and on a production instance only when the process was started with CHAOS_ENABLED=true on purpose. The page still opens where it is refused — the strip under the header says why — so past runs and the catalog stay readable.

One rule decides whether a fault may run in this process: refused in cloud mode (CLOUD_META_DB_URL set), refused when NODE_ENV=production unless CHAOS_ENABLED=true, allowed everywhere else (development, test, staging). Every chaos route answers the refusal with its reason instead of a 404; the socket drills on the Realtime page and the older POST /api/chaos/run follow the same rule. Arming, stopping and recording runs needs an administrator (a chaos-operator permission is planned).

The Faults tab lists the catalog: each fault says what it proves, where it acts (its fault points, such as http.request or mail.send), how far it can reach (everything, routes matching a pattern, one table, one person, a share of traffic, one replica, a socket room) and how long it may run at most. The server clamps every parameter and the duration to the catalog’s caps whatever the form sends.
Fault | Proves | Acts at | Cap / Slow requests | Slow answers stay honest: loading states show, traces and the Traffic Map see the latency. | http.request (100–5000 ms) | 300 s / Mail transport down | Mail fails cleanly: sends land in the mail log and the outbox retries. | mail.send | 300 s / Redis unreachable | Redis fails open: requests keep answering, sessions hold, caches miss, crons pause. | disconnects this process’s Redis client | 300 s / Socket drill | Sockets reconnect and catch up after drops, latency or forced disconnects. | the Realtime page’s own drill form (/realtime?tab=verify) | 600 s
Run opens a small form under the row: the target, the strength within the caps, the duration, the note, and the limits that should hold (pre-filled from the fault’s defaults). The pre-flight checklist sits beside it. A fault that is armed right now shows an “Armed now” mark that opens its run.

Every run is a row with a timeline: armed, each sample, alerts and readiness changes, notes, the stop or abort. While it runs the Runs tab shows the cockpit; afterwards a summary with the verdict, what was armed on what, how long it ran, which limits held and the timeline. Every run is also a job run (kind chaos) on the Jobs console. Runs made outside the registry — a CI job with toxiproxy, a game-day step measured by hand — are posted to POST /api/chaos/runs/record and appear in the same list.
• **held** — every limit stayed inside its bound for the whole window. • **broke** — a limit was crossed while the fault ran, but not far enough or long enough to stop it. • **aborted** — a limit was crossed past its tolerance three samples in a row and the fault was stopped by itself; or an operator stopped it after a breach. • **refused** — pre-flight failed; nothing was armed and the failed checks are kept on the run.
Runs are stored in the nivaro_chaos_runs and nivaro_chaos_run_events tables (migration 497). On a database that does not have them yet they live in Redis for 7 days, so the console works there too.

Before a run starts it states what should stay true as a list of limits: a sampler, a comparison, a limit and a tolerance — “request p95 < 2000 ms ± 200”, “server errors < 1 % ± 0.5”. Samplers read figures the process already measures: request p95, server-error share, request rate and failed record saves (from the request funnel the Traffic Map uses), main and background pool wait, event-loop lag, heavy reads waiting at the read gate, socket reconnects. The baseline is the five minutes before arm. While the run is armed, the replica that started it samples every 5 seconds and writes a compact sample event; crossing a limit past its tolerance three samples in a row stops the fault by itself and the run ends aborted. A run with no limits never aborts on its own — it just records.

Green ticks gate the Run button and the server runs the same checks again when the run starts: chaos is allowed here; this is not a production instance (an environment named Production in the Environments registry with a component answering on this host); no deploy or migration is running (one API version on the instance roster, the migration table not locked); no maintenance window; no open incident on the Ops Console; inside working hours (Monday–Friday 08:00–18:00 Eastern); the main pool and event loop are healthy; no other drill is armed. Each failed tick says why. An administrator may run outside working hours by ticking the override; the run records it. No other check can be overridden.

The header carries the one red control, Stop all: it clears every fault on every replica at once, socket drills included, and closes every open run. It works even when Redis is down — each process clears itself first and tells the others afterwards. The Faults tab is the catalog; the Runs tab lists every run with the running ones first and opens the selected one on the right. ?tab=runs&run=<id> deep-links a run.

While a run is armed its page shows a countdown ring emptying as the window runs out, a large red Stop this run beside Stop all, one sparkline per sampler drawn against the baseline (dashed) with the abort limit (red) and its tolerance band, and the timeline of events as they happen. Hypothesis samplers come first; the others are watched for context. The page is live over the socket and polls every 5 seconds as a net.

While any fault is armed on this instance, every app — the admin and headless frontends built on @nivaro/react — shows a striped red strip at the top: which fault, on what, who started it, when it ends, and the note “this is a planned test, not an outage”. Administrators get a Stop link to the console. The strip shows labels and names only, never the targeted people or the parameters, and it asks the server nothing more once the gate has said chaos is refused here.

The experiment builder is how a drill is set up on the Chaos page. It opens under a fault when you press Run on the Faults tab, and at full width on the Builder tab. It walks through eight steps and keeps a summary beside them that reads the run back in plain words.
Step | What you choose / Fault | Which fault to arm, with the claim it proves and how far it can reach. / Target | Everything, a route pattern (picked from the Traffic Map’s last 15 minutes or typed, such as /api/items/*), one table, one person, a share of traffic or one replica. / Strength | The fault’s settings, such as the added delay. Sliders stop at the caps. / Duration | How long it stays armed. It ends by itself when the time is up. / What stays true | The steady state: lines such as “server errors < 1 %”, each checked every 5 seconds. / Abort limits | How many bad samples in a row stop the run (1 to 10, usually 3; one sample every 5 seconds, so 3 is about 15 seconds), and the tolerance on each line. Past the tolerance for that many samples in a row the run aborts on every replica. / Blast radius | An estimate from the last 24 hours of traffic of what would stop or slow down if the fault’s dependency went fully down. Faults that take no whole dependency down show “no estimate”. / Pre-flight | The checks that must pass before Run, re-run by the server at the start.
Run takes two clicks: Run, then a red “Confirm — arms <fault> on <target> for <n>s”. The confirm button goes back to Run after a few seconds if you do not press it. The server checks the target, the strength and the duration again whatever the page sends, including the per-environment caps when chaos settings set them.
The limits come from this instance’s chaos settings. Chaos operators who are not administrators get the same limits as administrators: the builder reads them from GET /api/chaos/operator.
Link straight into the builder with /chaos?tab=builder&fault=<fault key>, &preset=<preset key>, or &spec=<JSON> carrying fault_key, target, params, seconds, hypothesis and abort_after. The Traffic Map’s “Inject fault here” and Ask AI’s drafts use these links.

A preset is a saved experiment: fault, target, strength, duration, what stays true and how many bad samples stop it, with a sentence on what it proves and the claims it tests. The Presets tab lists the shipped presets and the ones saved on this instance. Run opens the preset in the builder to check and confirm; nothing arms from the list.
There is a shipped preset for every claim a fault on this instance can prove. Each is a small first run: a short window (two minutes at most), a narrow target where the fault allows one, and a light strength.
Area | Shipped presets / Requests and mail | Slow answers stay honest · Mail down fails clean / Database | Slow database queues at the read gate · Database errors fail one request · Background pool held, requests stay fast / Redis | Redis outage fails open · Slow Redis is tolerated · Read-only Redis is survived · Lost query cache rebuilds · Signed-out sessions stay signed out · Redis eviction is tolerated · Cut-off replica catches up / Scheduler | Scheduler pauses when its lease expires · No job runs twice when the lease splits / Partners and services | Partner errors are contained · Full disk fails uploads cleanly · AI down answers 503 · Refused AI model falls back · Sign-in down, sessions hold · Slow sign-in says so · Microsoft Graph down fails clean / One replica | A stalled replica is drained · The heap guard catches memory pressure · Clock skew is safe · Sockets reconnect and catch up
• Presets for one replica pick the first replica in the builder, or the replica that answers when started straight from the API. • The Redis key-loss and eviction presets are refused on development when Redis runs on database 0, which every local instance shares. The refusal shows when you start the run. • Taking a web task down has no preset: it runs only inside a game day with a host runbook. • Save as preset in the builder stores the current draft under a name and key. Opened from a preset, it can also update that preset. • Editing a shipped preset saves your own copy under the same key. Deleting that copy brings the shipped one back; shipped presets themselves cannot be deleted. • Saved presets are configuration (nivaro_chaos_presets) and move between instances with config promotion and show up in Environment Config diffs. • A preset whose fault this instance does not have is listed as “Fault not on this instance” and cannot run. • Runs started from a preset record its key, so the run history shows where it came from.
Route | What it does / GET /api/chaos/presets | Shipped and saved presets, each with whether its fault is installed. / POST /api/chaos/presets | Save a preset {key, label, proves, claim_keys, spec}. / PATCH /api/chaos/presets/:key | Edit a preset (a shipped key becomes a saved copy). / DELETE /api/chaos/presets/:key | Delete a saved preset. / POST /api/chaos/presets/:key/run | Start a drill from the preset; the body may override target, params, seconds, hypothesis and abort_after.

Administrators can ask Ask AI, the Telemetry page’s Ask, or a connected MCP client what happens if a dependency dies: the database, Redis, the file share, email, the AI provider, the sign-in provider, partner APIs, sockets or one replica. The answer lists the claims about it and when each was last proven by a drill, the routes, screens and jobs the blast-radius estimate expects to fail or slow down, the last drills against it, and a draft experiment.
The answer never starts a drill. Its draft is a link that opens the builder pre-filled, where a person still checks pre-flight and presses Run and Confirm.
The same answer is GET /api/chaos/what-if?dependency=redis (administrators). The MCP tool is chaos_what_if, offered to administrator connections only.

sections.label: Chaos: database, partner, storage and process faults

blocks.h: Chaos: database, partner, storage and process faults
blocks.t: These faults are started from the Chaos console like every other drill. Each one is time-boxed, ends by itself, and stops at once with Stop all. They are refused in cloud mode and on production unless CHAOS_ENABLED=true. On the shared development database keep pool and error drills small and short: the faults run in your API process, but the database server is shared.

Fault | What it does | Targets | Caps / Slow database (db_latency) | Adds a delay to every statement that reaches the database. Configuration reads the metadata cache answers are not slowed. | everything, one table, a route pattern, one person, a share of statements; main pool, background pool or both | 5,000 ms per statement; 5 minutes / Database errors (db_errors) | Fails a share of statements with a deadlock victim (1205), a request timeout (ETIMEOUT) or a connection reset (ESOCKET), shaped like the errors the SQL Server driver throws. An optional wait comes first, so a timeout can take as long as a real one. Sign-in reads (users, roles, API keys, settings) and the Stop paths are never touched, so a drill can always be stopped. | as above | 100% of statements, 15 s wait; 3 minutes / Pool exhaustion (pool_hold) | Holds N connections of the main or the background pool for the window. No statement runs on them. | everything or one replica | 5 connections and 60 s off production; 10 connections on production / Partner failing (partner_faults) | Answers instead of an external API: added latency, a 500, a 429 with Retry-After, a 200 whose body says ERROR, malformed JSON, or a TLS failure. Works the same whether the API is live or in mock mode; the saved API is never changed. ERP pushes go through the same call. | every API or one (name or id); everything or a share of calls | 30 s added; 10 minutes / Storage failing (storage_faults) | A slow driver, a full disk (ENOSPC) or a read-only volume (EROFS) on file uploads, downloads and deletes, plus help-video upload parts and render scratch. A full disk still allows deletes. | everything or a share of calls | 30 s added per call; 10 minutes / Event-loop block (event_loop_block) | Blocks the replica for N ms every M seconds. | one replica or every replica | 2,000 ms per block; 3 minutes / Memory pressure (memory_pressure) | Grows the heap in steps toward a share of its limit, then holds it. The memory is dropped when the fault ends. | one replica or every replica | 75% of the heap limit; 5 minutes / Clock skew (clock_skew) | Moves the application clock of one replica by minutes or hours. SLA timers, maintenance windows and the cron run slot follow it. Sign-in and expiry checks (sessions, API keys, public dashboard links, help-video media tickets, delegations) only ever get stricter: a clock set back is ignored for them, and session stamps stay on real time. Log timestamps do not move. | one replica | ±24 hours; 10 minutes

• Readiness: the replica that started the run takes the readiness scorecard at the start, at the midpoint (windows of 30 s or more) and at the end. Each reading is a readiness event on the run with the score, the failing and warning checks, and what changed since the start. • Alerts: log alert rules, metric alerts (Traffic Map alerts included) and monitors that turn failing while a fault is armed add an alert event to the run, once per alert per minute. • Synthetic partner answers carry the header x-nivaro-chaos: 1 in the call log, so they can be told apart from real failures.
The event-loop and memory drills prove what exists today: event-loop lag, request times and /api/ready. There is no event-loop watchdog or heap guard yet; when they land, the same drills prove them.

sections.label: Chaos: Redis, scheduler, partition and outbound faults

blocks.h: Chaos: Redis, scheduler, partition and outbound faults
blocks.t: These faults start from the Chaos console like every other drill. Each one is time-boxed, ends by itself and stops at once with Stop all, which reaches every replica even while Redis is the thing failing: the chaos channel and the nvr:chaos:* keys are never touched by these faults. They are refused in cloud mode and on production unless CHAOS_ENABLED=true.

Fault | What it does | Targets | Caps / Slow Redis (redis_latency) | Every Redis command waits the added delay, plus or minus the jitter, before it is sent. Commands sent together keep their order. | everything or one replica | 2,000 ms; 5 minutes / Redis read-only (redis_readonly) | Every write answers the READONLY error a replica gives during a failover; reads still answer. Redis itself sends the error, so a group of commands sent together fails as a whole, as it would for real. | everything or one replica | 2 minutes / Redis keys lost (redis_key_loss) | Deletes one family of keys: sessions, the custom-query cache, the shared metadata cache, the scheduler lease and job locks, the realtime journal, idempotency keys, or every nvr:* key. With "Bring old keys back" on, the keys are copied first and put back when the window ends, wherever nothing newer was written, the way a lagging replica brings old keys back after a failover. | everything (runs once, on the replica that started it) | 20,000 keys; 5 minutes / Redis evicting keys (redis_evict) | Every few seconds, deletes a share of the nvr:* keys, the way Redis evicts keys when it runs out of memory. | everything (runs on the replica that started it) | 100% and 5,000 keys per sweep; 5 minutes / Scheduler lease split (cron_lease_split) | The scheduler lease on the chosen replica lapses (expire), is dropped (drop), or is dropped while that replica goes on believing it leads (split). Another replica takes the lease in the middle of whatever is running. | one replica or every replica | 5 minutes / Replica cut off from Redis pub/sub (redis_partition) | The chosen replica stops hearing and sending pub/sub messages: the socket adapter and the record-event channel. Its database connection is untouched. Its event-stream reader pauses and keeps its place, so record events written meanwhile reach its sockets when the window ends. | one replica | 5 minutes / AI gateway failing (ai_gateway_fault) | AI calls fail with a 5xx, time out, are slow, or the pinned model is refused (the next model in the fallback chain answers). | everything or a share of calls | 60 s wait; 10 minutes / Sign-in provider down (oidc_down) | The identity provider cannot be reached, or answers slowly, at discovery, at the token exchange or both. Discovery fails even when it was cached, as on a replica that just started. | everything | 30 s wait; 10 minutes / Microsoft Graph down (graph_down) | Directory lookups, their token and the sign-in profile and photo cannot reach Graph, or reach it slowly. A delay past a call’s own timeout fails it the way the timeout would. | everything | 30 s wait; 10 minutes
On development, Redis keys lost and Redis evicting keys run only on a Redis database other than 0: a shared development Redis keeps every instance’s sessions, caches, scheduler lease and event stream in database 0, and REDIS_CHANNEL_PREFIX separates channels, not keys. On a deployed stack with its own Redis they run on database 0 too, except the sessions family, which also needs REDIS_CHANNEL_PREFIX there. A refused run says so in its timeline.

• Sign-out holds: run Redis keys lost on the sessions family with "Bring old keys back" on, sign out during the window, and check the session is still signed out after the old keys return. The sign-out marker wins over the returned session. • Scheduler: GET /api/chaos/checks/cron-overlap?since=<time> lists every job that ran twice at once, runs left running past their budget, and the jobs not declared safe to run twice. A lease-split drill writes the same check into its timeline when the window ends. • Partition: before cutting a replica off, start POST /api/chaos/partition/probe on another replica with the socket id of a test client connected to the replica you will cut. Then GET /api/chaos/checks/partition?probe=<id> on the cut replica lists events lost and events delivered twice. The drill notes how many messages were dropped and how many stream events were caught up. • Redis counters: GET /api/chaos/checks/redis shows this replica’s fault counters, its Redis database and whether keys (and sessions) may be dropped here. • Steady state: two figures can be used in a drill’s hypothesis: Redis errors per minute (redis.errors_per_min) and the metadata cache hit rate (cache.metadata_hit_pct).

blocks.h: A safe job for the lease drill
blocks.t: CHAOS_TEST_CRON=1 starts a separate test scheduler on that process with one job, chaos-test-overlap, which only sleeps (CHAOS_TEST_CRON_MS, default 12 s) every 10 seconds. It competes for its own lease key and ticks even where scheduled jobs are off, so a lease-split drill can be proven on two development replicas without any real job running. It never starts on production or where the chaos gate refuses.

blocks.h: Sign-in while the provider is down
blocks.t: People already signed in keep working: a session never calls the identity provider. Someone signing in is sent back to the sign-in page, which says the provider is not answering. It never shows a raw error, and it never sends them back to the provider in a loop.

Every chaos drill ends with a report, and the reports add up to a scorecard: which claims about how Nivaro degrades are proven, which broke, and which nobody has checked lately. All of it is for administrators and stays readable on instances where drills cannot run.

Open a finished run from the Runs tab (Full report) or go to /chaos/runs/<id>. While the run is still going the same address shows the live cockpit.
• The verdict: held, broke or aborted, and the limit that broke it. • One chart per limit, before, during and after the fault, with the normal range from before the drill, the limit line, and the alerts and notes marked where they happened. • Time to detect: from arming the fault to the first alert, the first "noticed" note or a declared incident. • Time to fix: to the first "fixed" note. • Time to recover: from the end of the fault until every limit was back inside its normal range. "Not back while watched" means the samples after the fault never returned to it. • The alerts that fired, what the readiness checks said, and the errors people actually saw: server errors by route (ids removed), client error reports and rage or dead clicks, as counts only. • The participants’ notes and the full timeline.
Copy link gives a stable address other administrators can open. Export postmortem downloads the report as Markdown (timeline, figures and notes, never record data) to paste into a postmortem.

The Matrix tab shows every dependency (the database, Redis, the file share, each partner API, the AI gateway, sign-in, sockets and mail) against the ways it can fail: down, slow, errors and cut off. Each cell takes the colour of its newest drill and fades as that drill gets older; an outlined cell has never been proven. Click a cell to open its last report or run it again with the start form already filled in.
Under the matrix, Claims lists what Nivaro says about degrading (for example, "when Redis is unreachable, requests keep answering") with the drill that last proved each one. A claim is proven when its newest drill held within the last 30 days, stale when that drill is older, broke when its newest drill broke or stopped itself, and never proven when nothing has run. A fault proves a claim when it names the claim in its catalog entry.
The readiness check "Resilience claims are proven" warns when a claim is stale or its last drill broke. Claims never proven are listed but do not warn. It is skipped where drills cannot run (cloud, or production without CHAOS_ENABLED).

The Trends tab shows median time to detect and time to recover per month or quarter, a calendar of the days drills ran (Eastern dates; an outlined day had a drill that did not hold), each dependency’s verdicts month by month, and the claims never proven. The strip on top (the last 90 days) is also served as JSON for a recovery-time panel.

Route | Returns / GET /api/chaos/runs/:id/report | The run, its report, errors people saw, actor names and the share link / GET /api/chaos/runs/:id/postmortem | The report as a Markdown download / GET /api/chaos/claims | Every claim with its status and last run / GET /api/chaos/matrix | Rows, fault kinds and one cell per pair with its last verdict and re-run spec / GET /api/chaos/trends?months=12 | Monthly and quarterly timings, drills per day, verdicts per dependency, never-proven claims and the recovery feed

A game day is a planned drill: a date and time, the people taking part, and a timed list of things that will go wrong. It lives on the chaos console (Operations → Health → Chaos) under Game days. Chaos is refused in cloud mode and on production unless CHAOS_ENABLED=true, so game days are for staging and development.

• Plan a game day opens the editor. Start from a blank plan or the monthly staging template (kill a web task, drop Redis, block the file share, slow the database, with checkpoints before and after). • Times are Eastern. The length is 15 minutes to 8 hours. • People: a lead (faults are armed as the lead), an optional scribe, and responders. Everyone named gets an invitation at once and reminders 24 hours and 15 minutes before (notification category "Chaos drills and game days"). • Injects run at +mm:ss after the start: arm a fault from the catalog for a number of seconds, post an announcement to the day’s channel (as the lead, through the normal chat send), or reach a checkpoint. A fault key this instance does not have is a warning when you save and is skipped on the day. • Chat channel: a private channel for the participants. A timeline bot posts each fault and checkpoint as it happens, with fixed wording only — never the plan’s own labels. Start a huddle from the channel header. • Repeat monthly: when the day ends or is cancelled, the same slot next month (same weekday, same week of the month, same Eastern time) is planned with the same people.

• The lead presses Start now, or the scheduler starts the day at its time when "Start automatically" is on. Each fault inject goes through the drill pre-flight; a refusal is recorded on the timeline instead of stopping the day. • Injects fire on time from the chaos-gamedays job (every minute, one server) and from a timer on the server that started the day; whichever comes first fires it, and it fires once. An inject more than ten minutes late is marked missed and never fired late. • Fire now runs a waiting inject by hand. End day closes the day, stops any fault still armed and writes the result; Abort does the same with the verdict aborted. Stop all on the console always works and ends a running day too. • The day’s verdict is the worst of its fault runs (held, broke or aborted).

While a day runs, anyone taking part can stamp what happened in one click — Noticed, Found cause, Fixed — or type a note. The marks become the day’s time to detect, time to find the cause and time to fix, measured from the first fault that went live, and show on the inject track and in the report. Notes stamped on one of the day’s fault runs land on the day itself.

• A blind day hides its faults from the responders: no drill banner for them, and drill-tagged alerts are not marked as a drill for them. The lead and chaos operators (administrators) still see everything. • Declare incident (Ops Console header) is open to everyone signed in. It stamps a "Declared incident" mark on every running game day and blind drill — the responders’ time to detect — and always answers the same way, so it never gives away that a drill is running. • The lead reveals the drill at any time; the faults then show on the banner for everyone and the channel gets a line saying so.
