A single drill can also be started blind through POST /api/chaos/blind/runs.

The API never writes to Docker. The "Kill a web task" fault queues the host runbook chaos-kill-web-task in the Runbooks host queue; the host agent on the swarm manager runs it and swarm replaces the task. A deployment declares that runbook in its extension (runs on the host, no dry run needed, a target such as staging). Without it the fault is refused with that reason. Stopping the fault withdraws a kill still waiting in the queue.

Route | Who | What / GET /api/chaos/gamedays | admin | Every game day / GET /api/chaos/gamedays/:id | admin | Plan, timeline, fault runs, people, time to detect / fix / GET /api/chaos/gamedays/active | signed in | The days I take part in (titles and times only) / POST /api/chaos/gamedays | chaos operator | Plan a day; PATCH /:id edits it while planned / POST /api/chaos/gamedays/:id/start | step | end | cancel | reveal | chaos operator | Run the day; step takes {inject_id}, end takes {how} / GET / POST /api/chaos/runs/:id/notes | admin or participant | Scribe marks {mark, text} / POST /api/chaos/declare | signed in | Declare incident / POST /api/chaos/blind/runs | chaos operator | One drill, blind; /blind/runs/:id/reveal reveals it

Four things keep chaos drills safe in day-to-day operations: who may run them, how far a run may reach on each instance, a Chaos Monkey that runs small drills at random times when you switch it on, and a Stop button that reaches your phone.

Administrators may always run faults. In **Chaos → Settings** an administrator can name roles whose members may also start, stop and record drills (and read the chaos console). Only administrators change these settings, so an operator can never widen their own reach. API keys limited to named collections are refused. Only administrators may override the working-hours pre-flight check.

Each instance keeps its own limits, so development and staging can differ even when they share a database. The server applies them to every run started there — from the console, a game day, Chaos Monkey or a script — whatever the form sent.
Limit | What happens over it / Faults allowed | A fault off the list is refused (403 CHAOS_CAP). / Share of traffic | A larger share is lowered to the limit. A run aimed at everything becomes that share when the fault can take a share; any other target (some routes, a table, a person, a replica) is sampled at the limit on top. A route pattern with fewer than two fixed parts (/*, /api/*) is refused. / Added delay | Every delay measured in ms is lowered to the limit. / Run length | The window is shortened (never under 5 seconds). / Replicas | A run that would reach more replicas is narrowed to the one it started on, or refused when the fault cannot aim at one replica.
Whatever was lowered is recorded on the run (meta.caps). Empty means no limit beyond the fault’s own.
Socket drills started from the Realtime page (/realtime → Verification) are the one path outside these limits and the pre-flight: they are administrator-only, pass the same gate, and keep their own 5–600 s window and share/room/person targets. Stop all on the Chaos page ends them too. Start a socket drill from the Chaos console (fault “Socket drill”) when you want the limits, the pre-flight and a run with a verdict.
Stored under the chaos key of this instance’s nivaro_settings_overrides row (GET/PATCH /api/chaos/settings, administrators). No migration.

An alert that fires while a fault is armed — log alert rules, request rules, monitors, metric alerts, integration alerts, a readiness check turning to fail — is never silenced or rerouted: everyone who normally hears about it still does, by every channel they normally get. Its message gains a line naming the run: “May be caused by the chaos drill …” when the alert is about what the fault touches (a database alert during a database fault), otherwise “Fired during the chaos drill …”. The drill’s people (whoever started it, the game day’s lead, scribe and responders; for Chaos Monkey, administrators and chaos operators) are told too, in-app, when they were not already. The Ops Console, Telemetry and the Integrations console show a **Drill** tag on alerts that fired during a run. In a blind game day the note is left out of the normal recipients’ copy; the alert itself still reaches them.

Off until an administrator turns it on in **Chaos → Monkey**. Every 15 minutes, inside the days and hours you set (Eastern time), it may start one drill from the faults you approved, at random moments so that about the weekly number land across the week. Each drill is small (a share of traffic, else one replica) and short, and the instance’s limits apply on top. Administrators and chaos operators are told when it starts and when it ends, with the verdict.
• Never on an instance that looks like production (its instance key, or NIVARO_TIER=production), and never while another drill is armed. • Pre-flight still judges every drill (deploys, maintenance, open incidents…); a refusal is kept as a refused monkey run and does not count toward the week. • **Try now** runs one tick at once, skipping only the dice. • The chaos-monkey job ticks only where scheduled jobs run, on one server at a time.

When a drill starts, and again if it stops itself because what should stay true broke, the person who started it and its participants get a browser notification with **Stop all faults**. Tapping it ends every fault on the instance, even when that phone is not signed in.
The button carries a signed token that works once, only for that person and run, and only until the drill’s window ends (five minutes after an abort). The person must still be a chaos operator. It keeps working while Redis is down and during maintenance.

Browser chaos mode makes **your own tab’s** requests fail or slow down for a few minutes, so you can watch how screens cope: error messages, retry buttons, autosave and the offline outbox. Nothing is injected on the server and nobody else is affected.
Available to administrators when the server allows chaos drills (GET /api/chaos/status). It is refused in cloud mode and, on a production server, unless CHAOS_ENABLED=true. When the server has no chaos route the controls do not appear at all.

Open it from your user menu → **Browser chaos**, or press **⌘ Shift .** (Ctrl Shift . on Windows) anywhere. Pick what breaks, how hard and for how long, then Start. While it runs, a pill in the bottom-right corner shows what is on and the time left; its × stops it at once.
Preset | What your tab sees / Flaky network | A share of requests (5–90%) fail as if the network dropped them; the rest arrive late. / API down | Every API call answers 503, as a proxy does when no API server is behind it. / Slow API | Every API call waits longer (0.25–10 s). / Offline | Requests fail as if the network is gone, and the browser reports itself offline, so the offline banner and outbox take over. / Socket gone | Live updates stop; at the end the tab reconnects and reloads what it missed. / Fail my next saves | The next N creates, edits or deletes answer 500. Reads keep working. Combines with any preset or runs on its own.
• It always ends on time (1 to 30 minutes). A reload of the tab keeps it on until then; closing the tab ends it. • Signing in and out, the chaos controls themselves and the error reporter are never broken. • Crash reports sent while chaos is on are marked and not filed as issues. • With several tabs open, live updates come over one shared connection: Socket gone silences only this tab, the others keep theirs.

While designing a dashboard or a form, you can see how it looks when something it depends on fails. On a dashboard use **Pretend down** in the header; in the layout editor (and a record page’s Edit layout) open **Preview** and use the Pretend down list at the bottom.
• The list names what the view uses: the data behind each group of dashboard widgets, a form’s record widgets and panels (pipeline, owners, comments, tasks…), the AI gateway, partners and external APIs, and live updates. • Switch one on and the widgets that use it fail through their normal error handling, so you see exactly what a person would see. • Only your tab, only while the editor is open. Leaving the page turns everything back on. • The Preview button says how many things are pretended down, so it is never on unnoticed.

Headless front ends built on @nivaro/react get the same tools. Call installClientChaosFetch() first thing at boot (before anything creates an SDK client), mount <ClientChaosToolbar user={me} /> once, and add clientChaosAxiosInterceptor(AxiosError) to any axios instance. Sockets created through createWorkerSocket or createSocketRealtime are covered automatically; call bindClientChaosSocket(socket) for any other.
import { installClientChaosFetch, ClientChaosToolbar } from '@nivaro/react'

installClientChaosFetch() // before anything creates a client

<ClientChaosToolbar user={{ is_admin: me.is_admin }} />

Where chaos drills are allowed (never in cloud mode; on production only with CHAOS_ENABLED=true), the Traffic Map shows every armed fault on the nodes it acts on, so nobody reads a drill as a real outage. Where chaos is refused, nothing here appears.

A node a fault acts on is hatched in red with a dashed outline, and a label names the fault and the time it has left (the soonest to end, plus how many more). The edges into a faulted database, Redis, email or partner node are dashed. The toolbar shows the drill and links to its run; selecting a hatched node lists the drills acting on it, with Open run.
The fault acts at | Drawn on / Every request, a share or one replica (http.request) | Every API lane / Routes matching a pattern | The entities whose routes match / One person | That person on the callers side / The database (db.*), or one table | SQL Server, and that table’s entity / Redis (redis.*) | Redis / Email, SMS, push (mail.*, sms.*, push.*) | That channel / Partner calls (external.*) | Every partner node / File storage, AI providers | File storage, each AI node / Socket drills | The Sockets lane / The scheduler (cron.*) | The scheduled job nodes

Right-click a node, or use the inspector’s action row, for Inject fault here. It opens the chaos console on the Faults tab with that fault’s start form already aimed at the node: a route pattern for an endpoint or a lane, the table for a collection with a database fault, the person for a caller, everything for a data store, a channel or a partner. Nothing starts until you press Run there. Socket drills open the Realtime page’s own drill form.
The same right-click menu offers Simulate down on a dependency: what would break if it went away, worked out from recorded traffic, with nothing switched off (see Traffic Map: Act).
The console link is /chaos?tab=faults&fault=<fault key>&target=<kind>:<value>, for example target=route:/api/items/orders* or target=table:orders. A target the fault cannot take is ignored and the form opens with its usual default.

Four scripts in scripts/chaos/ prove recovery behaviour that cannot be tested from inside a running API: booting without the database, a lock left by a dead migration, links that slow down or drop, screens that meet a failing API, and a deploy that runs while people are using the system. Each one prints PASS or FAIL per check, always writes a JSON result file, and with --record <base-url> (and an admin token in CHAOS_RECORD_TOKEN) posts the run to the chaos console.
None of these may be pointed at production or at the shared development database. They start their own throwaway API or database, or (the deploy drill) measure a staging deploy you start yourself.

pnpm chaos:boot starts a throwaway API twice, once with the database unreachable and once with Redis unreachable (closed local ports) and a short BOOT_DEPS_WAIT_MS. A pass means the process logged its retries with backoff and exited 1 inside the window, which is what lets the orchestrator restart it cleanly. It also runs the unit test that proves a migration lock held past MIGRATION_LOCK_STALE_MS is freed and the migrations then run.
With CHAOS_SCRATCH_DB=<database> set to a scratch database (never an EFP_ database) the script also holds knex's lock row there, boots with migrations and MIGRATION_LOCK_STALE_MS=15000, and expects the "Freeing the stale lock" line and a live API. Run it before every release that touches the boot path.

deploy/chaos-ci/docker-compose.yml runs SQL Server, Redis, the API image and toxiproxy; the API reaches the database and Redis through toxiproxy and the test runner reaches the API through it too. pnpm chaos:toxiproxy adds latency, resets, timeouts and outages and checks: boot under database latency, concurrent reads under latency all answer, a database outage turns /api/ready to 503 and recovers without a restart, a session survives a Redis blip, and a socket reconnects and signs in again after its connection is reset.
• CI: .github/workflows/chaos-ci.yml runs it on pull requests that touch the database layer, plugins, server.ts, boot code or realtime. • Locally: docker compose -f deploy/chaos-ci/docker-compose.yml up -d --build --wait api, then node scripts/chaos/toxiproxy-suite.mjs. --mode host runs the API from your checkout instead of the image; --only db-outage,socket runs chosen cases. • SQL Server does not run under emulation on Apple silicon. Run the suite in CI or on an x86 host.

pnpm chaos:gallery opens admin screens in a browser at 1440 px, light and dark, while every /api call is answered by a mock: a 500 with a realistic error body, a request that never answers, or no network at all. It screenshots each one and writes reports/error-gallery/<date>/index.html (not committed) with a filterable grid and summary.json. --sample 15 (default) picks evenly spaced routes, --all walks every route, --routes /a,/b picks some. --start-admin starts a throwaway admin dev server for you.
Flag | Meaning / blank | The main area has no text at all. / raw-error | Stack, axios or "[object Object]" text is visible. / stuck-loading | A spinner or skeleton is still showing 10 seconds in. / no-error-shown | A request failed and the screen shows content or an empty state without saying so. / page-error | An uncaught exception reached the page. / error-boundary | The crash screen appeared.
A pass is a gallery with no flags. The point is a list to work through, and a re-run per release to see it shrink.

pnpm chaos:deploy-load measures a deploy; it never starts one. Staging only. Run it with --target <staging url> --token <bearer> --caller <k12|u<uuid>>, then start the deploy the usual way. It replays a slice of recorded traffic (traffic:replay, which keeps its own refusals) while polling /api/version and /api/ready every 250 ms, and once the version changes it keeps measuring for --after-s seconds. --load builtin --rps 20 uses a simple generator instead of a recorded slice.
It reports "this deploy dropped N of M requests", how many more answered 5xx, how long two versions answered together, the longest stretch with nothing ready, and how long one socket took to reconnect. A pass is nothing dropped and nothing errored. --dry-run proves the counting on a throwaway API that restarts itself, so it is expected to show drops.

Beyond the static ERD, /data-model/graph renders your whole schema as a live force-directed graph: collections sized by row count, relation edges heat-mapped by the last 7 days of write activity (M2M dashed amber). Drag nodes, zoom with the wheel, hover to isolate a neighborhood, click to open the table editor.

Before renaming or deleting a field, the crosshair icon on any Table Editor field row answers "what references this?" — layouts, queue columns and filters, display templates, computed formulas, field rules, visibility conditions, at-risk rules, alerts, watches, automation rules, workflow conditions, and saved views.
GET /api/data-model/:collection/fields/:field/impact   (admin)
Matching errs toward recall — every hit names its source with a link so you can judge before changing the schema.

All Nivaro tables use a nivaro_ prefix to coexist with existing application tables in the same MSSQL database. Migration history is tracked in nivaro_knex_migrations.
Table | Purpose / nivaro_roles | Role definitions. admin_access and app_access flags. / nivaro_users | Nivaro users linked to Microsoft OIDC via external_id. / nivaro_policies | Per-role permissions: collection + action + optional field list. / nivaro_sessions | Session store (Redis-backed; DB row is a fallback reference). / nivaro_collections | Metadata registry — display names, icons, archive config, etc. / nivaro_fields | Field metadata — type, interface, options, hidden, required, sort. / nivaro_relations | Relation definitions (M2O, O2M, M2M, M2A). / nivaro_settings | App-wide singleton settings (always id = 1). / nivaro_file_folders | Folder hierarchy for the file manager. / nivaro_files | File metadata — storage path, MIME type, dimensions. / nivaro_activity | Audit log — who did what, when, on which record. / nivaro_revisions | Full snapshot + delta history for item changes. / nivaro_notifications | In-app notifications per user. / nivaro_flows | Flow definitions — trigger, status, trigger_options. / nivaro_flow_operations | Flow operation nodes — type, position, options, resolve/reject links. / nivaro_workflow_templates | Workflow state machine blueprints. / nivaro_workflow_states | States within a template. Includes skip_criteria JSON for auto-advance rules. / nivaro_workflow_transitions | Edges: from_state → to_state with label, color, required_roles (JSON). / nivaro_workflow_bindings | Maps a template to a collection; optional state_field syncs state key to a record column. / nivaro_workflow_instances | Per-record runtime: current_state, started_at, completed_at. / nivaro_workflow_history | Immutable log of every transition taken (instance, from, to, user, comment). / nivaro_pipeline_owner_groups | Owner group per state — filters (JSON), sort, priority for tie-breaking. / nivaro_pipeline_owner_group_users | M2M link: owner group → nivaro_user. / nivaro_pipeline_owner_dimensions | Dimension config per binding — field (dotted path), label, is_row_axis, sort, required. / nivaro_pipeline_instance_owners | Per-record manual owner overrides. / nivaro_external_apis | Configured external API endpoints — base_url, auth_type, auth_config (JSON), headers (JSON), enabled, integration_type (plugin tag), integration_config (plugin JSON blob). / nivaro_external_api_endpoints | Predefined endpoint templates per API — name, method, path, default_body/query/headers (JSON), sort. CASCADE-deleted with parent API. / nivaro_comments | Per-record comments — collection, item, user FK, text (nvarchar(max)), timestamps. / nivaro_comment_mentions | M2M link from a comment to mentioned users — comment FK, user FK. / nivaro_dashboards | Dashboard definitions — name, user FK, is_shared, timestamps. / nivaro_dashboard_widgets | Widget rows per dashboard — type, title, collection, field, filters (JSON), grid position (col/row/width/height). / nivaro_workspaces | Workspace definitions — name, slug (unique), icon, color, timestamps. Default workspace seeded with fixed UUID.

Permissions are enforced by api/src/services/permissions.ts. The can(userId, collection, action) function returns true if any policy on the user's role grants the requested action on the requested collection.
Admin users (role.admin_access = true) bypass all checks. All other users must have an explicit policy.

MSSQL error 1785 fires when a foreign key introduces "cycles or multiple cascade paths." Three rules apply when adding new migrations:
• Self-referential FKs must use NO ACTION — not SET NULL or CASCADE. Affects nivaro_file_folders.parent and nivaro_revisions.parent. • Multiple FKs on the same table must use NO ACTION — nivaro_revisions has both activity and parent FKs; MSSQL rejects multiple cascade paths on the same table. • ON DELETE SET NULL requires a nullable column — MSSQL error 1761 if the column is NOT NULL.
When adding new FKs, default to onDelete('NO ACTION') and handle cascades in application code.
// Safe FK pattern for new migrations:
t.uuid('some_id')
  .nullable()
  .references('id')
  .inTable('some_table')
  .onDelete('NO ACTION');   // never CASCADE or SET NULL unless you've verified no cycles

Every field in a registered collection has per-field display settings that control how it is labelled and rendered in the item editor — without changing the underlying database column. Open Data Model → select a collection → hover a field chip in the Table Editor and click the gear icon to open the Display Settings popover. A cyan gear indicates the field already has overrides.

Setting | Applies to | Behavior / Label | All fields | Overrides the auto-generated label (title-cased field name). Leave blank to fall back to the default. / Interface | All fields | Overrides which input component renders the field. Options depend on the field's abstract type; choose "Default" to reset to auto-detection. / Placeholder | Text + number + textarea fields | Hint text shown inside the empty input. Stored as placeholder; presentation only — never saved as a value. / Note (helper text) | All fields | Short guidance for the field. Stored as note and surfaced as a tooltip info icon (ⓘ) next to the field label in the item editor. / Required | All fields | Marks the field as required in the editor. / Hidden | All fields | Hides the field from the item editor entirely. / Read-only | All fields | Renders the field as non-editable. / Inline edit | M2O relations | On by default. When enabled, the related record can be opened and edited inline next to the relation picker; when disabled, the field is a plain pick-only combobox. / Max values | M2M relations | Integer limit on how many related records can be linked. Leave blank for unlimited. Setting it to 1 switches the field to a single-select combobox.

Max values, and Unique rows by on an inline grid, are judged in the form. Each carries a switch, "Refuse on the server too", that makes the relation refuse the write wherever it comes from: another layout, an import through the items service, the API. The write answers 409 with LINK_LIMIT_REACHED or DUPLICATE_ROW and names the rule.
The switch is off by default because a limit is often true of one layout only. A form that takes one region beside another form that takes several must not switch it on. Stored as enforce_on_write: true beside the option, on the field or on the assignment in the collection's active layout.

blocks.h: Picker rules the server refuses too
blocks.t:
A relation picker offers only what its rules allow: the cascade filters (a project of the chosen zone and funding year), the field's own option filter, the target collection's picker filter and its picker exclusions. Those rules shape the form only, so a script, an import or another application may store a value the form would never offer. A relation field's settings carry "Enforce on API writes": the server then judges every write that names the field against the same rules, with the record as it would be stored, and refuses a value outside them with 400 PICKER_RULE_VIOLATED. The answer names the rule (cascade, option_filter, picker_filter or picker_exclusion), the field, and for a cascade the parents it read.
Off by default: integrations write legacy combinations the form no longer offers, and a rule enforced on the field binds every writer. Only fields present in the write are judged; changing a parent alone never re-judges the children. On an update, a parent the write does not carry is read from the record's own links. Stored as enforce_picker_rules: true on the field, or on its assignment in the collection's active layout, where the layout's own option filter is the one judged.

Text fields can carry an input mask that formats as the user types — e.g. (###) ###-#### for a phone number or AA-#### for a reference code. Three tokens: # accepts a digit, A a letter, * any character; everything else in the mask is a literal that inserts itself automatically. The mask shapes only what is on screen — the stored value is the clean characters with the literals stripped, so filters and integrations never see the punctuation. The mask also doubles as the input placeholder when the field has no explicit one.

Numeric fields accept a display unit: $ renders the value as currency, % appends a percent sign, and any other text becomes a suffix ("14 days"). Set it once on the field and it applies everywhere the shared display formatter renders that field. An explicit Format setting on the field wins over the unit.

Wide inline grids (O2M child tables) can pin their leading cells: the "Freeze first column" switch in the grid settings keeps the row handles and the first data column in place while the rest of the grid scrolls horizontally. Pinned cells need an opaque background, so they give up row tinting — the trade-off the switch’s help text spells out.

Field Rules are lightweight, per-collection automations that set or clear the value of one field based on the value of another. When a trigger field matches a condition, a target field is automatically set to a literal value or cleared. Rules run both server-side on save and in real time inside the item editor.
Field Rules are distinct from the global Rules engine (nivaro_rules). The Rules engine drives broader automation such as webhooks and notifications on create/update triggers. Field Rules are simple inline field defaults scoped to a single collection and stored in nivaro_field_rules.

• Each rule belongs to one collection and has a trigger (field + operator + optional value) and a target (field + action + optional value). • On save, applyFieldRules() runs inside createItem/updateItem before the row is written, evaluating every active rule whose trigger field is present in the payload. • In the item editor, changing a field calls POST /api/field-rules/evaluate, which returns only the fields the rules would change — those are merged into the draft immediately, with no save required. • Rules are evaluated in ascending sort order, so a later rule can override an earlier one.

Operator | Meaning | Uses value / eq | Trigger field equals the value | yes / neq | Trigger field does not equal the value | yes / null | Trigger field is empty (null/undefined) | no / nnull | Trigger field is not empty | no / contains | Trigger field (as text) contains the value | yes / in | Trigger field equals one of a comma-separated list | yes (comma-separated)
• set — assign a literal value to the target field. • clear — set the target field to null.

Open Data Model → select a registered collection → the "Field Rules" section in the right panel. Click Add Rule, then choose the trigger field, condition, target field, and action. Use the Active toggle to enable/disable a rule without deleting it, and the up/down arrows to reorder evaluation priority.

An inline-table field on a layout can carry its own per-row auto-fill rules (Table Editor → grid field settings → "Row auto-fill rules"): derive a line's category type from the picked category, its task from a project-type-filtered lookup, a lock on price for labor lines, and so on. The row editor evaluates them live as you edit, and the API runs the same rules when a child row is created directly.

In the row editor every rule target shows a small chip: "auto" when the value is exactly what the rules would derive, "overridden" when you (or an import) hold a different value. Fields the rules would leave empty show no chip. "↺ reset" beside an overridden value re-derives that one field from its rules. A value you change never gets flipped back by a slower rule response that was already in flight.

Row rules run on API creates and, by default, on API updates too: a PATCH that changes one of a rule's trigger fields re-derives its target, the same way the form does when you edit. A target the caller sends explicitly in the same request always wins. Untick "Re-run on API updates when a trigger field changes" on a rule to run it on creates only.

A cell a lock rule holds is read-only in both the inline editor and the row panel, and hovering it says which trigger locked it, using the row's own value: "Locked — Category is Installation - Labor". The evaluate call returns lock_reasons (trigger field, operator, value) beside locks.

blocks.h: Seed-only rules, conditional sources and pinned picker defaults
blocks.t:
A rule flagged **seed only** (Table Editor → rule footer) treats its target as an INPUT it merely fills when empty — a project's default category or default SKU for a new line. "Re-run rules" never blanks a seed-only target to re-derive it, Data Integrity never reports it as drift, and the row-input check still flags the line when it stays empty. Without the flag, a "default" rule would turn a hand-picked input into a target the re-run wipes. A seed-only value still equal to one of the rule family's own defaults counts as auto and FOLLOWS its trigger (switch a line from materials to equipment and the default SKU swaps); any other value is a hand pick and stays, and the row editor labels it overridden. When the new state derives nothing, the seeded value is left in place.
A precedence source may carry when: {field, op, value, related_field?} — the source only yields a candidate when the row (or the parent, via a $parent.<field> field) matches, with the same related-field hops as a trigger. One chain can therefore hold "alternate default when the parent record comes from a second source system, services default for labor lines, goods default otherwise" in front of a generic fallback. A source whose row field is empty is closed unless the op is about emptiness.
An M2O picker column can float a context-dependent default to the top of its list: options.pinned_options: [{when:{field,op,value}, parent_field, parent_collection, source_field, tag}] — when the ROW matches when (a materials line), the value the parent's linked record holds in source_field (order → project → default materials SKU) is pinned first with a tag, above search results and sort. Nothing is pinned without a match or a value. Entries are tried in order (project first, then the project type, say); when.field may name a $parent.<field> to key on the parent record (a record from a second source system gets that system's default). Works on the plain and the grouped picker alike.

A rule added or changed after lines were created never touched them. The grid toolbar's "re-run rules…" opens a panel with two modes: **Fill blanks only** writes rule targets that are empty today — plus any target a rule LOCKS on that line, since nobody could have typed those — **Re-derive everything** treats every rule target as blank first so set rules win over hand-typed values (a rule that derives nothing never erases what a line had). Preview lists which fields would change on how many lines and writes nothing. On a staged grid (save mode pending) the re-derived values are queued as row edits: lines show as Edited and land with the record's Save, so they can still be cancelled. Lines not yet saved — a new record's lines, staged additions — are planned alongside the saved ones (sent as rows with a client key; the server never writes them) and their patches are written back into the staged rows; staged edits on saved lines are overlaid first so the plan judges what the grid shows. On an immediate-mode grid Apply goes through the normal update path right away, so each line gets a revision attributed to you and the lines timeline shows the batch. The same call is POST /field-rules/apply with {collection, fk_field, parent_id, parent_context, row_rules, mode, dry_run} — update permission on the child collection is required for a real run, read permission for a preview.

Dynamic Attributes let admins add custom fields to a collection without a database migration or schema change. Definitions describe the attribute (key, label, type), and values are stored separately as key/value rows keyed by collection + item id. The item editor renders the matching inputs automatically.
This is an Entity-Attribute-Value (EAV) model. It complements — does not replace — real columns. Use real columns (Data Model → Fields) for data you query or filter heavily; use Dynamic Attributes for sparse, optional, or frequently-changing metadata where a migration would be overkill.

• nivaro_attribute_definitions holds one row per custom field: collection, key (slug), label, type, options (for select), required, sort, is_active. UNIQUE(collection, key). • nivaro_attribute_values holds one row per item value: collection, item_id (varchar, supports both UUID and integer PKs), attribute_key, value. UNIQUE(collection, item_id, attribute_key). • All values are stored as nvarchar(max) text regardless of type; the frontend parses them by the definition type on render. • The item editor shows a "Custom Attributes" card only when at least one active definition exists for the collection.

Type | Editor input | Stored as / text | Text input | string / number | Numeric input | string (numeric) / boolean | Switch | "true" / "false" / date | Date input | ISO date string / select | Combobox of options | one of the option strings

Open Data Model → select a collection → the "Attributes" tab. Click Add attribute, then set the key (slug, fixed after creation), label, type, and — for select types — a comma-separated list of options. Toggle Required and Active per definition, and delete a definition to remove it (which also cleans up its stored values).

On any existing item, the Custom Attributes card lists every active attribute for the collection. Each field saves independently — on blur for text/number/date, immediately for boolean and select — via PATCH /api/attributes/:collection/:itemId.

Each registered collection can have multiple named layouts. A layout defines how fields are grouped and ordered in the item editor. One grouped layout is the default; others are picked by record rules or roles, opened by their link name (?layout=<slug>), or serve other views (summary, detail, PDF, addendum, grid columns).

Open Data Model → select a collection → Layout tab. It opens on "Which form does each record get?" — every layout of the collection in the order the server checks them, with the conditions in plain words — and opens a layout in the layout editor from there. Admins can also edit a record's form from the record page with Edit form. See Layout Editor for the overview, the editor, saving and history.
Action | How / Create layout | Overview → New form (pick the kind up front); Create first form when there is none / Make default | Overview → row menu → Make default / Duplicate layout | Overview → row menu → Duplicate (or Duplicate as summary) / Delete layout | Overview → row menu → Delete (lists references first; history is kept) / Rename layout | Overview → row menu → Rename

GET  /api/collection-layouts?collection=articles[&layout_type=grouped]
GET  /api/collection-layouts/active?collection=articles[&item=42|&slug=x]
GET  /api/collection-layouts/overview?collection=articles     (admin)
GET  /api/collection-layo…

Every form in Nivaro is a layout: which fields a record shows, in which sections, tabs or steps, with which panels and rules. The layout editor is where they are built. It opens from Data Model → a collection → Layout tab, and from any record page with Edit form (admins only, in Nivaro admin and in headless frontends such as efp-new). The canvas is the real record form, so what you arrange is exactly what people get.

blocks.h: Which form does each record get?
blocks.t:
The Layout tab opens on an overview that answers one question in plain words: which form does each kind of record open with, and why. Rows are listed in the order the server checks them, so reading top to bottom is reading the resolution itself. A ?layout=<id> link skips the overview and opens that layout in the editor.
Section | What it lists / Forms people fill in — checked in this order | One row per grouped layout. "When the record…" is the layout's record rules as a sentence with field and choice labels ("is not unit-specific and is sparing"), role restrictions by role name ("for Finance only"), and "anything else" on the default. "Opens" names the layout with a default or rule pill and a shape line ("4 steps · 34 fields"). "Also" shows the New-menu label or "hidden from New menu". A row that can never be reached (another layout always matches first) carries a quiet warning. / Opened by a link or button only | Grouped layouts nothing resolves to on its own but that have a link name: reached by ?layout=<slug>, a queue's item layout, a grid's layout_slug or a transition dialog. Known references are listed. / Other views of the same record | Summary (read mode), detail (drill-down panel), file (PDF), addendum and table (grid columns when the collection is shown inside another record), each with one line on what uses it. / Unused | Layouts nothing resolves to or references, with Delete. A layout with a link name is never called unused — it may be used by URLs or code. Delete lists any references it finds before asking you to confirm.
Order among grouped forms is computed (layouts with more record rules first, then role preferences, then the default), so those rows are not draggable. Drag to reorder exists only where sort decides — the first-by-sort fallbacks for table, addendum, detail and summary layouts.
• The header holds Test a record, Find a field (on every form), Analyze ▾ (Check coverage, Worst first, Compare forms…), ⋯ (Every form) and New form. When people suggested changes, the line under the title says how many; click it for the forms they are about. • One strip under the header gathers what needs a look across the forms: "4 things need a look" with a chip per kind — rule loops, placements that point at nothing, forms missing translations, fields labelled differently, near copies. A chip opens its rows; the heading opens them all. The last coverage check sits at the strip's end ("Coverage: 2 forms get no records") with Check again. • New form — asks for the kind up front (form, summary, detail, PDF, addendum, grid columns), then opens it in the editor. • Row menu — Open, Rename, Duplicate, Duplicate as summary, Make default, Delete. • No layouts yet — the empty state explains what a form layout is and offers Create first form, which seeds one section "Main" holding every visible field of the collection.

Test a record… picks a saved record and lights up the row it resolves to, with the reason in words, and says for every other form why it was passed over ("Its record rules do not match", "A form with record rules matched first", "Restricted to other roles"). Optionally test as a role. The test runs the live /active resolution itself — there is no separate preview logic — so the answer is what that person would get.
Pick Phone under Screen to see which form the record opens with on a small screen, and a day under On day to test active dates on another day.

Form settings → Who gets this form → Active dates limits a form to the days between From and Until (both included, in the instance time zone). Outside them the form takes no part in choosing a form: records open with the next form that fits, as if the form were restricted to other roles. A link that names the form falls through the same way. The overview shows the dates beside the form and warns when they have not started or have passed. Scheduled changes publish edits to a form; active dates decide when the form is used at all.

Form settings → Who gets this form → Phone version → Make a phone version copies the form as a lighter one for small screens (remove what a phone does not need). Record pages on a screen narrower than 640 px ask for the phone version (viewport=phone on /collection-layouts/active): after the usual rules pick a form, its phone version opens in its place. A phone version never opens on its own and needs no rules of its own; its roles and active dates still apply. On the overview it sits under the form it stands in for.

Check coverage runs the 500 newest records through the same matching the record page uses (as an administrator sees them) and says, under each form, how many of them open with it. A form nobody gets, and record rules that match none of the records, are flagged. Forms chosen by role are not counted. Check again samples afresh.
Each form carries a health score from 0 to 100. It loses points for many fields, many steps, fields nobody sees and what the Problems panel finds; it reads "Health 72" with a coloured dot, and hovering it shows what cost it points. Analyze → Worst first sorts each section by score — turn it off to read the matching order again. Analyze → Check coverage runs the coverage check; its result sits at the end of the strip under the header.

Three areas: on the left the layouts of the collection (grouped as on the overview, each with a one-line purpose) and an entry for Form settings; in the centre the canvas; on the right the inspector for whatever is selected. The top bar is one row: ‹ Forms, the form’s name and who else has it open, Undo / Redo, the view (Canvas, Table, States, Roles) and Rules, Preview ▾, Tools ▾, AI ▾, the Problems count, History, ⋯, the save status and Save ▾. Tools holds Auto-arrange, Find on this form, Find and replace, Outline, Compact / Expand all / Collapse all, Show how full each field is, Every form, Form map and Keyboard shortcuts. AI holds Rebuild or lighter version, Test as a role, Review the look, Tune from autofill, Ask…, Type a change… and Suggested changes (its count shows on AI). ⋯ holds Test, Share & watchers, Watch this form, Save as template, New form from this record and Download this form. On a narrow screen the view switch shows icons only and the Preview summary and the Rules, Tools and AI labels drop away, so the bar never wraps.

The canvas is the shared record form (ItemEditForm, or the read view for summary and detail layouts) running in design mode: same styles, spacing, steps or tabs, header strip and slot cards as a real record. Inputs are inert — nothing on the canvas writes to a record, takes a lock or runs a rule that saves. Click a field, section, tab, slot card, header strip item or widget to select it (from the keyboard: Tab to it, Enter). Empty sections show a drop zone; Show hidden reveals fields and sections the preview would hide, faintly, so they can still be selected.

Tab | What it holds / Look | Label on this form (or hidden), width, help text, placeholder, how the value is shown: input type, format, currency, unit, precision, input mask. / Rules | Required, read-only, hidden, lock conditions, default value for new records, maximum number of values. / Picker | Relation fields only: cascade filters, option field and sort, picker rules, pick or upload, inline editing, prefill from the parent, drill-down panel. / Grid / Table | Child-record grids only: columns, row rules, parent cascades, parent context fields, the row-rule tester. / Advanced | Raw overrides and the keys that have no editor of their own.
Sections, tabs and steps, slot cards (pipeline, comments, tasks, owners, PDF, extension panels), header strip items, the subtitle and widgets each get an inspector of their own.

blocks.h: This form only vs every form
blocks.t:
Every setting says where it applies. Most are this form only: they save with the layout (on Save, or at once with Autosave on) and can be undone. Some live on the field itself (format, currency, unit, mask, cascade filters, column presets, grid totals, file options, deprecation) and change every form that shows the field; a widget's own settings change every form that places it. Those are marked "every form", sit outside Undo and History, and save only after an inline confirm ("Save for every form") that names what else they affect.
Row rules, row lints, picker enforcement, max values and line SLA are enforced on the server from the default grouped form only. On any other layout the inspector labels those keys "enforced on the default form only".

Layout-wide settings in short named sections, each control with a one-line effect, searchable from the box at the top: Who gets this form (kind, record rules, roles by name, link name, New-menu label and hiding) · How it's laid out (tabs or steps, check each step before Next, one section open at a time) · Buttons & panels (hide comments, tasks, revisions, clone, delete, banners; Schedule and Hide-from-pickers buttons for everyone) · Read view & summary · PDF (file layouts only) · Addendum · Defaults for new records · Entering data (keyboard, tab order, guided steps, badge, presets) · Inheritance · AI review, previews, version history. Only the settings that apply to the layout's kind are shown — addendum layouts get every setting that applies to them. This page calls that last section Form settings → Tools.
"Schedule button for everyone" and "Hide-from-pickers button for everyone" give people who may edit the record "Schedule a change…" and "Disable in pickers" (administrators always have both). Nivaro admin shows them in the record header; the shared record form shows them in its More menu when the host turns on showGrantedTools (efp-new does). The server checks the same grant for both. A non-admin must be able to see the record (otherwise the answer is Not found), the form that record opens with for them must have the setting on, and they must be allowed to update this record — the update rules of their role for the collection, its row filter and any tree permission, not just access to the collection. A form opened with a ?layout= link counts only when it is a record form their role may open and its record rules match this record; naming any other form never grants the tool. Scheduling also checks every field in the change: each must be one the person may update, and a registered field with its own column that is not read-only, computed or an audit stamp; otherwise the request is refused naming the field. People who are not administrators see the scheduled changes on a record only when they can see the record, with values of fields they may not read left out, and may cancel only their own changes on records they can still update.

Add a field, section, panel or widget opens a searchable list showing labels (the key as secondary text), the type and an "on this form" mark for what is already placed. Click a row to add it after the selection, or drag it onto the canvas. A field already on the form can be added again ("Add another copy") — the same field may sit in two places, such as the header strip and a section.
On other forms lists, above the fields, the fields this collection's other forms of the same kind place and this one does not, most-carried first, with how many forms carry each and their names.

blocks.h: Entering data: keyboard, steps, badge, presets
blocks.t:
Form settings → Entering data holds what changes how people fill the form. Start on the first empty required field puts the cursor there when the form opens. Enter moves to the next field turns Enter into "next" (Ctrl or ⌘ + Enter saves; Enter still means a new line in long text and picks the highlighted item in an open list). Glossary tooltips in help text gives glossary terms in a field's help text a dotted underline with their definition from AI knowledge → Glossary (labels always have it).
Tab order: Tools → Set the tab order (or the button in Form settings) numbers the fields as you click them on the canvas. Click a number again to take that field out. Done stores the order as one undoable step; fields you skipped follow in page order. Tab and Shift+Tab then follow the order on the record form, while a field with two controls keeps its own order inside.
Guided steps for new people: the form shows as steps while a person has made fewer records of the collection than the number in Records before tabs (3 unless you change it), and as tabs after that. People can switch with the Guided steps / Tabs switch above the header; their choice is remembered in their browser. It needs a form with tabs or steps.
Form badge: a short tag (16 characters at most) in one of eight colours, shown above the record header, so people can tell which form they are in.
Presets: select a field, open Presets in its inspector, tick what to keep (width, required, help text, placeholder, input and format, lock rule), name it and save. Select one or several fields and pick a preset to apply it; that is one undo step. Presets belong to the form and are deleted under Form settings → Entering data. They never change a field's label.
Theme preview: Tools → Preview in dark shows the canvas in the dark theme without changing the app's theme. When the app is already dark the tool is off, because a dark app cannot show a light canvas.
These settings live in one JSON column, nivaro_collection_layouts.entry_config (migration 491): { focus_first, enter_next, tab_order, adaptive, adaptive_threshold, badge: { tag, color }, glossary, presets }. It is a layout setting like the others (layout_update ops, PATCH /collection-layouts/:id) and is returned by GET /collection-layouts/active.

• The whole element is the handle: field, section header, tab, step or slot card. Keyboard drag works too (focus, Space to lift, arrows to move, Space to drop, Escape to cancel). • The drag preview is a copy of the element as it looks on the form, under the cursor at any scroll position; the canvas scrolls when you near its edge. • An insertion slot opens where the element will land, within a section or across sections, including into an empty section. Dropping on a section header puts the field first in that section; sections reorder by dropping anywhere on the target section. • Widths change with the inspector's width control, snapping to the grid fractions. • Alt+arrow moves the selected item in one keystroke, without picking it up. A field: Alt+↑ / Alt+↓ moves it one place in its section; Alt+← / Alt+→ moves it to the end of the previous section or the start of the next. A section moves up or down the page; a tab or step moves left or right. Each keystroke is one Undo step.

Shift-click (or ⌘ / Ctrl-click) fields to select several; click one again to take it out. The inspector then shows what they share: width, Required, Read-only, Hidden and Section. Each change applies to all of them as one Undo step. "Section" moves them to the end of that section, in the order they are on the form; a field the section already holds stays where it is. Sections, header items and page cards are selected one at a time. Dragging moves one item; use Section to move several.

Auto-arrange packs fields into tidy rows of the 12-column grid. A row with room left takes the widest of the next few fields that fits, so the order mostly holds, and "Widen fields to fill rows" stretches the fields of a row that still has room. The popover lists what changes per section (rows, gaps closed, fields moved and widened) before you press Arrange; the whole change is one Undo step. The top bar arranges the whole form; a section's inspector arranges that section only. Hidden fields stay next to the field they followed.

Canvas | Table in the top bar switches the centre to a table of every field on the form, grouped by section: the label on this form, section, width, Required, Read-only and Hidden, all editable in place. Shift- or ⌘-click rows (or tick their boxes) to select several and change them together in the inspector. Fields that come from a parent layout are not listed. Table and PDF layouts keep their own canvases.

blocks.h: Finding your way on a long form
blocks.t: • Find on this form (⌘F / Ctrl+F in the editor, or Tools → Find on this form) finds a field, panel, step, tab or section by label or key. Picking a match opens the step or tab it sits on, unfolds its section, scrolls to it and selects it. Hidden fields and fields a rule hides are found too; picking one turns on Show hidden when the form would not show it. • Outline (Tools → Outline) lists the header strip, steps, tabs, sections and their fields beside the canvas. Clicking a row selects it on the canvas, and selecting on the canvas marks its row. Drag rows to reorder: the same moves as dragging on the canvas, one Undo step each. Parts that come from a parent layout show but do not move. The outline stays open for you until you close it. • The inspector's header shows where the selection sits, for example Field · Flow › Billing. Click a part to select that step, tab or section. • Tools has Compact canvas (smaller spacing and inputs in the editor only, kept for you in this browser; the record page is unchanged), Expand all (every section open and every step and tab laid out one under another) and Collapse all (every section folded; steps and tabs back to one at a time). • Press ? (when not typing) or the keyboard button for every shortcut, grouped by area: undo and redo, duplicate, moving with Alt+arrows or Space, find, the command palette and save.

blocks.h: Arrange: duplicate, wrap, split, join, convert, pin
blocks.t:
Right-click anything on the canvas (or press the context-menu key on it), or press Arrange… in a section's inspector, to open the Arrange menu beside it. Every action in it is one Undo step.
• Duplicate (⌘D / Ctrl+D) copies the selected section, tab, step or holder right after itself, with all its settings and every field's settings (label, width, rules). A holder brings its tabs. The copy's fields are the same fields, so they now show in both sections. A single field cannot be duplicated: a field shows once per section. • Wrap puts the selected fields in a new section right after the first one's section. Fields in a tab or step get a new tab or step beside it, since a section cannot sit in a holder. • Unwrap removes a section, tab or step and keeps its fields as ungrouped fields. When there are no ungrouped fields yet, they stay where the section was. • Convert to… turns a section into a tab or step (it joins the holder just above it when that holder shows the same way, else a new holder takes its place), a tab or step into a section (an emptied holder goes), tabs into steps and back, or a holder's tabs into sections. Each choice lists what it would change before you press Convert. A holder shows all its tabs one way, so one tab becomes a step only with its siblings. • Copy rules to other sections… copies Hidden for, Read-only for and (from a tab or step) Only when onto the sections you tick. Step conditions are skipped on plain sections, where they do nothing. • Pin in the editor marks a section so it cannot be dragged and takes no drops, with its fields and tabs, while you arrange the rest. Alt+arrow skips it too. The pin only affects the editor; the form people see is unchanged. • Split the section here (on a selected field) moves that field and everything after it to a new section right below, named “… (continued)”, in the same order. The first part keeps all its settings; the new part takes its look, rules and visibility, but not its intro, collapsed summary or field swap. A split cannot fall inside a row of fields side by side. • Join with … (on a section, tab or step) moves the fields of the section right below into this one, after its own, and removes the emptied section. This section keeps its settings; a field both hold shows once. • Put side by side under one label (with two to six fields of one section selected) puts them in one row, such as Street / City / Zip or Qty / Unit. The row shows one label and one required marker; each input is captioned with its own name. Rename or take a row apart in the section’s inspector under Side by side; take one field out from its own inspector.

blocks.h: Show more, sticky sections and empty text
blocks.t: • Behind “Show more” (a field’s Look tab) tucks an optional field under a “Show 4 more” button at the end of its section. The fold opens on its own as soon as one of its fields has a value, so nothing filled is ever hidden. Required fields and fields in a row always show. The read view and the PDF leave out an empty folded field. • Stick to the top (a section’s inspector) keeps that section, such as totals or status, at the top of the form while people scroll the rest. A form has one sticky section: turning it on for one turns it off for the other. It does not stick on phone widths, nor on the canvas, where it is tagged “Sticks to the top”. • When nothing is filled (a section’s inspector) is the text the read view and the PDF show for a section none of whose fields has a value, such as “No shipping details yet”, instead of a list of dashes. • Rows of fields side by side print the same way everywhere: one label on the record page, and on the read view and the PDF their values on one line, joined by a dot. • Select a field to get a width handle on its right edge: drag it to make the field full, half, a third or a quarter wide (or focus it and press ← →). While you drag a field or a width, faint guides show the form’s 12 columns, so widths line up across sections.

Find and replace (Tools) searches this form's field labels, section names, text blocks and help text, for example Oracle to Fusion. Where the form sets no label or help text of its own, the collection's is searched too; replacing it gives this form its own. Every match is listed with its before and after and a tick box; Replace changes the ticked ones as one Undo step.

The Outputs button (Tools) turns the saved form into files. Excel import template gives one column per field in the form's order: choice fields are dropdowns, number and date columns are checked, and required columns are amber. A Fields sheet explains every column. Export records to Excel writes up to 5,000 records in the same columns, limited to what you may read; pointers to other records show their names. Blank printable form is a PDF with a ruled line, checkboxes or lines for every field, for people filling it in on paper.
Download as a sheet writes every label, help text and placeholder on the form, with your unsaved edits, to Excel. Edit the amber columns and upload the file back: the editor lists every difference with a tick box, and Apply changes the ticked ones as one Undo step. Clearing a cell removes the text this form set, so the field's own text shows again. Rows for fields or sections that were removed are left out.
Section for notification emails (Form settings, Tools) picks the section whose fields notification emails show as the record summary, in place of the header strip. Each email is cut to the person it goes to: a section hidden for their role, a field their role may not read, or a record they cannot open adds nothing. None keeps the header strip. It needs migration 493, and only the default form's choice counts.

A layout that inherits from a parent shows the parent's placements on its canvas marked "from <parent>" and locked (an inherited step or tab gets a small dot instead, with the parent's name in its tip). The inspector offers Override here (copies the placement into this layout as the parent last saved it, then editable) and Edit in <parent>.
What this layout changes of the parent's is tagged "Overrides parent". Select it and the inspector offers Reset to parent: this layout's copy goes and the parent's shows again, as one Undo step. Resetting a section also resets the fields in it that the parent places; fields only this layout places move to Ungrouped. The States and Roles views mark rows the same way, with Reset or Override beside the name.

When Settings → Localization lists more than one language, the first is the one the form is written in and the others get a Translations section: a field's label and help text (Look tab) and a section's, tab's or step's name (its inspector). Translations save with the layout and version with it. The record form shows them to people reading in that language — their chosen admin language, else the page's, else the browser's — and the text as written where a translation is missing. A suggested translation (for example one drafted by AI) shows marked as a suggestion and stays off records until Approve; the overview counts it as missing until then. The overview counts the missing translations per form. Section names need migration 465; field labels and help text work without it. Record values are translated separately (field translations).

• Table layouts (the columns a collection shows when it is a grid inside another record) edit on a columns strip that looks like the real grid header: column order and width, plus the Apply values and Create with defaults zones. • File (PDF) layouts edit their sections in form style, labelled as the PDF prints them; Preview with sample values waits for the last change to save (unsaved changes are not in it — Save first), then renders the real PDF in a new tab. Theme, cover, logo, page size, orientation and button label live in Form settings → PDF, which has its own Preview PDF. • Summary and detail layouts edit on the read view they render as, with the same selection and drag handles.

On a record page an admin finds Edit form in the record's More menu (Nivaro admin ItemEdit and efp-new RecordDetail). It switches that page's form into design mode on the layout this record resolved to, with the layouts list, inspector and add panel as side panels over the page. The editor keeps the layout it opened on even if a save changes which layout the record resolves to. Back to record closes it at once; the record re-reads its layout as soon as the last change has saved, so it never shows the form from before your last edit. When the collection has no layout yet, the same menu row reads Create the first form and opens the Layout tab. When the page's ?layout= link names a form that doesn't exist, it reads Form not found and opens the collection's forms instead.
Edits are the same operations, saving and History as in the Layout tab. People who are not administrators never see the menu row and never download the editor: it is a separate chunk, loaded only when an admin turns the mode on (efp-new loads it through the @nivaro/react/layout-editor subpath export).

Changes wait for Save. The form shows each change at once, but nobody else sees it until you press Save (or ⌘S / Ctrl+S); the top bar counts them ("3 unsaved changes") and Save turns blue while there is something to save. The arrow beside Save opens the Save menu: Review changes on canvas, What changes, AI review, Schedule… and Autosave. One Save sends every change together, and History names them.
Autosave (Save ▾ → Autosave) saves every change as you make it instead; the status chip reads Saving… then Saved. It is off each time the editor opens and stays as you set it until you close the editor. Turning it on saves anything unsaved straight away; the bar then shows only the save status, with the arrow beside it to turn Autosave off.
Leaving with unsaved changes asks first, beside what you clicked: Save, Discard or Keep editing. That covers Back, Done, Escape, opening another layout in the rail and links elsewhere in the app; closing or reloading the browser tab gets the browser's own warning. If the editor closes some other way (the browser's back button), the changes stay with that layout: open it again to save or discard them.
Undo and Redo (⌘Z / ⇧⌘Z, Ctrl+Y) step back through this session's changes, saved or not, each named ("Undo Move Status"). Undoing an unsaved change just takes it away; undoing a saved one is a new change to save (or saves at once with Autosave). Typing in one box counts as one change until you leave the box, and a refresh never overwrites what you are typing or anything unsaved.
Changes go to the server as small operations against the revision the editor last saw. If another admin (or you in another tab) saved in between, your changes are replayed on top of theirs instead of thrown away: with Save they stay unsaved for you to Save again; with Autosave they are sent again at once. A change that no longer fits (they removed what it changed) is dropped and listed in a banner above the form for you to redo by hand; the rest are kept. Undo keeps every change that was kept, and a saved setting change as long as nobody changed that setting since. Nothing is silently overwritten. A refused Save keeps your changes and says why. Restoring a version from History drops unsaved changes.
Every field or section an unsaved change touched shows a small blue dot until you save. Click the unsaved count in the top bar to list the changes; click one to select what it changed and scroll to it (a form-settings change opens Form settings).

blocks.h: Your draft is staged until you save
blocks.t:
Unsaved changes are a private draft: only you see them, on the canvas and nowhere else. About a second after each change they are kept for you on the server (and in this browser), so a closed tab, a crash or a switch to another computer loses nothing. Opening the layout again offers Recover, which brings the changes back unsaved, and Discard, which drops them. The status chip's tip says where the draft stands ("Kept for you on the server").
If the layout was saved by anyone since (or staging took the night's layouts from development), Recover lays your changes on top of the layout as it is now; a change that no longer fits is listed in a banner instead of applied, the rest are kept. Save is still one step: every change lands together against the layout's current revision, or none does.
A small "Ana is drafting" chip beside the layout's name says who else has unsaved changes staged on it, and how many — never what they are. Saving, discarding or scheduling your changes clears your draft.

The other admins who have the same layout open show as avatars beside the layout's name. What each has selected gets an outline in their colour with their first name; click an avatar to jump to it. Only names and what is selected are shared, never unsaved changes.

Form settings → Tools → Ask why on every save makes Save ask for a short reason, or a reason and a ticket link. The reason and ticket lead the version's note in History. Autosave stays off for that layout, and the server refuses a save without them (turning the setting off needs a reason too).

Form settings → Tools → Freeze edits stops changes to a layout until a date (a go-live or an audit), with a reason people read. Until that day the server refuses every save, restore, settings change and delete of the layout with the reason (400 LAYOUT_FROZEN). An administrator can still save by giving an override note: the editor asks for it at Save, the note becomes the version note in History and an activity entry (layout-freeze-override). Lifting the freeze early is a save too, so it asks for a note. The freeze lifts by itself on its date; copies of a frozen layout are not frozen.

Select a section that starts collapsed and turn on Load when opened. Until someone opens it, the record page does not read what only that section holds: its grids' rows, its relation-path values and its widgets. Fields the folded section shows in its summary still load. Test → Cost counts these requests apart ("more once someone opens…"). It changes when data loads on live records, so it is off unless you turn it on for a section.

History lists the saved versions of the layout — one per editing burst, sections included — with who saved and the change's name. "What the last save changed" shows the newest difference first; any version can be compared with the layout now. Restore replaces the layout with that version exactly (sections added since are removed) after keeping the current one as a version first. Versions survive a layout delete.
Piece on a version restores one section or one field from it without rolling back the rest. It lists only what differs from the form now, each with what restoring does ("Back on the form · 2 settings", "1 field removed · Order"): a field comes back with its settings, in the version's section when it is elsewhere or gone (its place among its neighbours is kept as it is now); a section comes back exactly as the version had it — its settings, its tabs, its fields in that order, fields added since removed. Each restore is one change: one Undo step, one unsaved change to save (or one autosave). A field whose section is gone says so; restore the section instead.
This session (at the top of History) lists every Undo step since you opened the layout, oldest first, each marked saved or unsaved, and what Redo would bring back. Click a step to go back (or forward) to the layout right after it: that is the same as pressing Undo or Redo that many times, so it saves, or waits for Save, the same way.
Name a version to keep it: older unnamed versions are pruned (the newest 30 are kept), named ones never are. "Name the saved form…" keeps the form as it is saved now ("Go-live baseline"); Name / Rename on a version names that one, and clearing the name lets it be pruned again. Compare any later state against a named version like any other.
Show on canvas (from the comparison, or Canvas on a version) marks the difference on the form itself: added fields and sections are outlined green, moved ones amber with the section they came from, changed ones violet with the settings that differ, and removed ones come back faintly in their old place, tagged Removed (they cannot be selected or dragged). With unsaved changes, Save ▾ → Review changes on canvas does the same for what you are about to save. Close the comparison from the bar above the canvas.
Explain in words, under a comparison, says what the differences mean for the people filling the form, using the History notes of the saves in between (administrators, with AI set up). The exact differences and the notes stay one click away, and without AI they are what you get. Compare two forms and Merge two forms use the same explanation for two different layouts.
The selected section, or the one under the pointer, shows on its frame who last changed it and when. It is worked out from the versions the layout keeps, so a change older than the kept versions is not named.

With unsaved changes, Save ▾ → Schedule… applies them at a time you pick instead of now (for example the morning of a release). They leave the editor at once and nobody sees them until then. At that time the server applies them like a Save, as a version named "Scheduled change by <you>". If someone changed the layout meanwhile, your changes still apply when every one of them fits; if one no longer fits, nothing is applied and you get a notification saying why.
The overview shows each form's scheduled changes (when, who, how many) under its name; any administrator can cancel one. A change that could not be applied stays there with the reason until dismissed (or for a week).

Preview as picks a record: the canvas shows its real values, its steps, and the fields its rules show or hide. "As a role" previews the form the way a role sees it — hidden and read-only fields are marked.
The same Preview as popover holds the other preview modes. A strip above the canvas says what each active mode changes; its × turns that mode off. Nothing in them changes a record.
• Compare with a second role: the canvas splits in two, the same record as each role. Fields one role can edit and the other only read (or never see), and sections only one of them sees, are ringed and tagged Differs; hover the tag for both answers. Both halves are preview only: select to edit, but drag on a single canvas. • Workflow state: pick a state of a pipeline bound to the collection and the form shows it as if the record were there — the fields that state locks, and what each move out of it needs (tagged Needed to move on) — without finding a record in that state. • What if: pick a field a step’s "Only when" condition reads, then one of the values the condition tests, Empty, or any value. The canvas lays it over the record and tags the steps that appear (Appears) or disappear (Hides, seen with Show hidden). • Device: Desktop, Tablet (768 px) or Phone (390 px). The form measures its own width, so columns wrap exactly as on that screen. • Who sees each field: every field is tinted by how many roles see it (every role, most, some, few, none — legend in the strip) with a chip such as 3/5 roles; click the chip for the roles that can edit it, only read it, or never see it. It combines each role’s permissions with this form’s section and lock rules; administrators see everything and are not counted.

blocks.h: Test records, new-record walkthrough, form cost
blocks.t:
⋯ → Test in the top bar has three tabs. Test records: pin up to 5 records that cover the form's important cases, each as a role or as an administrator. They are stored with the layout (versioned with it, never sent to non-admins). Re-check runs the live resolver, the same one as Test a record, for each one against your draft and shows which form it gets, how many fields it sees and what changed: against the last save while changes wait for Save, otherwise against your previous check.
New record acts out creating a record on this form as a role, step by step, and stops where the form would stop them: at Next when the form validates each step, otherwise at Save. A required field blocks when the role may not write it, it is locked or read-only, or its step or section is hidden for the values you pick under "Values they enter". Required fields the form never shows are listed under "Saves without". Nothing is written.
Cost estimates how many requests a record page fires when it opens on this form: one per picker, three per inline grid, one per widget, panel, relation-path or remote-options field, plus the page's own reads. It warns above the Form cost limit (Form settings → Tools; default 40). It complements form-ready timing, which is measured after release.
What changes (Save ▾ → What changes, while changes wait) runs the same check before you save and lists what changes for the pinned records ("Record 284212 loses the Zone field", "lands on another form") and the form cost against its limit. It only reads.
After each deploy the readiness scorecard (Configuration → "Pinned test records still see their forms as before") opens every pinned record the way its role would and compares it with what the previous version showed: which form it opens on, which fields it shows and which its role may edit. A difference is a warning naming the record and the change. Accept what test records see now makes the current view the one later checks compare with. Show-when rules on tabs are not judged.

The Rules switch in the top bar (the branch icon; on by default, remembered per browser) puts small tags on the canvas that say why each field behaves as it does: Required here or Required field (this form or every form), Needed to Approve (a pipeline move requires it), Read-only here, Read-only field, Calculated, Locked for Finance, Locked in Approved, Hidden here, Hidden field, and Filled by a rule. Hover a tag for the whole sentence; click it to open what causes it: the field's Rules, Look or Advanced tab, the section, the pipeline or the field rules page.
Sections carry their rules as sentences too, worded as on the overview: "Shows when Is Sparing is Yes", "Skipped when Project is filled", "Hidden for Finance", "Read-only for Finance".
Hover a field whose value decides something else: every section it shows or hides, picker it filters, field a rule fills and grid whose lines or row rules read it gets a dashed amber ring, and the field a "Controls n" tag.
Without a preview record, each input shows in grey the value a new record on this form starts with: "Default: Open" from the form's defaults, "By rule: …" when a field rule fills it from those defaults, "From Project: …" when a cross-record default copies it from a record a default picks. Yes/no and multi-pick fields show it as a tag. Nothing is saved; preview a record to see its real values instead.
Rule loops are flagged in a banner above the canvas and on the overview: a section that shows only by a field placed inside that same section (once hidden, nobody can change the field back), or fields whose rules, cascades and section rules decide each other in a circle. The fields involved get a Rule loop tag; Show selects the first one. A loop of field rules alone is the same on every form, so the overview says it once above the list.

States in the top bar shows every field against the states of the collection's pipeline (a switcher picks one when several run on it), with an Every state column first. Click a cell to set the field to Editable, Read-only, Required or Hidden. Every state writes the field's own Read-only, Required and Hidden on this form. Read-only in one state adds that state to the field's Read-only when. Required in one state makes the moves that leave the state ask for the value (a record-fields requirement on those moves); that is saved to the pipeline at once, for every form, and its toast has Undo. A field cannot be hidden in one state only, and a state nothing leaves cannot require anything: those choices stay greyed with the reason. A dot on a cell marks a field that is read-only but required, which nobody could fill in.

Roles in the top bar shows every section and tab against every role. Click a cell to make the section Can edit, Read-only or Hidden for that role (the section's Hidden for and Read-only for). Each cell is one change to save. Administrator roles are greyed: they always see and edit everything. Field permissions still apply inside a section.

blocks.h: How a field behaves on live records
blocks.t:
Settings on a field that change what people see and do on a saved record. All of them are per placement (this form only) and off until you set them.
• Label and help by state or role (Look tab): different words in a workflow state or for a role, for example "Requested date" that reads "Delivered date" once Completed. Add a rule, pick the states or roles, and type the label and help text for that case; the first rule that matches wins. The record page, the read view and the PDF follow it, and Preview as a role or a state shows it on the canvas. • Recommended (Rules tab): between optional and required. The field gets an amber dot beside its label; saving lists the recommended fields still empty but never stops the save. The record header counts them on their own ("2 recommended to fill"), apart from the required-fields percentage. Required wins when both are on. • Confirm changes on saved records (Rules tab): changing the field on an existing record asks "Are you sure?" and a short reason before the save. The reason is stored with the change and shows in the record history. Tick states to ask only while the record is in them; with none ticked it asks in every state. New records are never asked. A transition button that would save the change asks first, then you start the move again. • Repeat last value (Rules tab): a Repeat last button beside the label fills in what this person entered for the field on their previous record of the collection, read from their own change history. It never offers another person's value, encrypted fields or system tables. • Counter and limit (Look tab, text fields): a counter under the input in characters or words. The limit starts at the database column size; past the limit the form will not save.
