Leave the limit empty to count without one. • Display formula (Add panel → Display formula): a read-only figure worked out on the page from fields already on the form, for example Remaining = {{budget}} - {{committed}}, shown as plain, whole, 0.00, money or a percent. It uses the same expression language as other client formulas, is never stored and creates no computed field. The inspector flags syntax errors, names that are not fields and fields that are not on this form (they read as empty there).

The Problems count in the top bar (the alert icon and a number) counts the errors and warnings on the form as you edit it; it opens the Problems panel listing them, worst first (Errors, Warnings, Tips). Click one to select it on the canvas. Many come with a fix that is one undo step.
• A required field the form hides, or one in a section hidden or locked for a role that can edit the record — or that must fill it to make a transition. • A picker that narrows its choices by a field that is not on the form. • Empty sections, steps and tabs holders. • Steps and sections no record reaches (their show-when rules can never hold, or contradict the record rules of the form, or every role but administrators is hidden from them), and fields that sit only there or are hidden everywhere they are placed. • Accessibility: fields without a label, a required field whose label (and so its required mark) is hidden, a half-width field that sits after a wider one although it would fit beside the field above it, and a chosen colour that reads below 3:1 on the light or dark background.
These checks are counted, never guessed. The AI review in Form settings → Tools also reads labels and help text.

• Stored as (Look tab): the database type and size behind the field, for example nvarchar(50). A warning shows when this form's default value, the input mask or the label cannot fit: a default longer than the column or past its digits, a mask that stores more characters than the column holds, or a label longer than the field's width shows. • Check the width against stored values (Look tab, single-line fields): reads the newest 5,000 stored values, never the whole table, and says how long 95% of them are and how much the current width shows. When the width cuts them off, or is far wider than needed, Use ⅓ (or the width it names) sets it in one Undo step. • Options for a record (Picker tab): pick a saved record and see the options this picker would offer it — the cascade filters and option filter worked out as the record form works them out (the draft you are editing included), then the picker exclusions — with the count left after each step and the first 50 options. When the target collection has a picker filter, the count it would leave is shown too: the record form's picker does not apply it; enforced API writes do. • Placements that point at nothing (overview): placements whose column was dropped, whose widget was deleted, whose grid's table or link column is gone (relations are a claim: the table and column must exist) or whose section no longer exists. Remove it / Remove N takes them off that layout in one save, with a version kept like any other edit.

AI → Type a change… (⌘K or Ctrl+K) takes a change in plain words. Enter shows every change it will make, in sentences; nothing changes until Apply, and one Apply is one undo step that waits for Save like any other change. Names match by label or key, in any case, with partial words and small typos; a name that fits two things asks you to be more specific.
• move Shipping Location to Materials · move Notes after Zone · move section Details after Extras · move Notes to ungrouped • make Zone required · make Notes optional · make Zone read-only / editable · hide Notes · show Notes • rename Notes to "Comments" · rename section Details to Basics • set width Zone 6 · set Zone width to half · make Zone a third • add Region to Location (a field not on the form yet) · add step Review after Details · add section Extras • remove Notes (the data is kept) · collapse Extras · expand Extras • Several commands in one go: separate them with ";" — they apply as one change.
Required is set per form, not per role: "make Zone required for Finance" makes it required on this form and says so when the form is not limited to Finance (give Finance its own form to require it only there). Text the palette cannot read can go to the AI (admins, when AI is set up): it answers in the same commands, shown in the same preview before anything changes. Without AI the typed commands still work.

When AI is set up, administrators get five helpers. Each one only proposes: a change lands through the draft as one undo step, and nothing is applied without Apply. The AI reads field names, labels, help text, roles and the workflow — never record values.
• AI review (Save ▾ → AI review): after a Save the AI reads what changed next to the roles and the workflow and warns about likely mistakes, such as hiding Amount from Finance, who must fill it before Approve. It never blocks or delays the save; warnings open beside the Save menu (their count shows on its arrow) and Undo reverses a saved change. Picking AI review asks before saving. A change that only renames, rewrites help text or reorders inside a section is not sent. • Help text that contradicts the form (Form settings → Tools → Review this layout): help text that says "optional" while a workflow move needs the field, or names a role that cannot edit it, is flagged with a rewrite. Use the rewrite changes only the help text on this form. • Fields that mean the same thing (same review): two fields with different labels that hold the same information, such as Vendor and Supplier. Identical labels are a separate finding. • Natural entry order: an order inside each section that follows how people fill the form in (who, what, when, cost), with fields that filter or show other fields first. Apply one section or Apply all — one undo step either way. • Personal and financial fields: fields that look personal or financial and are seen on this form by a broad role (one holding a fifth of active people, or roles that together hold half). The suggestion hides the field's section from those roles, leaving out roles that edit the field or need it for a workflow move, and says which other fields go with it. This is advice, not a security control: the API still returns a field to every role whose permissions read it.

The AI menu in the top bar (administrators) holds three reviews: Test as a role, Review the look and Tune from autofill. None of them changes the form by itself: every fix is shown in sentences first, and one Apply is one undo step that waits for Save like any other change. Findings appear as tags on the canvas; click one in the list to select that field or section, and Clear marks removes the tags.
• Test as a role: pick a role (and, if you like, what that person is trying to do). The AI plays someone in that role filling in a new record, step by step, and says where they would hesitate — a confusing step, label or field — with a suggestion; a clearer label can be applied with one click. Built-in checks run even without AI: a required field the role cannot see or change (the record could not be saved), a step with nothing for them to fill in, a label that reads like a database name, two fields with the same label. Only labels, help text, choices and the form's structure are sent, never stored data. Nothing is saved. • Review the look: the AI reviews how the form looks — density, the order and nesting of sections, alignment of widths — and pins each comment to its section. It gets a picture of the canvas (typed values hidden) when the AI provider can read pictures; with a preview record on the canvas, or with a provider that cannot read pictures, it gets the sections' structure and measured sizes instead, and says so. Built-in checks flag long full-width stacks, ragged rows and one-field sections. • Tune from autofill: for collections that use "Fill from document", the fields people most often change after the AI proposed a value (last 90 days, counts only). Fields changed in at least a quarter of their proposals start ticked. "Highlight after autofill" rings those fields with a Check this tag only when the form was filled from a document; "Add Check these section" moves them into a section at the top of the form (on a steps or tabs form, a first step).
AI fill per field: in the inspector's Look tab, a text field can get its own AI fill button with a prompt. Write {{field_name}} in the prompt (or pick from Insert a field) to use another field's current value; nothing else from the record is sent. A field's own setting wins over the form-wide "AI generate buttons" switch (turned off, it hides the button on that field). Anyone who may change the field on that record can use the button — not only administrators — and fields they cannot read stay empty in the prompt. The value goes into the form like typing; it is saved with the record.

Admins with AI set up can describe a rule in words beside the setting it changes. The AI answers in the form's own rule format; names it cannot match are left out and listed. It sees field names, labels, choices and the layout — never stored values.
• A step's "Only when" and a field's "Read-only when" → Write with AI. "Hide this step when Is Sparing is yes or Warehouse is 3" becomes conditions the step checks. Before Apply you see how many of the newest 500 records it shows on (or locks on), next to today's count. Apply is one undo step and saves with the form. • Steps can show and hide by a field's value; single fields cannot. A field locks by pipeline state or by role, not by another field's value. The AI says so instead of guessing. • Picker tab → Narrow the options → Write with AI: "only regions of the record's zone" becomes a cascade filter or an option filter. Pick a record to see its options today and with the change, side by side. Use this adds it to the field's every-form change, which you confirm. • Rules tab → Default for new records → Write a rule with AI: "Default Zone from the project's zone" becomes a field rule, tried on five records (now, after the rule, and what a new record gets). It is saved only when you confirm, and then runs on every form and API write. • Rules tab → Checks → Suggest checks: patterns, ranges and lengths learned from the values stored today, each with how many existing values it would refuse. Nothing is applied until you pick a check and confirm the every-form change. Without AI the pattern-based checks still appear.

Form settings → Tools → AI wording (administrators) checks the words on the form. Each tool lists its changes as sentences with a checkbox; Apply sends the ticked ones through the editor as one undo step, and nothing is saved until Save. A change whose text was edited since you asked is greyed out — run the tool again.
• Glossary terms — every label, help text and section name that uses another word for a term in the AI knowledge glossary (CAR for PUB'd), listed with where it shows, and rewritten to the term on this form. • Section intros — a one- or two-sentence note at the top of each step or section saying what to fill in and why. It is the section's Intro in the inspector, shown as a note or a warning. • Placeholders — example text for empty inputs from the shape of stored values (PO-######, typical amounts). Values never reach the AI, and an example that equals or contains a stored value is refused. • Choice labels — readable labels for coded choices such as $t:pending_approval or IN_PROGRESS. Per row, put them on this form only or on the field, which changes every form that uses the field's own list straight away (that one is not part of Undo). • Plain language — a plain-language score from 0 to 100 for every label, help text and intro, worst first, with a simpler rewrite that must score higher. Glossary terms do not count as unexplained abbreviations. • Translations — label and help drafts for a language set under Settings → Localization. Drafts are marked as drafts until someone approves them (Approve or Approve all); approved translations are never redrafted.
Without AI, Glossary terms, Placeholders, Choice labels and Plain language still work from rules; Section intros and Translations need AI.

Admins, when AI is set up. New form → Start with AI makes a new form; AI → Rebuild or lighter version in the editor rebuilds the open one (the same AI menu holds the reviews above). Every proposal is listed in plain sentences first. Nothing is written until Apply (or Create form), it lands as one undo step, and it still waits for Save.
• Describe it: "a returns form with a manager approval step". The steps or sections are built from the fields this collection already has. Any name the AI makes up is left out and listed. • From a picture or PDF: a screenshot, scan, PDF or spreadsheet of an old form (up to 10 MB). Its labels are matched to fields, and its order and grouping are kept. Labels with no field are listed as candidate new fields. They are never created for you. • From a process document: one step per stage, with the passage each step came from. You also get suggested read-only fields per pipeline state (ticked) and required fields (unticked: Required counts for every state). • Lighter version for a role: pick a role. You see the fields its people changed in the last 180 days, and the fields it would hide. Create lighter version makes a new form that inherits from this one, is shown only to that role, and hides the unused fields. • Sections by meaning: at the top of the Add panel (and under AI). Each field not on the form gets a suggested section, based on what the field means. This helps on a new collection that has no usage history yet.
The AI gets field names, labels, descriptions and the form layout. It never gets record values. An uploaded file is read once and never stored. The lighter version reads only which fields were changed, never the values. If the AI rebuild leaves a step or section still holding fields, it is kept and named.

AI → Ask… opens a panel on the right for questions such as "Why can't Finance see Zone on record 284212?" or "Which form does record 284212 get?". The AI answers with the same engines the editor shows: which form a record gets for a role (Test a record), the role's field permissions, where the field sits, the section rules (hidden or read-only for roles, shows when) and the checks. It reads your unsaved draft, changes nothing, and never sees record values: a section rule comes back as matched or not. Each answer lists the fields, records and forms it looked at; click one to select the field, preview the record or open the form. Administrators only; it needs AI to be set up.

Ask "Where do I turn off comments?" in the Ask panel and it lists the matching controls, each with where it lives (Form settings section or inspector tab) and a Show me button. Show me opens that panel, selects a field or section the control applies to when it is an inspector control, switches to its tab and highlights the control. The words of the question are matched first; only when they do not place it does the AI pick from the same list. Without AI the closest word matches are shown. In Form settings, a search typed as a question, or one nothing matches, offers Look everywhere, which asks the same way.

A connected assistant (Claude or ChatGPT over the MCP connector, or Claude Code) can propose changes to a form with the propose_layout_ops tool. A suggested change never changes the form: AI → Suggested changes (the count shows on AI) lists them, who sent each one and through which app, the note, and every change in plain words. Try on canvas applies it to your draft as one undo step (nothing is saved until Save, unless Autosave is on); Keep marks it applied, Take back undoes it, and Reject closes it. A suggested change that no longer fits the form says why and cannot be tried.

The overview looks across all the forms of a collection as well as at each one. Each form carries a small sketch: its sections as blocks, its fields as bars as wide as they are on the form, steps and tabs as a strip, page cards (pipeline, comments) as thin bars. The sketch is drawn from the saved layout and changes the next time the overview loads after a save.
• Fields labelled differently: a field that reads "Vendor" on one form and "Supplier" on another is listed with every label and the forms that use it. Pick the label to keep and every form gets it at once (one change per form, each in that form's History). The field's own label clears the label set on each form. A label hidden on purpose is left alone. • Near copies: two forms of the same kind that are 90% or more the same (the same fields in the same sections with the same width, label and visibility) are listed with what differs. Compare side by side opens both; Make … the parent links the copy to the other form so fields added there later appear on it too. The copy keeps every field it has: remove the ones it repeats unchanged in its editor to let changes flow through. • Analyze → Compare forms… puts two forms side by side, read only, each drawn as people see it. "Only here" marks fields and sections the other form lacks and "Differs" marks fields set up differently (its tip says how: section, width, label, visibility, other settings). Click a field to select it on both. List the differences gives the same as a table. Pick either side from its menu, or Swap. • Find a field (on every form) searches every collection by field name or label and lists each form, summary, detail, PDF or grid that places the field, with its section and width there and its label when the form changes it, including forms that inherit it from a parent. Click one to open it in the editor.

Every form (Tools → Every form in the editor, ⋯ → Every form on the overview) changes all layouts of the collection in one go. Each run shows a preview first: per form, what will change, what is already like that, and which forms are skipped and why. Untick a form to leave it out. A form with unsaved changes in the editor is left out until you save or discard them.
• Retire a field: takes it off every form — its placements, the header, section summaries, the quick picker, its form default, row order and PDF cover title. The preview counts the records that still hold a value; the values stay in the database. Rules that still read the field are named, not changed. • One change: place a field after or before another (forms without that field are skipped and listed), set its width, make it required, read-only or hidden (or the reverse), or remove it. • Macros: in the editor, Every form → Macros → Record writes down every change you make until Stop; name it and keep it. Replay previews it on the collection's forms: fields are matched by name and sections by label, a position becomes "after this field", and a step that does not fit a form is skipped and listed. Your macros are your own.
Each changed form saves its own version first (its History shows "Before <the change>"), so any one form can be put back from History. Right after a run, Undo this bulk change puts every changed form back at once — except a form someone changed since, which you restore from its History.

Merge two forms (⋯ → Merge two forms on the overview, or Merge into one… on a near-copies finding) folds one form into another. Pick the form to keep and the form to fold in, then Preview. What only the folded form has is added to the kept one; what only one of them has becomes a section shown just for the records (or roles) that form used to open for, as a show-when rule or a hidden-for-roles list. The kept form takes over who the folded one opened for: its record rules, roles, the default and its link name when the kept form has none.
• The preview lists what the kept form gets, who will open the merged form and what happens to the folded one, then checks the newest 2,000 records: how many move to the merged form, how many keep it, and any that will open a different form instead. • Worth a look lists what the merge cannot carry exactly: two forms picked in different ways (record rules and roles), record rules with nothing in common, fields set up differently on the two (the kept form's setup wins), page cards and header fields only the folded form has. • The folded form is renamed "… (merged into …)" and no longer opens for any record. Its sections and fields stay, so a queue, share link or child form that opens it by id keeps working; the preview names those places. • Apply changes both forms as one change: each saves a named "Before merge" version first. Undo the merge puts both back; either form can also be restored on its own from its History. A form someone changed since the preview is not touched: preview again.

⋯ → Change log on the overview exports every layout change in a period as a CSV: when, the form and collection, who made it (name and email), the change note and what it did (fields and sections added, removed or moved, settings changed). Pick 30 days, 90 days, this year or two dates, and this collection or every collection; Count changes shows how many first. History keeps the newest 30 versions of each form plus every named one, so the log cannot show older changes than that.

• Copy a section to another layout: drag a section from the canvas onto a form in the Forms list, or select it and use Copy to layout… in the inspector (which also reaches other collections). It lands at the end of that layout with its tabs, fields and settings. Fields already on that form stay where they are. • Section library: select a section and use Save to library…. Saved sections show under Add → Section library on every collection; a click adds one after the selection as one undo step. Remove one with the × beside it — forms keep their copies. • Layout templates: ⋯ → Save as template… in the editor saves the whole form (sections, panels, header, how it behaves). New form → Start with → Template makes a new form from one. Rules for who gets a form, defaults and links to other layouts stay behind. • Another collection: fields with no field of the same name get their closest match (by name or label), which you can change or set to Leave out. Step conditions, skip-if-filled, field swaps, lock conditions and grid bindings are written in the other collection's terms and are left out. • New form → Start with → Field list: paste names (one per line or separated by commas) or upload a CSV or text file. Names are matched to fields by name or label, with close spellings marked "?"; names with no match are left out. The form gets one section with the matched fields in that order. • New form from this record: Test a record on the overview, or the editor's ⋯ while previewing a record (also from a record's Edit form), makes a form with one section holding the fields that record has filled in, in field order. New form → Start with → A record does the same.

blocks.h: Usage: how a form is used
blocks.t:
Turn on Show how full each field is (the Usage tab, or Tools) and each field on the canvas shows how often it is filled across the collection's records ("62% filled"; under 10% its tip says it is rarely filled). It is off until you turn it on, and remembered per browser. The Add panel shows the same figure under each field ("filled on 3%"). The numbers are the Table Editor's Field usage figures and refresh every five minutes.
The record form records one small event each time someone closes it: which form, which record, how long they spent on each step, whether they saved, and, for a new record, the step they left it on without creating it. Design mode records nothing.
• Edit form on a record page adds how many people used this form on how many records today (UTC day) to its banner. • The editor's Usage tab shows today's opens, people and records; the last 30 days' opens, saves and new records left unfinished; the average time on each step with how many new records were left on it; and the fields changed most often within 24 hours of a record being created (last 90 days; on records opened with this form once 20 of them are known, otherwise across the collection). • Suggested sections: fields people change in the same save (Jaccard over the last 90 days of revisions) that sit in different sections. Move into (the section) moves the strays next to the others in one step, which Undo reverses. Not now hides a suggestion until the editor reopens. • Rarely opened sections: the form also counts, per visit, each section it showed and whether the person opened it (expanded it, clicked or typed in it). A section that starts open and was opened on 10% of visits or fewer (at least 20 visits) is suggested to start collapsed; the first section of the form or of a step is never suggested, nor any section on an accordion form. Start them collapsed is one change, which Undo reverses.

blocks.h: A/B test two versions of a form
blocks.t:
At the bottom of the Usage tab, Start test shows a new version of this form to half of one role: pick the role and either a copy of this form (it opens so you can change it) or another form of the collection that is not the default. Each person lands in the same half every time (a stable hash of their id), administrators always get the original, and a link name (?layout=) still opens either version. The new version never wins on its own: it only stands in for the original, so the overview lists it right after the original with an A/B pill, and Test a record shows the split.
The test compares the halves side by side: people in each half, visits, saves and save rate, average time from opening the form to saving, new records left unfinished, and records created by people in each half with how many were edited again within a day. The better side of each line is in bold once each half has 20 visits. End test asks which version everyone should get: Keep the original simply stops the test; Use the new version copies its sections, fields and settings onto the original (its name, link name and who gets it stay), so links and history are kept and History can put it back.
Usage is kept per form per day (nivaro_layout_usage_daily, nivaro_layout_usage_seen) and deleted after 180 days by the nightly layout-usage-prune job. Only counts are stored; people and records are counted, never listed.

When someone searches a relation picker on a record form and finds nothing, the form sends the words they typed when the picker closes. The server counts them per form and field for 14 days (in Redis); it never stores who typed them or on which record. Design mode sends nothing.
Select the field in the editor and open its Picker tab: Searches that found nothing lists the top ten, how many times each was typed, and a suggested fix for the top five — the field's option filter leaves matching records out (loosen it), the picker filter or hidden records leave them out, or nothing matches at all (add the record, or turn on Quick create). Clear list empties it for that field.

People who are not administrators get Suggest a form change in a record's More menu. They say what should change and can name a field. The suggestion becomes a Form change support request, so they follow it under My requests and it also shows on the Support desk. The overview's subtitle shows how many suggested changes are open and, on a click, for which forms. In the editor, Form settings → Tools → Suggested changes · from people lists them; Accept marks the request done and Decline cancels it, each with an optional note the person is told about. To turn suggestions off, deactivate the Form change type under Support → Request types. One person can send 10 suggestions an hour.

A diagram shows everything that opens a layout: other layouts, queues, grids and drill-downs, share links and public forms, generated files and extension code. Each box says whether it finds the layout by its id or its link name. Before you delete a layout, change its link name or change its kind, the diagram turns red for what that change would break. Renaming keeps every link working. Open it from the row menu (What relies on this…) or Form settings → Tools.
Extension code cannot be read for layout names, so extensions declare what they open with ctx.layouts?.dependsOn({ collection, slug | layout_id, label }) in register(). The diagram says so when no extension declares anything, rather than claiming nothing uses the layout.

Row menu → Compare with another environment (or Form settings → Tools) reads another environment's copy of this layout and lists what would change here: settings, sections and tabs, fields and order. The other copy comes from an API in the Environments registry (read by this server with that component's token), or from an uploaded file: Download this layout on the other side, or a Config Diff snapshot. The copy is matched by link name, then by name, and you can pick another. Apply here saves a version of this layout first, so History → Restore undoes it. Which layout is the default and its place in the list stay as they are here. Settings that cannot be carried (a template or layout this environment does not have, a name already taken, a value this instance refuses) are listed and left alone. Nothing is ever sent from here to the other environment.

blocks.h: Help, notes and the form map
blocks.t: • Help videos on a field or section: a field's Help tab, or the bottom of a section's inspector, attaches a published help video. The record page then shows a small play button beside that field's label or on that section's header, to the roles the video is visible to. The attachment belongs to the video (it appears in its Where list), so it shows for that field or section on every form of the collection. • Notes for editors: pin a short note to a field (Help tab) or a section (bottom of its inspector), such as "Finance asked for this in Q3". A sticky-note marker shows on the canvas with the note, its author and date. Notes save, undo and version like any other layout change, and record pages never receive them. • Form map (Tools → Form map): a clean printable map of the form: its steps or tabs, sections and fields in order, each field's width, required and read-only marks, and the rules that hide or lock things, in plain words. Print / Save as PDF prints it on a light page whatever the app theme. • Why can't I edit this? On a record, pointing at a locked field names the exact rule behind it: the role or pipeline step a lock rule lists, the section locked for the role and the form it is on, or the role's field permissions. Admins also see a "N fields hidden by rules" note above the form that lists each hidden field and the rule that hides it (step rules, sections hidden from roles, fields turned off on the form).

blocks.h: Owner, watching and sharing a form
blocks.t: • Watch: ⋯ → Watch this form in the editor top bar. While it is on you get a notification (your Profile → Notification rules decide the channels, category Watch) whenever someone saves a change to the form or restores one of its versions. It says who saved, what changed in counts (for example "2 fields moved, 1 section added") and the version note, and opens the editor with History showing. You never hear about your own saves. A watch is listed with your other notification subscriptions, where you can also remove it. • Owner: Share → Owner names the business owner of a form. The overview shows "Owner: …" under the form. The owner hears about every saved change even without watching, and is told first; change requests about the form go to the owner first too. • Review reminder: Share → Review reminder sets how long a form may stay unchanged before its owner is asked to review it: 3, 6 or 12 months, never, or the default (6 months). The reminder arrives on a weekday morning (category Watch) with the form's health score and its last 30 days of use (visits, people, saves, new records left unfinished), and comes again every that many months while the form stays unchanged. Any saved change starts the count over. • Preview link: Share → Preview link makes a read-only link that lasts 7, 14, 30 or 90 days, for people who are not administrators. It shows the last saved version of the form, with only the fields you may read, and never shows record data. Anyone with the link can leave a comment on a field or on the whole form; comments appear under Share → Comments from previews (the count shows on the Share button), where Select this field finds the field on the canvas and Resolve removes the comment. Turn off ends a link for everyone.

The first time someone opens a record form after it changed, a short note at the top of the form lists what is new, what moved to another section and what is no longer on the form, with who changed it and when. It only names fields that person may read. Dismissing it hides it for that person until the next change; the person who saved the change never sees it, and nothing shows the very first time someone opens a form.

blocks.h: React to form changes in flows and webhooks

blocks.t:
Layout configuration travels one way: development → staging every night (promote:config copies the layout, section and placement tables), staging → production at go-live. An edit made on staging is therefore gone the next morning. Set LAYOUT_EDIT_WARNING on such an instance and every layout editing surface — the overview, the editor and record-page Edit form — shows it as an always-visible banner. Unset = no banner. The editor still works either way.
# staging .env
LAYOUT_EDIT_WARNING=Layouts here are replaced every night from development. Make lasting changes on development.

Layout writes are admin-only. The older endpoints (PATCH a layout, PUT all placements, the field-groups routes) keep working for scripts; the editor uses the bundle + ops pair.
# Which form a record gets, checks and health (administrators)
GET  /api/collection-layouts/overview?collection=orders
     → { data: { rows: [...], warning: string | null } }   // sectioned, in /active order
GET  /api/collection-layouts/ex…
Op | Shape / place | { op, field, group_key, index, patch? } — add a placement / move | { op, from: { field, group_key }, to_group_key, index } / update_placement | { op, at: { field, group_key }, patch } / remove | { op, at: { field, group_key } } / group_create | { op, key, label, group_type, parent_key, index, patch? } — section, tab or step / group_update | { op, key, patch } — a group holding fields cannot become a container or a text block / group_move | { op, key, parent_key, index } — also moves slot cards on the page / group_remove | { op, key, placements: 'ungroup' | 'delete' } / layout_update | { op, patch } — any setting PATCH /collection-layouts/:id accepts
Placements are keyed by (field, group_key), matching the database's unique (layout_id, field, group_key): a field placed twice keeps both placements through every op and save path. After each op sort is renumbered per container, and the record page's top level (sections, the Ungrouped zone and slot cards) shares one order. GET /collection-layouts/active now also returns each placement's col_span, so slot cards keep their width on records.

A layout whose tabs are configured as steps renders as a linear stepper strip instead of a tab bar — the item editor walks the user through groups one at a time with Back / Next controls. Set tab_mode to steps (vs the default tabs) in Data Model → Layout → Settings.

Option | Effect / tab_mode: steps | Tab-type groups render as an ordered stepper strip with Back / Next navigation. / validate_before_next | Blocks advancing to the next step until all required fields on the current step are filled.
Steps mode reuses the tab groups of the layout — there is no separate step entity. With validate_before_next off, users can move freely between steps; validation still runs on save.

A layout can name an ordered list of relation fields (M2O or M2M) that form its dependency chain — Funding Year → Zone → Region → Project Type → Project → Sub Type. The quick picker walks that chain one step at a time in a compact popover: each slide shows only the options still valid given the earlier picks (the same cascade filters the form's pickers use), a sole remaining option is picked automatically, short lists render as chips and long ones as a searchable list. Back / Next move between slides and the track above shows every step with its chosen value; click any step to revisit it.

Surface | Behaviour / Collection browser "+ New item" | When the target layout configures steps, the popover opens beside the button first. "Create <record>" opens the new-record form with the picks prefilled (?prefill= carries scalars and M2M links). / Record form header — "Quick pick" | Opens the same popover bound to the live draft: every pick is a normal edit (cascade clears, field rules and validation all apply), Done just closes. Available on new and existing records. / Headless hosts (@nivaro/react) | QuickPickerDialog (anchorEl → popover, otherwise a dialog) + encodePrefill / decodePrefill for the handoff; useQuickPickerSteps reads a layout's steps.

A layout of type "detail" drives the drill-down sheet that opens when a related record is clicked (a PO from a workflow, an invoice from a PO). With display_mode "read" it renders as a read-only presentation instead of a form: a header band, section cards as definition grids, tab groups as child tables — and any widget slots the layout carries, which is how a read-only sheet gets actions.

blocks.h: Presentation settings (Data Model → Layout → settings, detail layouts)
blocks.t: Setting | Effect / Sheet width | Pixel width the drill sheet opens at (320–2000; default 640). A per-field drill config still wins. / Header band fields | Identity fields lifted out of the cards into a band above them — the first is the title (large), the rest compact label/value pairs. Empty ones drop out. / Hide empty values | Fields with no value are omitted from the cards instead of rendering as "—".

The review_list widget type lists child rows grouped by a key with a status decision per group (Approve / Reject / In review…), optional stamp fields and an action endpoint that owns the write. Two ways to find the rows: a relation path from the host record (workflow → purchase orders → invoices), or SIBLING mode — rows of the host's own collection sharing a field value (every line of this invoice, hosted on one line). An optional enrich endpoint (POST {ids}) returns per-row chips (a 3-way-match verdict) and whether the caller may decide each row; groups with an undecidable row show "View only" instead of buttons.
{
  "host_collection": "invoices", "collection": "invoices",
  "path": [], "sibling_field": "invoice_id",
  "group_by": "invoice_id", "aggregate_sum": "amount", "aggregate_sum_format": "currency",
  "line_columns": ["line_item_number", {"fi…
A group with exactly one entry (sibling mode) opens expanded. Without an action endpoint the widget PATCHes each row directly with the note as the change reason.

Summary mode is the record form rendered as a read-only presentation: the active grouped layout as section cards and definition grids, child tables instead of editable grids, related records as labels and drill links. Nothing on the record itself can be changed until the viewer switches to Edit — but the Notes and Tasks slots stay live, so a reviewer can comment on or assign work from the summary without leaving it.

When the collection has Summary mode enabled, the record header carries a Summary / Edit segmented control with the active side filled. The choice lasts for the current visit only — nothing is stored per user; every open runs the opening-mode rules again. New records always open in Edit. The right-hand summary rail collapses while in Summary mode and returns when switching back.

What Summary mode shows is a layout of type "summary" (Data Model → collection → Layouts → layout type). It renders the same way a read-only detail sheet does — section cards, definition grids, child tables, the header band and hide-empty settings — and it carries its own groups and field assignments, so the summary can differ from the edit form: fewer fields, a different order, a header band with the identity fields. Start one with "Clone as Summary" on the grouped layout, which copies every group, assignment and override, then trim. A collection without a summary layout renders its grouped layout read-only, which is the pre-layout behaviour. Each section has a read-view width (Data Model → Layout → group settings → "Summary / read-view width": auto, full, half or one third) — the board is six tracks wide, so two half sections sit side by side and a lines grid takes the row; auto is half for a short fact list and full when the section holds a grid or widget. Child grids with no rows and links with nothing linked count as empty, so an empty Files section disappears. Widget slots with nothing to show (an empty rollup, a review list with no rows) are hidden in Summary mode, and a section left with nothing collapses with them. Data-integrity findings do not render as a banner in Summary mode; the affected fields (or child grids) carry an amber mark whose tooltip lists the issues.

blocks.h: Which mode a record opens in
Edit lock while a record waits

blocks.t: A layout can show a collapsible summary sidebar that lists every field and its live value as the record is edited. Toggle it on per layout with summary_enabled in layout settings; on the ItemEdit page the Summary button opens and closes it.

Option | Effect / summary_enabled | Enables the summary sidebar for the layout and shows the Summary button on ItemEdit. / summary_hide_empty | Leaves fields with no value out of the summary.
Clicking a field row in the summary navigates the editor to that field's tab or step, making the panel a fast jump-to index for long forms.

In the Layout tab, the built-in Pipeline, Comments, and Tasks panels appear as draggable "page slots" that sit in the same ordered list as field groups. Drag a slot to reposition it among the groups so the panel renders exactly where you want in the item editor.

• Visibility toggle — show or hide the panel for this layout. • Custom label — rename a slot (e.g. "Comments" → "Notes"). • Default state — start the panel expanded or collapsed. • Position — drag the slot anywhere in the layout order, interleaved with field groups.
Slot settings are scoped to the layout, so different layouts of the same collection can order, rename, and hide the Pipeline / Comments / Tasks panels independently.

A layout can be restricted to specific roles so different users see different forms for the same collection. Set the role conditions in the "Visibility" section of layout settings. The role list is an ALLOW-LIST enforced by the server on every path: a user whose role is not listed can never resolve the layout, pin it by slug (?layout=… from queues, links or the collection browser), list it in New-item menus or queue builders, or drill into it — record-condition matches included. Admins always pass.

Each layout has a toggle that turns the AI helpers on or off for records edited through it. When disabled, the item editor hides the Summarize button and the per-field AI generate buttons, and skips AI validation and duplicate-detection checks entirely for that layout.
This is a presentation/UX gate at the layout level — collection-level AI validation rules (which are also enforced server-side) still apply to writes that come through other layouts or the API. Use it to keep AI affordances out of forms where they are not wanted.

A Multi-collection Hierarchy lets admins define a named tree where each level is a *different* collection, linked by regular foreign-key columns. For example: Divisions (level 0) → Regions (level 1, via regions.division) → Zones (level 2, via zones.region). Each collection keeps its own schema, workflows, RBAC, computed fields, and revision history.
This is distinct from the same-collection tree (nivaro_tree_configs), which uses a single self-referential parent_id on one collection. The same-collection tree remains the right choice for homogeneous recursive trees such as categories, folders, and org charts. Use a multi-collection hierarchy when each level is a conceptually different entity that needs its own structure.

Feature | Same-collection Tree | Multi-collection Hierarchy / Node types | All same collection | Each level a different collection / Schema per level | Shared | Independent / Workflows/RBAC | Shared | Per-collection / Depth | Unlimited (recursive) | Fixed (defined levels) / Use cases | Categories, folders, org charts | Divisions/Regions, Product Types/Sub-types, Project Type/Sub-type

interface HierarchyLevel {
  collection: string;       // e.g. 'divisions'
  label_field: string;      // e.g. 'name'
  parent_fk: string | null; // column on THIS collection pointing to parent level's id. null = root
}

interface Hierarchy…
A hierarchy config is stored as a single row in nivaro_hierarchy_configs, with the ordered levels array serialized to a JSON column. No schema changes are required beyond the FK columns that already link the collections.

Location | Behaviour / Sidebar → Content → Hierarchies | New "Hierarchies" item (Network icon). Master-detail list of configs. / /hierarchies | Left panel lists configs; right panel shows the edit form and levels editor. / /hierarchies/:id | Same page with a config selected. / /hierarchies/:id/tree | Full tree browser: indented tree, each node shows a collection badge, "Open" links to the item edit page, "Add Child" creates a record in the next level's collection.

A multi-collection hierarchy is built on top of collections that already exist and that are already linked by foreign-key columns. The hierarchy config simply records the order of the collections and which FK column links each child level to its parent.

blocks.h: Step 1 — Create the collections with FK columns

blocks.t: In the admin sidebar, go to Content → Hierarchies. The list of existing hierarchy configs appears in the left panel.
Click "New Hierarchy" and give it a name (e.g. "Territory Hierarchy") and an optional description.

Add one level per collection, top-down. Level 0 is the root collection with parent_fk set to null. Each subsequent level names the child collection and the FK column on that child collection that points back to the parent level.
Level setting | Description / collection | The collection for this level. E.g. divisions for level 0, regions for level 1. / label_field | The field used as the display label for nodes at this level. E.g. name. / parent_fk | The column on THIS level's collection that points to the parent level's id. Set to null for level 0 (the root).
Saving writes a row to nivaro_hierarchy_configs with the ordered levels array serialized to JSON.

Click "View Tree" to open /hierarchies/:id/tree. Root records appear at the top; expand each to see children fetched from the next level's collection. Each node shows its collection badge, an "Open" link to the item editor, and an "Add Child" action to create a record in the next level's collection with the parent FK pre-filled.
parent_fk is the exact column name on the CHILD collection, not a field alias. It must be the column whose value equals the parent record's id. This is never the same as parent_id in a same-collection tree.
All hierarchy endpoints live under /api and require authentication (Bearer static token or session). Config write endpoints (POST/PATCH/DELETE on /hierarchy-configs) require admin access.

Method | Path | Auth | Description / GET | /api/hierarchy-configs | Authenticated | List all hierarchy configs. → { data: HierarchyConfig[] } / POST | /api/hierarchy-configs | Admin | Create a hierarchy config. → { data: HierarchyConfig } / GET | /api/hierarchy-configs/:id | Authenticated | Fetch a single config. → { data: HierarchyConfig } / PATCH | /api/hierarchy-configs/:id | Admin | Update a config. → { data: HierarchyConfig } / DELETE | /api/hierarchy-configs/:id | Admin | Delete a config. → 204 / GET | /api/hierarchy/:id/tree | Authenticated | Full hierarchy as nested JSON. → { data: HierarchyNode[] } / GET | /api/hierarchy/:id/nodes | Authenticated | Flat list of all nodes. → { data: FlatHierarchyNode[] } / GET | /api/hierarchy/:id/node/:collection/:nodeId/children | Authenticated | Direct children (next level) of a node. → { data: FlatHierarchyNode[] } / GET | /api/hierarchy/:id/node/:collection/:nodeId/ancestors | Authenticated | Ancestor chain, root-first. → { data: FlatHierarchyNode[] }

Field | Type | Description / id | number | string | Primary key of the underlying record. / collection | string | The collection this node belongs to. / label | string | Value of the level's label_field. / level_index | number | Zero-based index of the level in the config. / parent_id | number | string | null | Parent record id (value of this level's parent_fk). null at the root. / parent_collection | string | null | Collection of the parent level. null at the root. / raw | Record<string, unknown> | The full row from the DB. / children | HierarchyNode[] | Child nodes from the next level (nested endpoint only).
Identical to HierarchyNode but without the children array. Returned by /nodes, /children, and /ancestors.

    {
      "id": 5,
      "collection": "divisions",

{

The levels array is stored as JSON in nivaro_hierarchy_configs.levels. Always parse it on read and serialize it on write — the column is nvarchar(max).

This walkthrough builds a two-level "Territory Hierarchy" where Divisions contain Regions. Each level is its own collection with its own schema; the hierarchy is held together by a single FK column on regions.

Create two collections in Data Model. Each has its own fields; regions adds an integer division column that references divisions.id.
Collection | Fields / divisions | id, name, short_code / regions | id, name, short_code, division (INT — FK to divisions.id)

blocks.h: Step 2 — Create the hierarchy in the UI
blocks.t:
Go to Content → Hierarchies in the sidebar. Click "New Hierarchy", enter the name "Territory Hierarchy", and click "Create hierarchy".
In the detail panel, scroll to "Hierarchy Levels" and click "Add Level" twice to create two levels:
Level | Collection | Label field | Parent FK / 0 (root) | divisions | name | — (disabled, root has no parent) / 1 | regions | name | division
Parent FK for level 1 is division — the column on the regions table that stores the parent division's id. Click "Save Levels" to persist.
Everything is configured through the UI. The levels editor stores the config as a JSON array internally — you never edit JSON directly.

-- Divisions (root level)
INSERT INTO divisions (name, short_code) VALUES ('Western Division', 'WST');   -- id 5
INSERT INTO divisions (name, short_code) VALUES ('Eastern Division', 'EST');   -- id 6

Authorization: Bearer <token>

blocks.h: Step 5 — Browse and add children in the UI

blocks.t:
When a collection participates in a multi-collection hierarchy as a non-root level, the Collection Browser automatically shows a scope filter above the filter bar.
Example: if "regions" is level 2 in the "Sales Territory" hierarchy (under "divisions"), browsing /collections/regions shows a "Scope by Division" dropdown. Selecting a division narrows the table to only regions that belong to that division.
M2O levels filter directly via the FK column. M2M levels resolve child IDs via the hierarchy API and filter by ID.

• On page load, all hierarchy configs are fetched. • If the current collection appears at level_index > 0 in any config, the scope bar appears. • Selecting a parent adds an implicit filter to the items query (not shown in the active filter bar). • Clear the scope with the "Clear" link to restore the full table.

The item editor automatically shows a "Hierarchy Membership" card for any item that belongs to a multi-collection hierarchy as a non-root level.
For M2O levels the card displays a breadcrumb trail linking up through parent levels. For M2M levels it shows the first resolved ancestor path, with a note that multiple paths may exist.
Each ancestor is a clickable link navigating to that item's edit page. If no parent is assigned the card shows "No parent assigned".
The panel appears only when the collection is configured in at least one hierarchy. It is silently omitted for root-level collections and for same-collection trees (which use the breadcrumb in the page header instead).

Any Nivaro collection can become a hierarchical tree by enabling a tree configuration through Data Model → collection detail → Tree / Hierarchy section. No schema changes are required beyond having a self-referential parent field (e.g. parent_id) already defined on the collection.
Once a tree config is saved, the collection browser gains a Table / Tree view toggle, item edit pages show a breadcrumb trail above the form, and the parent field renders as a TreePicker instead of a plain input.

• A nivaro_tree_configs row links a collection to its parent_field, label_field, and optional order_field. • Tree queries use MSSQL recursive CTEs anchored at root nodes (WHERE parent_field IS NULL) with OPTION (MAXRECURSION 100) for unlimited depth. • The flat node list endpoint returns each node with a computed depth integer and a path string (e.g. /1/4/12). • The nested endpoint returns the same data shaped as a recursive children array for direct use in tree UIs. • Move operations run isDescendantOf() before updating to prevent a node becoming its own ancestor.

Location | Behaviour / Data Model → collection detail | "Tree / Hierarchy" section: enable toggle, field selectors for parent_field, label_field, order_field. / Collection browser toolbar | Table / Tree toggle appears when a tree config exists for the collection. / Tree view | Collapsible node rows with expand/collapse, Add Child, Move, and Edit actions per node. / Item edit page | Breadcrumb trail above the form shows the full ancestor path with clickable links. / Parent field widget | Renders as a TreePicker when the field matches the configured parent_field.
Tree features activate only when GET /api/tree-configs/by-collection/:col returns a non-null config. If you remove a tree config the collection browser reverts to table-only mode immediately.
Follow these steps to turn any collection into a hierarchical tree. The collection must already have a nullable integer (or uuid) field that references itself — this becomes the parent pointer.

blocks.h: Step 1 — Add a parent field to the collection

blocks.t:
Navigate to Data Model → select the collection → scroll to the "Tree / Hierarchy" section → click "Enable Tree View". Configure the three fields:
Setting | Description / parent_field | The field name that holds the parent record ID. Must already exist as a column. E.g. parent_id. / label_field | The field used as the display label for each node in the tree UI. E.g. name or title. / order_field | Optional. An integer field used to sort siblings. If omitted, siblings are ordered by their primary key. Required for drag-to-reorder (see Reorder Siblings). / Maintain path column | Optional switch. Adds materialized path + depth columns to the table, kept current on create/move (see Breadcrumb Path Column).
Click Save. Nivaro creates a row in nivaro_tree_configs and the collection browser immediately shows the Table / Tree toggle.

Open the collection browser and click the Tree icon in the toolbar. Root nodes (records where parent_field IS NULL) appear at the top level. Click the chevron on any node to expand its children. Use the node action menu to Add Child, Move, or Edit the record.
The parent_field value must be the exact column name in the underlying table, not a field alias. Use the same name you see in Data Model → Fields for that collection.
Return to Data Model → collection → Tree / Hierarchy → toggle off → Save. The nivaro_tree_configs row is deleted. Existing data is unaffected; the parent_field column remains in the table.
Render tree-enabled collections as interactive top-down organizational charts instead of indented lists. Perfect for org structures, reporting hierarchies, and project teams.
• Collection browser → collection with tree config. • Click "Tree" view button in toolbar. • Toggle "List | Org chart" switch (right side of toolbar).

Feature | Description / Node cards | Display label (from label_field) + child count. / Collapse nodes | Click arrow to hide subtree; shows hidden child count. / Zoom controls | Use −/% /+ buttons to scale; "Fit" auto-scales to viewport. / Click to edit | Click any node card to open item editor. / Search | Filter by node label (hides non-matching branches). / Print | Print to PDF (preserves hierarchy structure).
Maintain a custom sort order for sibling nodes. Configure an integer order_field on your tree config and use drag-and-drop or the API to reorder siblings.
• Data Model → select collection → Tree / Hierarchy section. • Set "Order Field" to an integer column (e.g., sort_order). • Save — tree list view now shows grip handles on every node.
• Grab the grip handle (≡) on a node row. • Drag up/down within the same sibling group. • Drop to update sort values immediately. • Dragging under a different parent is a MOVE operation, not reorder.

import { reorderTreeSiblings } from '@nivaro/sdk'

// Reorder siblings atomically
const result = await nivaro.request(
  reorderTreeSiblings('org_units', 'any-sibling-id', [
    { id: 'node-4', sort: 0 },
    { id: 'node-9', sort: 1 },
    …

blocks.h: API: Move node to new parent

blocks.t: Optionally maintain path and depth columns on the collection table. Path is a materialized breadcrumb (/rootId/.../selfId) that enables fast subtree queries without recursive CTEs.
• Data Model → collection → Tree / Hierarchy section. • Toggle "Maintain path column". • Click "Rebuild paths" to backfill existing rows.
Column | Type | Meaning | Example / path | varchar | Breadcrumb: /root_id/.../self_id (ID-based, not label-based) | /1/5/12 / depth | int | Distance from root (0 = root) | 2

• Subtree queries become trivial: WHERE path LIKE '/12/%' returns all descendants of node 12. • No recursive CTE needed — single index scan. • Perfect for custom queries, external reporting, and API consumers. • Inherited field resolution uses batched path parsing instead of per-row recursion. • Path never goes stale (ID-based, changes only on move).

-- Find all org units under "Sales" (ID 5) with their depth
SELECT id, name, depth, path
FROM org_units
WHERE path LIKE '/1/5/%'  -- sales org_unit is at /1/5
ORDER BY depth, name

-- Result: all Sales children, grandchildren, etc. (fast!)

• Paths auto-maintain on create/move/delete. • If paths get out of sync (bulk data import), rebuild: POST /api/tree-configs/:id/rebuild-paths. • SDK: rebuildTreePaths(configId).
Path uses IDs not labels — remains valid even if ancestor labels change. Depth is computed from path length on every rebuild; kept in sync automatically.

Mark fields as inheritable so they cascade values down the tree. If a child has no value, it inherits from the nearest non-null ancestor. Perfect for org settings, cost codes, compliance levels, and defaults that vary by branch.
• Data Model → select collection (must have tree config). • Open a field in the editor. • Toggle "Inheritable" (nivaro_fields.is_inheritable).

Item view shows:

┌─────────────────────┐
│ Name: Boston Office │
│ Currency: USD       │ ← Shows "Inherited from parent" chip
│ Budget: 50000       │ ← Shows "Overridden (parent: 100000)" chip
└─────────────────────┘

- Inherited field: va…

• If field has a non-null value on this record, use it. • Walk ancestors from immediate parent up to root. • First ancestor with non-null value: use that. • No ancestors have it: field is null (use field default if set). • Include _inherited: { field: ancestorId } sidecar in response.

• If path column maintained: ancestors parsed from path string + single batched fetch. • If no path column: recursive CTE per row (slower but works). • Inheritance resolves BEFORE computed fields (formulas see effective values). • List reads include _inherited per row.
Inheritance is virtual — values not stored on child rows, resolved at read time. Clearing a field reverts to inherited value on next read.
Restrict role access to a subtree of a tree-enabled collection. A single rule anchors to a node and applies read/update/delete permissions to that node and all descendants.

• Sales role can only read/edit their own org unit and children (not Finance branch). • Department managers can view team org units but not corporate parent. • Regional admins govern their region and all subsidiaries.

• Data Model → collection → Tree / Hierarchy → "Subtree permissions" (admin only). • Click "New rule". • Pick a node from the tree (the rule applies to it + descendants). • Choose role. • Choose action: read / update / delete / * (all). • Choose allow or deny.

Scenario | Rule Wins | Result / Rule on node vs ancestor | Node rule (deepest wins) | Use node rule / read rule vs * rule on same node | read rule (specific beats wildcard) | read rule applies / allow vs deny on same node+action | Deny (deny overrides allow) | Access denied / No matching rule | Falls back to nivaro_policies | Use base role permissions / Admin user | All rules bypassed | Admin sees everything

• Single item read denied: return 403. • List read (batch): denied rows silently filtered out. • Update/delete denied: return 403. • Admins bypass all tree permissions. • Collections with no rules: zero performance penalty (60s cache).

• Restriction-only: can only narrow access, never grant beyond base policies. • If nivaro_policies says a role cannot read "org_units", tree perms cannot override it. • Best combined with row-level security (RLS) for additional control.
Rules stored in nivaro_tree_permissions. Deepest matching rule in ancestor chain always wins.

All tree endpoints require authentication. Config management endpoints (/tree-configs) require admin access. Data read/move endpoints (/tree/:collection/...) require at minimum read permission on the collection.

Method | Path | Auth | Description / GET | /api/tree-configs | Admin | List all tree configurations. / POST | /api/tree-configs | Admin | Create a tree config for a collection. / PATCH | /api/tree-configs/:id | Admin | Update a tree config. / DELETE | /api/tree-configs/:id | Admin | Delete a tree config (disables tree mode for the collection). / GET | /api/tree-configs/by-collection/:col | Authenticated | Return the tree config for a collection, or null if none exists. / GET | /api/tree/:collection/nodes | Authenticated | Flat list of all nodes with depth and path. / GET | /api/tree/:collection/nested | Authenticated | Full tree as nested JSON (children arrays). / GET | /api/tree/:collection/:id/ancestors | Authenticated | Ordered list of ancestors from root to the immediate parent (breadcrumb). / GET | /api/tree/:collection/:id/descendants | Authenticated | All descendants of a node at any depth. / GET | /api/tree/:collection/:id/children | Authenticated | Direct children only (depth + 1). / PATCH | /api/tree/:collection/:id/move | Authenticated | Reparent a node. Body: { "parent_id": <id|null> }. Returns 409 if target is a descendant. / PATCH | /api/tree/:collection/:id/reorder | Authenticated | Bulk-update sibling sort values. Body: { "order": [{ "id", "sort" }] }. Requires the config's order_field; all ids must share the same parent. / POST | /api/tree-configs/:id/rebuild-paths | Admin | Full rebuild of the materialized path/depth columns (maintain_path configs).

blocks.t: Extensions can query tree data directly via ctx.database (the Knex instance) using raw recursive CTEs, or by calling the tree API routes with callExternalApi or a plain HTTP client.

blocks.t: This walkthrough builds a four-level organisational unit tree: Company → Region → Zone → Site. The same pattern applies to any hierarchy — product categories, project types, cost centres, file taxonomies, and so on.

Go to Data Model → New Collection → name it org_units. Add these fields:
Field | Type | Notes / name | string | Required. The node label displayed in tree view. / type | string | Optional discriminator — e.g. 'company', 'region', 'zone', 'site'. / sort_order | integer | Optional. Used to order siblings. Leave null to sort by id. / parent_id | integer | Nullable. Self-reference — the parent org unit. / description | text | Optional. Free-form notes.
parent_id must be added as a plain integer field. You do not need to define a formal relation in Nivaro — the tree engine finds children via the raw column value.

Data Model → org_units → scroll to "Tree / Hierarchy" → Enable Tree View. Set:
Parent field:  parent_id
Label field:   name
Order field:   sort_order   (optional)

-- Root (company)
INSERT INTO org_units (name, type, parent_id) VALUES ('Acme Corp', 'company', NULL);        -- id 1

-- Regions
INSERT INTO org_units (name, type, parent_id) VALUES ('North America', 'region', 1);        -- id 2
INSERT INT…

Open Collections → org_units → click the "Tree" toggle in the toolbar. You will see:
▼ Acme Corp
  ▼ North America
    ▼ US East
        New York HQ
        Boston Office
      US West
      Canada
    Europe
Click "Add Child" on any node to create a new record with parent_id pre-filled. Click a node label to open its edit page. The breadcrumb at the top of the edit page shows the full path:
Acme Corp › North America › US East › New York HQ
